courses.summary: Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements and their equivalence, heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps, reversibility and irreversibility, Carnot cycle and theorem, thermodynamic temperature scale, Clausius inequality, entropy change of ideal gases and solids/liquids, principle of increase of entropy, and availability (exergy) basics.
outcomes: State and apply Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements
Compute Carnot efficiency and COPs
Calculate entropy changes and entropy generation
Use the availability concept for maximum useful work

lessons.title: Statements of the second law; engines, refrigerators, heat pumps

story.title: Why not run ships on ocean heat?

scenes.text: The ocean holds enormous thermal energy.
Yet a ship can't run by just cooling sea water — it needs a colder sink. That is the second law.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:
**Kelvin–Planck:** no cyclic device can convert all heat from a single reservoir into work (no 100% efficient engine; PMM2 impossible).
**Clausius:** heat cannot flow from a colder to a hotter body without external work.
The two are equivalent (violating one violates the other).

steps.title: Performance
steps.body:
Engine: η = W/Q_H = 1 − Q_L/Q_H.
Refrigerator: COP_R = Q_L/W. Heat pump: COP_HP = Q_H/W = COP_R + 1.
Units: refrigeration tonne (TR) ≈ 3.517 kW (211 kJ/min).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Engine takes 500 kJ, rejects 300 kJ: W = 200 kJ, η = 40%.

**Example 2.** Refrigerator removes 6 kW with 1.5 kW input: COP_R = 4; heat rejected 7.5 kW.

**Example 3.** Heat pump with COP 3.5 supplies 7 kW heating: input 2 kW. A 1.5 TR AC removes ≈ 5.3 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- COP can exceed 1 (it is not an efficiency).
- Using COP_R for heating duty.
- Forgetting the first law still holds: Q_H = Q_L + W.

activity.prompt: Device → performance measure

quiz.why: The Kelvin–Planck statement says no cycle can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. So 100% conversion is forbidden.
options: 100% conversion of heat to work in a cycle

quiz.why: The Clausius statement says heat cannot flow by itself from a cold body to a hot one. It needs work, as in a refrigerator.
options: heat flow cold → hot needs work

quiz.why: COP_HP = Q_H/W and COP_R = Q_L/W. Since Q_H = Q_L + W, their difference is (Q_H − Q_L)/W = 1.

quiz.q: Engine η with Q_H 1000 kJ, Q_L 650 kJ

quiz.why: A perpetual motion machine of the second kind would convert heat from one reservoir fully to work. That violates the second law (Kelvin–Planck).

lessons.title: Reversibility, Carnot cycle and thermodynamic temperature

scenes.text: No real engine can beat a reversible engine between the same temperatures.
Carnot's limit depends only on the two temperatures.

steps.title: Irreversibilities and Carnot
steps.body:
Irreversibilities: friction, heat transfer across finite ΔT, unrestrained expansion, mixing, combustion, electrical resistance, inelastic deformation.
Carnot cycle: two reversible isotherms + two reversible adiabats. η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H (kelvin).
**Carnot theorem:** no engine is more efficient than a reversible one between the same reservoirs; all reversible engines have the same efficiency. This defines the thermodynamic temperature scale: Q_H/Q_L = T_H/T_L.
COP_R,Carnot = T_L/(T_H − T_L); COP_HP,Carnot = T_H/(T_H − T_L).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Engine between 800 K and 300 K: η_max = 62.5%. An inventor claims 70% ⇒ impossible.

**Example 2.** Fridge at −5 °C (268 K) in a 30 °C room (303 K): COP_max = 268/35 = 7.66.

**Example 3.** Claim: engine receives 1000 kJ at 600 K, rejects 450 kJ at 300 K ⇒ η = 55% > 50% Carnot ⇒ impossible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in Carnot formulas.
- Thinking a reversible engine has 100% efficiency.
- Forgetting that small temperature differences make COP high (and engine efficiency low).

activity.prompt: Carnot engine between 527 °C and 27 °C. Efficiency (%)?

quiz.why: The Carnot efficiency is η = 1 − T_L/T_H, with temperatures in kelvin. It is the maximum between those two reservoirs.
The Carnot cycle has two reversible isothermal processes (heat in and out) and two reversible adiabatic processes (isentropic expansion and compression).

quiz.q: Heat transfer across finite ΔT is
quiz.why: Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference is irreversible, since it cannot be reversed without external work. Reversible heat transfer needs an infinitesimal ΔT.

quiz.q: COP of Carnot fridge, T_L 250 K, T_H 300 K
quiz.why: Carnot COP of a refrigerator = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 250/(300 − 250) = 250/50 = 5.

quiz.q: All reversible engines between same reservoirs have
quiz.why: By Carnot's theorem, all reversible engines working between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever the working fluid.

lessons.title: Clausius inequality and entropy

scenes.text: Ice melting in a warm drink never reverses by itself.
Entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

steps.title: Entropy
steps.body:
Clausius inequality: ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 (= 0 reversible). Entropy dS = δQ_rev/T, a property.
**Ideal gas:** Δs = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁) = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁).
**Solids/liquids:** Δs = c ln(T₂/T₁).
**Reservoir:** ΔS = Q/T.
Principle of increase of entropy: ΔS_isolated = S_gen ≥ 0. Reversible adiabatic ⇒ isentropic.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1 kg water heated from 20 °C to 80 °C (c = 4.18): Δs = 4.18 ln(353/293) = 0.779 kJ/K.

**Example 2.** Air heated at constant pressure 300 → 600 K: Δs = 1.005 ln 2 = 0.697 kJ/kg K.

**Example 3.** 1000 kJ of heat flows from a 600 K reservoir to a 300 K reservoir: ΔS = −1000/600 + 1000/300 = +1.667 kJ/K (irreversible).

**Example 4.** 1 kg iron (c = 0.45) at 500 K dropped into a large 300 K lake: ΔS_iron = 0.45 ln(0.6) = −0.230; ΔS_lake = 0.45 × 200/300 = 0.300 ⇒ S_gen = 0.070 kJ/K.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a system's entropy can never decrease (it can, if surroundings increase more).
- Using Q/T for non-isothermal heat transfer without integrating.
- Units kJ/K vs kJ/kg K.

activity.prompt: Air: constant pressure heating from 300 K to 450 K (c_p 1.005). Δs (kJ/kg K, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Entropy depends only on the state of the system, so it is a property (state function). Heat is not.

quiz.q: For a reversible adiabatic process ΔS =
quiz.why: In a reversible adiabatic process, there is no heat and no irreversibility, so ΔS = 0 (isentropic).
Irreversible processes generate entropy, so S_gen > 0. Reversible processes have S_gen = 0, and negative values are impossible.

quiz.q: ΔS of a reservoir receiving 600 kJ at 300 K
quiz.why: For a reservoir at constant temperature, ΔS = Q/T = 600/300 = 2 kJ/K. It is positive as heat is received.
The Clausius inequality says that for any cycle ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality for reversible cycles.

lessons.title: Availability (exergy) and irreversibility

scenes.text: A tank of hot water at 60 °C stores energy, but in a 30 °C room little of it can become work.
Exergy measures the useful-work potential relative to the surroundings (dead state).

steps.title: Key results
steps.body:
Dead state: in equilibrium with surroundings (T₀, p₀).
Available part of heat Q from a source at T: Q(1 − T₀/T) (Carnot fraction).
Closed-system availability: φ = (u − u₀) + p₀(v − v₀) − T₀(s − s₀).
Flow exergy: ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz.
**Gouy–Stodola:** irreversibility I = T₀ S_gen. Second-law efficiency η_II = η/η_rev (or exergy recovered/exergy supplied).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1000 kJ at 1000 K with T₀ = 300 K: available = 700 kJ, unavailable 300 kJ.

**Example 2.** The same 1000 kJ first passes to a 500 K body: available becomes 1000(1 − 300/500) = 400 kJ ⇒ loss 300 kJ = T₀ΔS_gen = 300(1/500 − 1/1000)·1000 ✔.

**Example 3.** An engine with η = 30% between 900 K and 300 K: η_rev = 66.7% ⇒ η_II = 45%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating exergy as conserved (it is destroyed by irreversibilities).
- Using T instead of T₀ in Gouy–Stodola.
- Forgetting that energy is conserved even when exergy is destroyed.

statements.s: Exergy is conserved in all processes.
Irreversibility I = T₀ S_gen.
Heat at higher temperature has more available energy.
At the dead state exergy is maximum.

quiz.q: Available part of Q at T
quiz.why: The available part of heat Q at temperature T is what a Carnot engine could convert, Q(1 − T₀/T), where T₀ is the surroundings. The rest is unavailable.
The Gouy–Stodola theorem says the lost work (irreversibility) equals T₀ times the entropy generated: I = T₀S_gen.
Second-law efficiency compares actual performance with the best possible (reversible) one: η_II = η/η_rev.
The dead state is the state where the system is in thermal and mechanical equilibrium with the surroundings, so no more work can be obtained from it.

quiz.q: Available energy of 500 kJ at 600 K, T₀ = 300 K

questions.q: A heat pump's COP is
questions.why: The COP of a heat pump is the useful heat delivered per unit work: COP = Q_H/W. Q_L/W is for a refrigerator.

questions.q: Entropy unit
questions.why: Entropy is heat divided by temperature, so the unit is kJ/K (or J/K).

questions.q: Carnot efficiency between 400 K and 300 K
Refrigerator: Q_L 5 kW, W 1.25 kW ⇒ COP
Heat rejected by that refrigerator
questions.why: By energy balance, heat rejected = Q_L + W = 5 + 1.25 = 6.25 kW.

questions.q: Δs for water 1 kg, 300 → 360 K (c 4.18)

Assertion (A): No engine can be more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs.  Reason (R): Otherwise combining it with a reversed reversible engine would violate the Kelvin–Planck statement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. If an engine could beat a reversible one, running a reversible engine backward from its output would give net work from one reservoir. That would violate Kelvin–Planck. R explains A.

questions.q: Max COP of a heat pump supplying 22 °C from 2 °C
questions.why: Maximum COP of a heat pump = T_H/(T_H − T_L) = 295/(295 − 275) = 295/20 = 14.75.

questions.q: S_gen when 500 kJ flows from 1000 K to 250 K
questions.why: S_gen = ΔS_cold + ΔS_hot = 500/250 − 500/1000 = 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 kJ/K. It is positive, so the heat transfer is irreversible.

questions.q: Air: 1 → 5 bar isothermal at 300 K: Δs
questions.why: For an isothermal ideal-gas change, Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = −0.287 × ln 5 = −0.287 × 1.609 ≈ −0.462 kJ/kg K. Compression lowers entropy as heat leaves.

questions.q: Case: An inventor claims an engine absorbing 2000 kJ at 750 K and rejecting 1100 kJ at 300 K. Verdict
questions.why: Check Clausius: ∮δQ/T = 2000/750 − 1100/300 = 2.67 − 3.67 = −1.0 kJ/K < 0. So it is possible but irreversible. Its efficiency is 900/2000 = 45%, below Carnot, 1 − 300/750 = 60%.

questions.q: Second-law efficiency of an engine with η = 40% between 1000 K and 300 K
Iron 2 kg (c 0.45) at 600 K quenched in a 300 K lake: S_gen
Exergy destroyed in that process (T₀ = 300 K)
COP_R of reversed Carnot with T_L = −23 °C and T_H = 27 °C
questions.why: T_L = 250 K and T_H = 300 K. COP_R = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 250/50 = 5. Convert °C to kelvin first.

courses.title: Thermodynamics · Unit 4 · Pure substances, steam and thermodynamic cycles
courses.summary: Phase-change processes, p–v, T–s and h–s diagrams, saturation, quality and steam tables, Rankine cycle and improvements, air-standard Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles, and vapour-compression refrigeration.
outcomes: Use steam tables with quality, superheat and interpolation
Analyse the Rankine cycle and its improvements
Compute efficiencies of Otto, Diesel and Brayton cycles
Analyse vapour-compression refrigeration with COP
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Pure substances and steam tables

scenes.text: Water enters a boiler as liquid and leaves as superheated steam at 500 °C.
Steam tables give the properties at every stage.

steps.title: Phases and quality
steps.body:
Compressed liquid → saturated liquid (f) → wet mixture → saturated vapour (g) → superheated vapour. Critical point (water: 22.06 MPa, 373.95 °C) — above it no distinct phase change.
Quality x = m_vapour/m_total. Wet mixture: v = v_f + x v_fg, h = h_f + x h_fg, s = s_f + x s_fg.
Superheated tables need p and T; compressed liquid ≈ saturated liquid at the same T.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** At 1 bar: h_f = 417.5, h_fg = 2257.5 kJ/kg. For x = 0.9: h = 417.5 + 0.9 × 2257.5 = 2449.2 kJ/kg.

**Example 2.** Steam at 1 bar with h = 2000 kJ/kg: x = (2000 − 417.5)/2257.5 = 0.70.

**Example 3.** Heat to make 1 kg of saturated steam at 1 bar from water at 25 °C (h ≈ 104.9): q = 2675 − 104.9 = 2570 kJ/kg.

steps.title: Reading tables
steps.body: Always first decide the region: compare T with T_sat(p), or v/h/s with f and g values at that p. Then use the right table.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using saturated tables for superheated steam.
- Quality outside 0–1 (means you're not in the wet region).
- Forgetting to interpolate linearly between table rows.

activity.prompt: At 1 bar, h_f = 417.5 and h_fg = 2257.5 kJ/kg. Enthalpy for x = 0.8 (kJ/kg, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: Quality x is the mass fraction of vapour. Saturated vapour is all vapour, so x = 1.
For a liquid–vapour mixture, h = h_f + x h_fg, i.e. liquid enthalpy plus the fraction of latent heat.
The critical pressure of water is about 22.06 MPa (at about 374 °C). Above it there is no distinct liquid–vapour change.
In the superheated region, p and T are independent, so both are needed to fix the state. In the wet region, they are linked.
A compressed liquid behaves almost incompressibly, so its properties are approximated by those of saturated liquid at the same temperature.

lessons.title: Rankine cycle

scenes.text: About three-quarters of India's electricity has come from steam power plants.
They run on the Rankine cycle: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser.

steps.title: Ideal Rankine
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic pump; 2→3 constant-p heating in boiler; 3→4 isentropic expansion in turbine; 4→1 condensation.
w_p = v₁(p₂ − p₁); w_t = h₃ − h₄; q_in = h₃ − h₂; η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in. Back-work ratio small (pump work ≪ turbine work).
Improvements: higher boiler pressure/temperature (superheat), lower condenser pressure, **reheat** (raises dryness at exit), **regeneration** (feedwater heaters), supercritical cycles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting pump work in q_in (h₂ = h₁ + w_p).
- Exit dryness < ~0.88 causes blade erosion — use reheat.
- Using T_sat at the wrong pressure.

activity.prompt: Ideal Rankine cycle processes in order (starting at condenser exit)
items: Isentropic compression in the pump
Constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler
Isentropic expansion in the turbine
Constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser

quiz.why: The pump in a Rankine cycle handles liquid, so w_p = v(p₂ − p₁), using the small specific volume of the liquid.
Reheating sends steam back to the boiler after partial expansion. It raises the dryness at the turbine exit, so blade erosion by water droplets is reduced.
Lowering the condenser pressure lowers the temperature at which heat is rejected (T_L), so efficiency rises. The limit is the cooling water temperature.
Regeneration heats the feedwater with steam bled from the turbine. This raises the mean temperature of heat addition and so the efficiency.
Steam rate is the steam flow per unit energy output, in kg/kWh. A lower value means a more compact plant.

lessons.title: Air-standard cycles: Otto, Diesel, Brayton

scenes.text: Petrol engines follow the Otto cycle, diesel engines the Diesel cycle, jet engines the Brayton cycle.
Each efficiency depends on a pressure or compression ratio.

steps.title: Efficiencies (cold air standard, γ = 1.4)
steps.body:
- **Otto:** η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1) (r = compression ratio).
- **Diesel:** η = 1 − (1/r^(γ−1)) × (ρ^γ − 1)/(γ(ρ − 1)), ρ = cut-off ratio. For the same r, Otto > Diesel; diesel engines use higher r.
- **Brayton (gas turbine):** η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), r_p = pressure ratio. Back-work ratio high (≈ 40–60%). Regeneration, intercooling, reheating improve it.
Mean effective pressure MEP = W_net/(V_max − V_min).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using pressure ratio in the Otto formula (it uses volume ratio).
- Exponent (γ − 1)/γ belongs to the Brayton pressure-ratio form.
- Expecting real engines to reach air-standard efficiency (they are much lower).

bands.text: Higher ratio: efficiency rises but knock risk rises.
Very high for petrol — needs high-octane fuel or direct injection.

quiz.q: For same r, Otto vs Diesel
quiz.why: At the same compression ratio, the Otto cycle (constant-volume heat addition) is more efficient than the Diesel, because the cut-off ratio reduces Diesel efficiency.
Brayton efficiency is η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), so it depends on the pressure ratio.
A gas turbine's compressor takes a large share of the turbine work, so it has a high back-work ratio (often 40–60%). A steam plant's pump takes very little.
In the Otto cycle, heat is added at constant volume (the spark ignites the mixture near top dead centre). In Diesel it is at constant pressure.

lessons.title: Vapour-compression refrigeration

scenes.text: Your refrigerator moves heat from inside to the room using a refrigerant like R-134a or R-600a.
Compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator form the cycle.

steps.title: Ideal VCR cycle
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic compression (saturated vapour → superheated); 2→3 condensation; 3→4 throttling (h₃ = h₄); 4→1 evaporation.
Refrigerating effect q_L = h₁ − h₄; compressor work w = h₂ − h₁; COP = (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁). Capacity in TR = ṁq_L/3.517 kW.
Subcooling the liquid increases q_L; superheating at evaporator exit protects the compressor. Refrigerants are chosen for low GWP/zero ODP (e.g. R-290 propane, R-600a isobutane, R-32, R-744 CO₂).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** h₁ = 395, h₂ = 425, h₃ = h₄ = 255 kJ/kg: q_L = 140, w = 30 ⇒ COP = 4.67.

**Example 2.** For 2 TR (7.034 kW): ṁ = 7.034/140 = 0.0502 kg/s; compressor power = 1.51 kW.

**Example 3.** Carnot COP between −10 °C and 40 °C: 263/50 = 5.26 — the actual 4.67 is 89% of it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating expansion as isentropic (it's throttling, isenthalpic).
- Using h₂ − h₄ for refrigerating effect.
- Forgetting 1 TR = 3.517 kW.

activity.prompt: VCR: h₁ = 400, h₂ = 440, h₄ = 260 kJ/kg. COP?

quiz.why: The expansion device (valve) is a throttling process, with no work or heat, so enthalpy stays constant: h₃ = h₄. Pressure falls and the refrigerant flashes partly to vapour.
The refrigerating effect is the heat absorbed in the evaporator per kg: h₁ − h₄, from the evaporator exit to its inlet.
Subcooling the liquid before the expansion valve lowers h₄ (the enthalpy at the evaporator inlet). That raises the refrigerating effect h₁ − h₄ and so improves COP.
One ton of refrigeration is the heat to melt 1 ton of ice in 24 h, i.e. about 3.517 kW (12 000 Btu/h).
R-290 (propane) is a natural refrigerant with very low global-warming potential and no ozone depletion. R-12, R-11 and R-22 harm the ozone layer.

questions.q: Quality of saturated liquid
questions.why: For a saturated liquid, no vapour has formed yet, so the quality x = 0.

questions.q: Rankine cycle condenser process
questions.why: In the condenser of a Rankine cycle, steam condenses at constant pressure, rejecting heat to the cooling water.

questions.q: Heat addition in Diesel cycle
questions.why: In the ideal Diesel cycle, heat is added at constant pressure as fuel burns while the piston moves. The Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume.

questions.q: Quality for h = 1800 kJ/kg at 1 bar (h_f 417.5, h_fg 2257.5)
Brayton η for r_p = 6
VCR COP: q_L 150 kJ/kg, w 40 kJ/kg
Assertion (A): Reheat in a Rankine cycle reduces moisture at turbine exit.  Reason (R): Steam is re-superheated at an intermediate pressure before final expansion.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Steam is sent back to the boiler after expanding to an intermediate pressure and is re-superheated, so the final expansion ends drier. R explains A.

questions.q: Otto cycle r = 9: efficiency
questions.why: η = 1 − r^(−0.4) = 1 − 9^(−0.4) = 1 − 0.415 ≈ 58.5%. Lower r than 10 gives lower efficiency.

questions.q: Rankine: w_t = 1000, w_p = 5, q_in = 3000 kJ/kg ⇒ η
questions.why: Net work = 1000 − 5 = 995 kJ/kg. η = w_net/q_in = 995/3000 ≈ 33.2%. The pump work is small compared with turbine work.

questions.q: Diesel r = 16, ρ = 2.5 (γ 1.4): η
Case: A 1.5 TR split AC has COP 3.2. Electrical input
questions.why: 1.5 TR = 1.5 × 3.517 ≈ 5.28 kW of cooling. COP = cooling/work, so work = 5.28/3.2 ≈ 1.65 kW.

questions.q: Steam rate for w_net = 900 kJ/kg
questions.why: Steam rate = 3600/w_net (kJ/kg) = 3600/900 = 4 kg/kWh, since 1 kWh = 3600 kJ.

questions.q: Refrigerant flow for 3 TR with q_L = 150 kJ/kg
Pump work: v = 0.001 m³/kg, p from 10 kPa to 15 MPa
questions.why: w_p = v Δp = 0.001 × (15 000 − 10) kPa = 0.001 × 14 990 ≈ 15 kJ/kg. Liquid pumping needs little work.

questions.q: Brayton back-work ratio is typically
questions.why: A Brayton cycle's compressor uses 40–60% of the turbine work, which is the back-work ratio. This is far above the 1–2% pump fraction in steam plants.

lessons.title: Formula sheet: basics, first law

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Engineering Thermodynamics.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Work, heat, first law
steps.body:
- W = ∫p dV; isobaric pΔV; isothermal p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁); polytropic (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1)
- Q − W = ΔU; ΔU = mc_vΔT; ΔH = mc_pΔT; c_p − c_v = R
- Adiabatic T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ); polytropic Q = W(γ − n)/(γ − 1)
- SFEE: h + V²/2 + gz; nozzle V = √(2Δh); throttle h₁ = h₂; filling T₂ = γT_line

steps.title: Units
steps.body: kPa·m³ = kJ; V²/2 in J/kg (÷1000 for kJ/kg); always kelvin in ratios.

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.why: At constant pressure, W = pΔV = 200 kPa × 0.5 m³ = 100 kJ.
For an adiabatic nozzle, V = √(2Δh) = √(2 × 200 000 J/kg) = √400 000 ≈ 632 m/s. Convert kJ to J first.

quiz.q: Q at constant volume, 1 kg air, ΔT 100 K
quiz.why: At constant volume, no work is done, so Q = ΔU = mc_vΔT = 1 × 0.718 × 100 = 71.8 kJ. Using c_p gives the constant-pressure answer.

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Engineering Thermodynamics.

steps.title: Second law and entropy
steps.body:
- η = 1 − Q_L/Q_H; η_C = 1 − T_L/T_H; COP_R = Q_L/W; COP_HP = COP_R + 1
- Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁); liquids c ln(T₂/T₁); reservoir Q/T

steps.title: Cycles
steps.body:

- Rankine η = (w_t − w_p)/q_in; w_p = vΔp
- Otto 1 − r^(1−γ); Brayton 1 − r_p^(−(γ−1)/γ); Diesel with cut-off ρ
- VCR COP = (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁); 1 TR = 3.517 kW

- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.

steps.body:

items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time

quiz.why: Volume depends on the amount of matter, so it is extensive. Pressure, temperature and density do not depend on the mass, so they are intensive.
Heating a rigid tank causes no change in volume, so the boundary work p dV is zero. All the heat raises internal energy.
For an ideal gas, c_p − c_v = R, and for air R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. (1.005 − 0.718 = 0.287)
In an adiabatic nozzle with no work, h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2, so the enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy.
The Clausius statement says that heat cannot flow from a colder to a hotter body without work being done, as in a refrigerator.
options: heat flow cold to hot needs work

quiz.q: Mock 1: Entropy change of reversible adiabatic
quiz.why: A reversible adiabatic process has no heat transfer and no irreversibility, so the entropy is constant (isentropic): ΔS = 0.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Quality 0.5 at 1 bar: h (h_f 417.5, h_fg 2257.5)

quiz.why: In a vapour-compression cycle, the expansion valve is a throttling device, where enthalpy remains constant (h₃ = h₄).

questions.q: Unit of specific enthalpy
questions.why: Specific enthalpy is enthalpy per unit mass, so its unit is kJ/kg.

questions.q: Zeroth law defines
questions.why: The zeroth law says bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other. This allows temperature to be defined and measured.

questions.q: Carnot cycle has
questions.why: The Carnot cycle has two reversible isothermal processes and two reversible adiabatic (isentropic) processes.

questions.q: 1 TR equals
questions.why: A ton of refrigeration is about 3.517 kW, from the heat to freeze 1 ton of water into ice in 24 hours.

questions.q: Isothermal work: 2 kg air at 400 K, V doubles
questions.why: Isothermal work: W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 2 × 0.287 × 400 × ln 2 = 229.6 × 0.693 ≈ 159.2 kJ.

questions.q: Heat engine Q_H 800 kJ, η 30% ⇒ Q_L
questions.why: Work = η × Q_H = 0.3 × 800 = 240 kJ. Heat rejected = 800 − 240 = 560 kJ.

questions.q: Compressor 1 kg/s, Δh = 250 kJ/kg (adiabatic): power
questions.why: For an adiabatic compressor, power = ṁΔh = 1 kg/s × 250 kJ/kg = 250 kW.

questions.q: Δs: air at constant volume 300 → 600 K
questions.why: At constant volume Δs = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) = 0.718 × ln 2 = 0.718 × 0.693 ≈ 0.498 kJ/kg·K.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Diesel engines achieve higher efficiency than petrol engines in practice.  Reason (R): They operate at much higher compression ratios, which outweighs the cut-off penalty.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Diesel engines use much higher compression ratios (about 15–22 against 8–10), and this more than offsets the efficiency loss from the cut-off. So R explains A.

questions.q: Rankine with h₃ 3400, h₄ 2300, h₁ 200, w_p 10 kJ/kg: η
questions.why: Net work = turbine work − pump work = (3400 − 2300) − 10 = 1090 kJ/kg. Heat in = h₃ − h₂ = 3400 − (200 + 10) = 3190. So η = 1090/3190 ≈ 34.2%.

questions.q: Brayton r_p = 12: η
Final T: evacuated tank filled from 350 K air line
questions.why: For filling an initially empty tank adiabatically, T_final = γT_line = 1.4 × 350 = 490 K. Flow work heats the gas.

questions.q: Max COP of fridge: −20 °C inside, 35 °C ambient
questions.why: Maximum COP = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 253/(308 − 253) = 253/55 ≈ 4.6, using kelvin.

questions.q: Case: A turbine receives 4 kg/s at 3200 kJ/kg, 30 m/s and leaves at 2400 kJ/kg, 120 m/s, adiabatic. Power
S_gen: 300 kJ from 900 K reservoir to 300 K reservoir
questions.why: S_gen = 300/300 − 300/900 = 1 − 0.333 ≈ 0.667 kJ/K. Positive, so the heat transfer is irreversible.

questions.q: Steam at 10 kPa with s = 7.0 kJ/kg K (s_f 0.6493, s_fg 7.5009): x
questions.why: x = (s − s_f)/s_fg = (7.0 − 0.6493)/7.5009 ≈ 0.847. The steam is wet with about 85% vapour.

questions.q: Otto: 1 kg air, heat added 1500 kJ, r = 8: net work
questions.why: Otto efficiency for r = 8 is 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 0.565. Net work = 0.565 × 1500 ≈ 847 kJ.

questions.q: Polytropic expansion n = 1.25, W = 200 kJ (air, γ 1.4): heat
questions.why: For polytropic expansion, Q = W(γ − n)/(γ − 1) = 200 × (1.4 − 1.25)/0.4 = 200 × 0.375 = 75 kJ. It is positive: heat is added.

questions.q: Available energy of 2000 kJ at 800 K with T₀ = 300 K
Refrigerant flow for 5 TR, q_L = 175 kJ/kg

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics · Unit 1 · Fluid properties and fluid statics
courses.summary: Density, specific weight, viscosity (Newton's law), surface tension and capillarity, compressibility, pressure at a point, hydrostatic law, manometers, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved surfaces, buoyancy and stability of floating bodies (metacentric height).
outcomes: Use viscosity, surface tension and capillary-rise relations
Measure pressure with piezometers and manometers
Compute hydrostatic force and centre of pressure on surfaces
Assess stability of floating bodies with metacentric height
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Fluid properties

scenes.text: Honey pours slowly; water splashes.
Viscosity measures resistance to shear — a key fluid property.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
Density ρ (water 1000 kg/m³), specific weight w = ρg, relative density S = ρ/ρ_water.
**Newton's law of viscosity:** τ = μ du/dy (μ dynamic viscosity, Pa·s; ν = μ/ρ kinematic, m²/s). Newtonian fluids obey it; non-Newtonian (paints, blood, toothpaste) don't. Liquid viscosity falls with temperature; gas viscosity rises.
**Surface tension** σ (N/m): pressure inside droplet Δp = 4σ/d, bubble (two surfaces) 8σ/d, jet 2σ/d.
**Capillary rise** h = 4σ cos θ/(ρgd) (water–glass θ ≈ 0; mercury θ ≈ 130° ⇒ depression).
Bulk modulus K = −dp/(dV/V).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Plate moving 0.5 m/s over oil film 1 mm thick, μ = 0.8 Pa·s: τ = 0.8 × 500 = 400 Pa.

**Example 2.** Capillary rise of water (σ = 0.073 N/m) in a 1 mm tube: h = 4 × 0.073/(1000 × 9.81 × 0.001) = 29.8 mm.

**Example 3.** Pressure inside a 2 mm water droplet: 4 × 0.073/0.002 = 146 Pa above ambient.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing poise (0.1 Pa·s) and Pa·s.
- Using radius instead of diameter in 4σ/d formulas.
- Forgetting cos θ (mercury depresses).

activity.prompt: Shear stress: μ = 0.5 Pa·s, velocity gradient 200 s⁻¹. τ (Pa)?

quiz.why: Newton's law of viscosity says shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient: τ = μ du/dy. The constant is the dynamic viscosity.
In liquids, viscosity comes from cohesion between molecules, which weakens as temperature rises, so viscosity decreases. In gases it increases.
A soap bubble has two surfaces (inside and outside), so the pressure excess is twice that of a droplet: Δp = 4σ/r = 8σ/d.
1 poise = 1 dyne·s/cm² = 10⁻⁵ N × s/10⁻⁴ m² = 0.1 Pa·s.
For mercury in glass, cohesion is stronger than adhesion and the contact angle is more than 90°, so the level falls: capillary depression.

lessons.title: Pressure measurement and manometers

scenes.text: A technician uses a U-tube manometer to check gas pressure.
Height differences of liquid columns reveal pressure differences.

steps.title: Hydrostatics
steps.body:
dp/dz = −ρg ⇒ p = p₀ + ρgh (depth h). Pressure at a point is the same in all directions (Pascal).
Absolute = atmospheric + gauge; vacuum = negative gauge. Standard atmosphere 101.325 kPa = 760 mm Hg = 10.33 m water.

steps.title: Manometers
steps.body: Piezometer (low gauge pressures, liquids only). **U-tube:** p_A + ρ₁gh₁ − ρ_m g h_m = p_atm (walk through the tube adding ρgh going down, subtracting going up). Differential manometer: p_A − p_B = (ρ_m − ρ)gh_m for same fluid at same level. Inverted U-tube for small differences. Micromanometer/inclined manometer for sensitivity: h = L sin θ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Water pipe; mercury U-tube; centre of pipe 0.2 m below the mercury level in the left limb; mercury difference 0.3 m: p_A = 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.3 − 1000 × 9.81 × 0.2 = 40 024 − 1962 = 38.06 kPa (gauge).

**Example 2.** Differential manometer between two water points at the same level, Hg difference 0.15 m: Δp = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.15 = 18.54 kPa.

**Example 3.** Pressure at 10 m depth in sea water (ρ = 1025): 100.6 kPa gauge.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding ρgh going up (it should be subtracted).
- Using mercury density for the connecting fluid columns.
- Forgetting atmospheric pressure when absolute pressure is asked.

activity.prompt: Gauge pressure at 5 m depth in water (kPa, g = 9.81)?

quiz.why: The hydrostatic law: pressure at depth h in a static fluid is p = p₀ + ρgh. It increases linearly with depth.

quiz.q: Standard atmosphere in m of water
quiz.why: Standard atmosphere = 101.325 kPa = ρgh for water, giving h = 101 325/(1000 × 9.81) ≈ 10.33 m of water.
A piezometer is an open tube that works for liquids at positive gauge pressure. It cannot measure gases (they escape) or vacuum (air would enter).

quiz.q: Differential head with Hg/water, 0.1 m Hg
quiz.why: The mercury column of 0.1 m is equivalent to (13.6 − 1) × 0.1 = 1.26 m of water, since the water above it offsets 1 part of the density.
In an inclined manometer, the tube is tilted, so a small vertical rise h appears as a longer reading along the tube, L = h/sinθ. This magnifies small pressure differences, so it improves sensitivity.

lessons.title: Hydrostatic forces on surfaces

scenes.text: An engineer sizes a dam's sluice gate to withstand water pressure.
Total force acts at the centre of pressure — below the centroid.

steps.title: Plane surfaces
steps.body:
Total force F = ρg A h̄ (h̄ = depth of centroid). Centre of pressure depth h_cp = h̄ + I_G sin²θ/(A h̄) (vertical: h̄ + I_G/(A h̄)). Always below the centroid (for submerged surfaces).
Vertical rectangle b × d with top at surface: F = ρgbd²/2, h_cp = 2d/3.

steps.title: Curved surfaces
steps.body: F_H = force on the vertical projection of the surface (as a plane surface). F_V = weight of fluid vertically above the surface (real or imaginary). Resultant F = √(F_H² + F_V²), angle tan⁻¹(F_V/F_H), passing through the centre for circular surfaces.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Vertical gate 2 m wide, 3 m deep, top at the free surface: F = 1000 × 9.81 × 6 × 1.5 = 88.3 kN at 2 m depth.

**Example 2.** Circular plate d = 1 m, vertical, centre 2 m deep: A = 0.785, F = 9810 × 0.785 × 2 = 15.4 kN; h_cp = 2 + (π/64)/(0.785 × 2) = 2 + 0.031 = 2.031 m.

**Example 3.** Quarter-circle gate radius 2 m, width 1 m, water on the concave side up to the top: F_H = 9810 × 2 × 1 = 19.6 kN; F_V = 9810 × (π × 4/4) × 1 = 30.8 kN; F = 36.5 kN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the resultant at the centroid.
- Using surface area instead of vertical projection for F_H.
- Forgetting sin²θ for inclined surfaces.

activity.prompt: Vertical rectangular gate 1 m wide, 4 m deep, top at surface. Total force (kN, g = 9.81)?

quiz.q: Total hydrostatic force on a plane
quiz.why: The total hydrostatic force on a submerged plane surface is F = ρg A h̄, i.e. the pressure at the centroid times the area.

quiz.q: Centre of pressure relative to centroid
quiz.why: Pressure rises with depth, so the force is bigger on the lower part. The centre of pressure is therefore below the centroid.

On a vertical rectangle with its top edge at the surface, pressure rises linearly from zero, giving a triangular load. The resultant acts at the centroid of the triangle, 2d/3 below the surface, which is below the centroid (d/2).

quiz.q: Vertical component on a curved surface equals
quiz.why: The vertical force on a curved surface equals the weight of the fluid directly above it up to the free surface (or the equivalent). It is not the force on the projected area.

quiz.q: Horizontal component on a curved surface equals force on
quiz.why: The horizontal force on a curved surface equals the force on its projection on a vertical plane, because only the horizontal pressure components contribute. It acts at the centre of pressure of that projection.

lessons.title: Buoyancy and stability of floating bodies

scenes.text: A loaded ship stays upright even when waves tilt it.
Its metacentre lies above its centre of gravity — positive metacentric height.

steps.title: Archimedes and stability
steps.body:
Buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid, acting at the centre of buoyancy B (centroid of displaced volume).
Floating: weight = buoyancy. Stability: metacentric height GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V (I = second moment of the waterline area about the tilt axis, V = displaced volume). GM > 0 stable, = 0 neutral, < 0 unstable.
Submerged bodies: stable if G is below B.
Period of rolling T = 2π√(k²/(g GM)) — large GM: stiff, uncomfortable roll; small GM: slow roll.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Wooden block 1 m × 0.5 m × 0.4 m (height), S = 0.6, floating in water: depth of immersion = 0.24 m. B at 0.12 m, G at 0.20 m ⇒ BG = 0.08 m. I (about long axis) = 1 × 0.5³/12 = 0.01042; V = 0.12 ⇒ BM = 0.0868 ⇒ GM = 0.0068 m > 0 (just stable).

**Example 2.** Iceberg (S = 0.92) in sea water (1.025): fraction submerged = 0.898.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full volume instead of displaced volume for BM.
- Taking I about the wrong axis (use the axis about which it tilts; the smaller I is critical).
- Forgetting floating bodies can be stable even with G above B (if M is above G).

activity.prompt: Body with BM = 0.5 m and BG = 0.3 m. Metacentric height GM (m)?

quiz.why: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force on a body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. It equals the body weight only when the body floats freely.
A floating body is stable if the metacentre M lies above the centre of gravity G, i.e. GM > 0. Then the buoyancy couple on tilting restores the body to upright.
The distance from the centre of buoyancy to the metacentre is BM = I/V, where I is the second moment of the waterline area about the tilt axis and V is the displaced volume.
A fully submerged body has no waterline area, so its metacentre coincides with the centre of buoyancy B. It is stable only if G is below B.

quiz.q: Fraction of ice (S 0.9) submerged in fresh water
quiz.why: A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid, so the submerged fraction = ρ_body/ρ_fluid = 0.9/1 = 0.9. Ice floats with 90% of its volume under water.

questions.q: SI unit of dynamic viscosity
questions.why: Dynamic viscosity μ = τ/(du/dy) = (N/m²)/(1/s) = Pa·s. The unit m²/s belongs to kinematic viscosity.

questions.q: Pressure increases with depth
questions.why: In a fluid of constant density, p = p₀ + ρgh, so pressure increases linearly with depth. For gases, density changes so the variation is not exactly linear.
options: linearly in a liquid of constant density

questions.q: Archimedes' principle concerns
questions.why: Archimedes' principle describes buoyancy: the upthrust on a submerged or floating body equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

questions.q: Kinematic viscosity of oil μ = 0.09 Pa·s, ρ = 900 kg/m³
questions.why: Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ = 0.09/900 = 1×10⁻⁴ m²/s. Divide dynamic viscosity by density.

questions.q: Pressure at 2 m depth in oil S = 0.8 (gauge)
questions.why: Gauge pressure p = ρgh = 800 × 9.81 × 2 = 15 696 Pa ≈ 15.7 kPa. Oil with S = 0.8 has density 800 kg/m³.

questions.q: Capillary rise of water in 0.5 mm tube (σ 0.073)
questions.why: Capillary rise h = 4σ cosθ/(ρgd) = 4 × 0.073/(1000 × 9.81 × 0.0005) ≈ 0.0595 m = 59.5 mm, with a contact angle near zero for water in clean glass.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The centre of pressure on a submerged vertical plane lies below its centroid.  Reason (R): Pressure increases with depth, so lower parts carry more force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Pressure increases with depth, so the lower part of a vertical plane takes a larger share of the force, which pulls the resultant below the centroid. R explains A.

questions.q: Force on a vertical circular plate d = 2 m, centre 3 m deep
questions.why: F = ρg A h̄ = 9810 × (π × 2²/4 = π) × 3 = 9810 × 3.1416 × 3 ≈ 92.5 kN. The centroid depth 3 m is used.

questions.q: h_cp for that plate
U-tube Hg manometer on a water pipe: Hg difference 0.25 m, pipe centre 0.15 m below left Hg level. p_A (gauge)
questions.why: Pressure at A = mercury column − water column: 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.25 − 1000 × 9.81 × 0.15 = 33 354 − 1472 ≈ 31.9 kPa gauge.

questions.q: Case: A rectangular pontoon 6 m long, 3 m wide floats 1 m deep; G is 1.2 m above the bottom. GM (tilting about long axis)
questions.why: Displaced volume = 6 × 3 × 1 = 18 m³. I = 6 × 3³/12 = 13.5 m⁴, so BM = 13.5/18 = 0.75 m. KB = 0.5 m, KG = 1.2 m, so GM = 0.5 + 0.75 − 1.2 = 0.05 m. It is barely stable.

questions.q: Pressure inside a 1 mm air bubble in water (σ 0.073), above ambient
questions.why: An air bubble inside a liquid has one surface, so Δp = 2σ/r = 4σ/d = 4 × 0.073/0.001 = 292 Pa. A soap bubble has two surfaces and so gets twice that.

questions.q: Quarter-circle gate r = 1 m, width 2 m: F_V (water above, full quadrant)
questions.why: The vertical force equals the weight of water above the curved surface: ρg × (πr²/4) × width = 9810 × 0.785 × 2 ≈ 15.4 kN.

questions.q: Shear stress for μ = 1.5 Pa·s, plate 2 m/s over 3 mm film
questions.why: For a linear velocity profile, τ = μ U/h = 1.5 × 2/0.003 = 1000 Pa. Convert the film thickness to metres.

questions.q: A floating body with GM < 0 will
questions.why: If GM < 0, the metacentre lies below G, so a small tilt produces an overturning couple and the body capsizes. It is unstable, though it does not sink.

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics · Unit 2 · Fluid kinematics and dynamics
courses.summary: Types of flow, streamlines and pathlines, continuity equation, velocity potential and stream function, Euler's and Bernoulli's equations, applications (venturimeter, orifice meter, pitot tube, orifices), and the momentum equation for forces on bends and jets.
outcomes: Classify flows and apply continuity
Use stream function and velocity potential
Apply Bernoulli to flow meters and tanks
Use the momentum equation for forces on bends, plates and jets
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Flow types, continuity and flow description

scenes.text: Partly covering a hose outlet makes water shoot farther.
Continuity: smaller area ⇒ higher velocity.

steps.title: Classifications
steps.body:
Steady/unsteady (∂/∂t = 0?), uniform/non-uniform (∂/∂s = 0?), laminar/turbulent, compressible/incompressible, rotational/irrotational, 1-D/2-D/3-D.
Streamline (tangent to velocity), pathline (particle path), streakline (dye from a point) — identical in steady flow.

steps.title: Continuity
steps.body:
ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂; incompressible: Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂.
Differential (incompressible): ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y + ∂w/∂z = 0.
Acceleration = local (∂V/∂t) + convective (u∂V/∂x + …).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Pipe 0.2 m to 0.1 m diameter, V₁ = 2 m/s: V₂ = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s; Q = 0.0628 m³/s.

**Example 2.** Check u = 2x, v = −2y: ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 2 − 2 = 0 ⇒ possible incompressible flow.

**Example 3.** Convective acceleration for u = 2x at x = 1: a_x = u ∂u/∂x = 2 × 2 = 4 m/s².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- V ∝ 1/d (it is ∝ 1/d²).
- Thinking steady flow has zero acceleration (convective acceleration can exist).
- Mixing streamline and pathline in unsteady flow.

activity.prompt: Pipe narrows from 300 mm to 150 mm diameter; V₁ = 1.5 m/s. V₂ (m/s)?

quiz.why: For incompressible flow, the volume flow rate Q = AV is the same at all sections, so A₁V₁ = A₂V₂. This is the continuity equation.
In steady flow, the fluid properties at any given point do not change with time. The velocity may still vary from place to place.
options: properties don't change with time at a point

quiz.why: Area ∝ d², so halving the diameter cuts the area to 1/4. By continuity, the velocity becomes 4 times.

quiz.q: In steady flow streamlines and pathlines
quiz.why: In steady flow, every particle passing a point follows the same path, so a streamline, a pathline and a streakline coincide.
Continuity for incompressible 2-D flow needs ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. Here ∂u/∂x = 1 and ∂v/∂y = −1, so the sum is zero everywhere: the flow is incompressible.

lessons.title: Stream function, velocity potential and flow nets

scenes.text: Engineers sketch flow nets to see how water speeds up around piers.
Streamlines and equipotential lines cross at right angles.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Stream function ψ: u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x (satisfies continuity automatically). Difference ψ₂ − ψ₁ = flow rate per unit width between streamlines.
Velocity potential φ (irrotational flow): u = −∂φ/∂x, v = −∂φ/∂y (sign convention varies; some texts use +). Exists only for irrotational flow; satisfies Laplace's equation if incompressible.
Rotation ω_z = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y); vorticity = 2ω.
ψ = const and φ = const are orthogonal ⇒ flow net.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ψ = 3xy: u = 3x, v = −3y; ∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y = 0 ⇒ irrotational. At (1, 2): V = √(9 + 36) = 6.71 m/s.

**Example 2.** Flow between streamlines ψ = 2 and ψ = 5 m²/s ⇒ q = 3 m²/s per metre width.

**Example 3.** u = y, v = 0 (shear flow): ω_z = −½ ⇒ rotational ⇒ no φ exists.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign convention mix-ups for ψ and φ — state your convention.
- Claiming a velocity potential exists for rotational flows.
- Forgetting ψ difference is per unit width.

activity.prompt: Stream function

quiz.why: The stream function ψ is defined so that u = ∂ψ/∂y and v = −∂ψ/∂x. Substituting gives zero in the continuity equation, so ψ always satisfies continuity. It satisfies irrotationality only for potential flow.
A velocity potential φ exists only if the flow is irrotational (curl V = 0), since V = ∇φ and the curl of a gradient is always zero.
In 2-D irrotational flow, streamlines (ψ = constant) and equipotential lines (φ = constant) cross at right angles, forming the flow net.

quiz.q: Discharge between ψ = 1 and ψ = 4 (per m width)
quiz.why: The flow between two streamlines equals the difference in their stream function values: 4 − 1 = 3 m²/s per metre width.
Rotation ω_z = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y) = ½(0 − 1) = −0.5, which is not zero. So the flow is rotational: a simple shear flow.

lessons.title: Bernoulli's equation and flow measurement

story.title: Measuring flow in a water main

scenes.text: A water utility measures flow with a venturimeter in the main pipe.
Pressure drops at the throat because speed rises — Bernoulli.

steps.title: Bernoulli
steps.body: Along a streamline, steady, incompressible, inviscid: p/ρg + V²/2g + z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + datum head). With losses: add h_L to the downstream side; pumps add head, turbines remove it.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
**Venturimeter:** Q = C_d A₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁² − A₂²), h = differential head (for Hg/water: h = x(13.6 − 1)); C_d ≈ 0.95–0.99.
**Orifice meter:** same form, C_d ≈ 0.6–0.65 (more loss, cheaper).
**Pitot tube:** V = C_v√(2gh) (stagnation − static).
**Small orifice in a tank (Torricelli):** V = √(2gH); Q = C_d a√(2gH); C_d = C_c × C_v.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using manometer reading directly as h (convert with (S_m/S − 1)).
- Applying Bernoulli across a pump without adding its head.
- Forgetting C_d.

activity.prompt: Torricelli: velocity from a tank orifice under 5 m head (ideal, m/s, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: Bernoulli's equation assumes steady, incompressible, frictionless (inviscid) flow along a streamline, with no energy added or removed.
options: steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline

quiz.why: A venturimeter has a smooth converging–diverging shape with little loss, so its coefficient of discharge is high, about 0.95–0.98.
A Pitot tube measures the stagnation pressure, and with the static pressure gives the velocity at the point where it is placed.

quiz.q: Hg/water manometer 0.1 m equals water head
quiz.why: With mercury (S = 13.6) over water, the head in water is (13.6 − 1) × 0.1 = 12.6 × 0.1 = 1.26 m. The water in the legs offsets one part of the density.
The coefficient of discharge is the product of the contraction coefficient and the velocity coefficient, C_d = C_c × C_v, since actual Q = C_v × C_c × ideal Q.

lessons.title: Momentum equation and forces

scenes.text: Firefighters brace against the hose's reaction force.
The momentum equation predicts forces from changing momentum flux.

steps.title: Momentum equation (steady, control volume)
steps.body:
ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in) (vector, each direction). Include pressure forces p A on inlet/outlet faces and body forces.
- Jet on a fixed flat plate (normal): F = ρaV².
- Jet on a moving plate (velocity u): F = ρa(V − u)² (single plate).
- Pipe bend: Fₓ = p₁A₁ − p₂A₂ cos θ − ṁ(V₂ cos θ − V₁) (force by fluid on bend; sign by direction).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Jet 50 mm dia at 20 m/s on a fixed plate: a = 0.001963; F = 1000 × 0.001963 × 400 = 785 N.

**Example 2.** Same plate moving away at 5 m/s: F = 1000 × 0.001963 × 225 = 442 N; work rate = 442 × 5 = 2.2 kW.

**Example 3.** 90° bend, 0.3 m pipe, Q = 0.3 m³/s, p = 200 kPa throughout (neglect losses): V = 4.24 m/s; ṁ = 300 kg/s; Fₓ = pA + ṁV = 200 000 × 0.0707 + 300 × 4.24 = 14 140 + 1272 = 15.4 kN, same in y ⇒ resultant 21.8 kN at 45°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting pressure forces at the inlet/outlet.
- Using V instead of relative velocity for moving plates.
- Sign confusion between force on fluid and force on bend.

activity.prompt: Water jet 0.002 m² area at 15 m/s on a fixed normal plate. Force (N)?

quiz.why: The momentum equation for a control volume says that the net force equals the rate of change of momentum: ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in).

quiz.q: Force of jet on fixed normal plate
quiz.why: A jet striking a fixed plate normally loses all its momentum in that direction. So F = ṁV = ρaV × V = ρaV².
For a moving plate, only the relative velocity of the jet matters: mass strikes at the rate ρa(V − u), and its velocity change is (V − u). The force is ρa(V − u)² for a single plate.
For a bend, the force on the fluid includes pressure forces at the inlet and outlet sections (and weight), as well as the momentum change. Leaving out pressure gives a wrong answer.

quiz.q: Doubling jet velocity changes force on fixed plate by
quiz.why: F = ρaV², so the force is proportional to V². Doubling the velocity gives a force 2² = 4 times as large.

questions.q: Continuity is based on conservation of
questions.why: Continuity expresses conservation of mass: the mass flow entering a control volume equals that leaving it in steady flow.

questions.q: Velocity head
questions.why: The velocity head is V²/2g, the height from which a body would need to fall to gain the velocity V. It is one of the three terms in Bernoulli's equation.

questions.q: Orifice meter C_d about
questions.why: An orifice meter has a sharp edge and the jet contracts, with losses, so C_d is about 0.6, much lower than for a venturimeter.

questions.q: Q in 0.1 m dia pipe at 2 m/s
Pitot head 0.8 m: velocity
ψ = 2xy: velocity at (1, 1)
Assertion (A): A velocity potential exists only for irrotational flow.  Reason (R): Curl of a gradient is zero, so a potential flow cannot have vorticity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. A velocity potential means V = ∇φ, and the curl of any gradient is zero, so such a flow cannot have vorticity. R explains A.

questions.q: Bernoulli: pipe 1 (p 200 kPa, V 2 m/s) to pipe 2 (V 6 m/s), same level: p₂
questions.why: By Bernoulli at the same level: p₂ = p₁ − ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = 200 − ½ × 1000 × (36 − 4)/1000 = 200 − 16 = 184 kPa. Higher speed means lower pressure.

questions.q: Orifice Q: d = 25 mm, H = 2 m, C_d 0.6
Jet 0.001 m² at 30 m/s on plate moving away at 10 m/s: force
questions.why: For a moving plate the jet strikes at relative velocity (30 − 10) = 20 m/s, so F = ρa(V − u)² = 1000 × 0.001 × 20² = 400 N.

questions.q: Case: A 200 × 100 mm venturi (C_d 0.97) shows 0.2 m Hg on water. Q
Is u = x², v = −2xy a valid incompressible flow?
questions.why: The flow is incompressible if ∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. ∂u/∂x = 2x and ∂v/∂y = −2x, so the sum is zero. The flow satisfies continuity everywhere.

questions.q: Rotation ω_z for u = −y, v = x
questions.why: Rotation ω_z = ½(∂v/∂x − ∂u/∂y) = ½(1 − (−1)) = ½ × 2 = 1 rad/s. It is solid-body rotation.

questions.q: 90° bend, pA = 10 kN at each face, ṁV = 2 kN: force component in x on bend
questions.why: The force on the bend in the x-direction is the pressure force plus the momentum term: 10 + 2 = 12 kN, since the fluid is turned and both act in the same sense.

questions.q: Tank drains through orifice: if head drops to one quarter, outflow becomes
questions.why: Q ∝ √H. If the head drops to a quarter, Q becomes √(1/4) = 1/2, i.e. half the flow.

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics · Unit 3 · Viscous flow and flow through pipes
courses.summary: Reynolds number and flow regimes, laminar flow between plates and in pipes (Hagen–Poiseuille), turbulent flow and the Darcy–Weisbach equation, friction factor and the Moody chart, minor losses, hydraulic and energy grade lines, pipes in series and parallel, and power transmission through pipes.
outcomes: Classify flow regime with Reynolds number
Use Hagen–Poiseuille for laminar pipe flow
Compute major and minor head losses
Solve series/parallel pipe problems and draw HGL/EGL
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Reynolds number and laminar pipe flow

scenes.text: Thick crude oil moves smoothly in layers through a pipeline.
Reynolds number tells whether flow is laminar or turbulent.

steps.title: Reynolds number
steps.body: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν. Pipes: laminar Re < 2000, transitional 2000–4000, turbulent > 4000 (approximate).

steps.title: Hagen–Poiseuille (laminar, circular pipe)
steps.body:
Velocity profile parabolic: u = u_max(1 − r²/R²), u_max = 2V_avg.
Pressure drop Δp = 32μVL/D² ⇒ head loss h_f = 32μVL/(ρgD²).
Friction factor f = 64/Re (Darcy). Shear stress varies linearly from 0 at the centre to τ_w at the wall.
Between fixed parallel plates: u_max = 1.5 V_avg; Δp = 12μVL/t².

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Oil μ = 0.1 Pa·s, ρ = 900, D = 0.1 m, V = 1 m/s: Re = 900 ⇒ laminar. Δp per 100 m = 32 × 0.1 × 1 × 100/0.01 = 32 kPa; h_f = 3.62 m.

**Example 2.** f = 64/900 = 0.0711 — check with Darcy: h_f = f(L/D)V²/2g = 0.0711 × 1000 × 1/19.62 = 3.62 m ✔.

**Example 3.** Water at 20 °C (ν = 10⁻⁶) in 25 mm pipe at 1 m/s: Re = 25 000 ⇒ turbulent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Fanning f (= f_Darcy/4) with the Darcy equation.
- Applying 64/Re to turbulent flow.
- Taking u_max = V_avg.

activity.prompt: Water ν = 1×10⁻⁶ m²/s, D = 0.05 m, V = 0.03 m/s. Reynolds number?

quiz.why: Pipe flow is laminar for Re below about 2000, and turbulent above about 4000. Between is the transition.
For laminar flow in a pipe, the Darcy friction factor is f = 64/Re. It depends only on Re and not on roughness.
The laminar profile in a pipe is a parabola, with maximum velocity at the centre equal to twice the average velocity.

quiz.q: Δp in laminar pipe flow is proportional to
quiz.why: By Hagen–Poiseuille, Δp = 32μLV/D², which is linear in V. In turbulent flow, it rises roughly as V².
Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces: Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν.

lessons.title: Turbulent flow and Darcy–Weisbach

scenes.text: A plumber chooses pipe sizes so the top floor still gets enough pressure.
Friction loss grows with V² — the Darcy–Weisbach equation.

steps.title: Major loss
steps.body:
h_f = fLV²/(2gD) (Darcy f). In terms of Q: h_f = 8fLQ²/(π²gD⁵) ≈ fLQ²/(12.1D⁵).
Friction factor: smooth pipes Blasius f = 0.316/Re^0.25 (Re < 10⁵); rough pipes depend on ε/D — Colebrook equation, Moody chart; fully rough f depends only on ε/D. Haaland explicit approximation: 1/√f = −1.8 log[(ε/3.7D)^1.11 + 6.9/Re].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Water 0.15 m pipe, 500 m long, V = 2 m/s, f = 0.02: h_f = 0.02 × 500 × 4/(19.62 × 0.15) = 13.6 m.

**Example 2.** Doubling the flow (same f) ⇒ h_f × 4 = 54.4 m.

**Example 3.** Halving the diameter at the same Q ⇒ h_f × 32 (∝ 1/D⁵).

steps.title: Quick sizing
steps.body: Because h_f ∝ 1/D⁵, a small increase in diameter hugely reduces losses — often cheaper than a bigger pump.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fanning vs Darcy f confusion.
- Using the laminar formula in turbulent flow.
- Units of D in mm.

activity.prompt: h_f = fLV²/(2gD): f = 0.025, L = 200 m, V = 1.5 m/s, D = 0.1 m. h_f (m, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The Darcy–Weisbach equation gives the head loss due to friction in a pipe: h_f = fLV²/(2gD). The other formula with 32μ is for laminar flow only.

quiz.q: Halving D at same Q multiplies h_f by
quiz.why: For the same Q, V ∝ 1/D². Then h_f ∝ V²/D ∝ 1/D⁵. Halving D multiplies h_f by 2⁵ = 32.
The Blasius formula, f = 0.316/Re^0.25, is for smooth pipes in turbulent flow with Re up to about 10⁵. It does not apply to rough pipes or laminar flow.
The Moody chart gives the Darcy friction factor f for turbulent flow as a function of Reynolds number and relative roughness ε/D.
options: friction factor vs Re and ε/D

quiz.q: In fully rough turbulence f depends on
quiz.why: In the fully rough zone at high Re, the viscous sublayer is thinner than the roughness, so f depends only on relative roughness ε/D and no longer on Re.

lessons.title: Minor losses, HGL and EGL

story.title: Why many fittings slow the flow

scenes.text: A pipeline with many elbows and valves delivers less water.
Each fitting adds a minor loss K V²/2g.

steps.title: Minor losses
steps.body:
h_m = K V²/(2g).
- Sudden expansion: h = (V₁ − V₂)²/(2g) (Borda–Carnot).
- Sudden contraction: h ≈ 0.5 V₂²/(2g) (or (1/C_c − 1)²V₂²/2g).
- Pipe entrance (sharp) 0.5 V²/2g; exit to a tank 1.0 V²/2g.
- Elbows, valves: K from tables (e.g. globe valve open ≈ 10, gate valve open ≈ 0.2).
Equivalent length L_e = KD/f.

steps.title: HGL and EGL
steps.body: Energy grade line EGL = p/ρg + V²/2g + z; hydraulic grade line HGL = p/ρg + z (EGL − V²/2g). EGL slopes down by friction losses, drops at fittings, rises at pumps. Where HGL falls below the pipe, pressure is below atmospheric (siphons, cavitation risk).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Expansion from 0.1 m (V = 4 m/s) to 0.2 m (V = 1 m/s): h = 9/19.62 = 0.46 m.

**Example 2.** Two reservoirs joined by a 300 m, 0.2 m pipe, f = 0.02, with entrance (0.5) and exit (1.0): H = (0.5 + 1 + 0.02 × 300/0.2)V²/2g = 31.5 V²/2g. For H = 10 m: V = √(10 × 19.62/31.5) = 2.50 m/s; Q = 0.0785 m³/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the exit loss (full velocity head).
- Using upstream velocity for contraction losses (use downstream).
- Drawing HGL above EGL.

activity.prompt: Sudden expansion: V₁ = 5 m/s to V₂ = 2 m/s. Head loss (m, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: When a pipe discharges into a large reservoir, all the kinetic energy is lost, so the exit loss is V²/2g (K = 1).
For a sharp-edged pipe entrance from a reservoir, the loss coefficient is about 0.5, i.e. 0.5V²/2g. A well-rounded entrance gives about 0.04.
The energy grade line is above the hydraulic grade line by the velocity head: EGL − HGL = V²/2g.
The HGL is p/ρg + z. When it lies below the pipe, p/ρg is negative, so the pressure is below atmospheric. This is the case at siphon crests and risks cavitation.
For a sudden enlargement, the loss is (V₁ − V₂)²/2g (Borda–Carnot), from the momentum balance with the shock at the expansion.

lessons.title: Pipes in series and parallel; power transmission

scenes.text: A town's water flows through mains, branches and loops.
Series pipes add losses; parallel pipes share the same loss.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
**Series:** Q same; H = Σh_fᵢ (+ minor). Equivalent pipe (Dupuit): L_e/D_e⁵ = ΣLᵢ/Dᵢ⁵ (same f).
**Parallel:** h_f same in each branch; Q = ΣQᵢ.
**Power transmission through a pipe:** P = ρgQ(H − h_f); maximum when h_f = H/3 ⇒ η_max = 66.7%.
**Water hammer** (sudden valve closure): pressure rise Δp = ρcV (c = wave speed ≈ 1000–1400 m/s).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Series: 300 m of 0.3 m and 200 m of 0.2 m (f same) ⇒ equivalent 0.3 m pipe length: L_e = 300 + 200 × (0.3/0.2)⁵ = 300 + 1519 = 1819 m.

**Example 2.** Two parallel pipes of equal length and f, D₁ = 0.2, D₂ = 0.1: Q ∝ D^2.5 ⇒ Q₁/Q₂ = 2^2.5 = 5.66.

**Example 3.** Water hammer: V = 2 m/s stopped instantly, c = 1200 m/s: Δp = 1000 × 1200 × 2 = 2.4 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding flows in series or losses in parallel.
- Using D² instead of D⁵ in equivalent pipe.
- Closing valves too fast in long pipelines (water hammer damage).

activity.prompt: Series or parallel rule?

items.text: Same head loss in each pipe

quiz.q: Max power transmission efficiency through a pipe
quiz.why: For maximum power transmission through a pipe, the friction head loss is one third of the supply head: h_f = H/3. The efficiency is then (H − H/3)/H = 66.7%.
Pipes in parallel connect the same two junctions, so they share the same head loss, while the total flow splits between them.

quiz.q: Q ratio for parallel pipes D 2:1 (same L, f)
quiz.why: For equal head loss, h_f ∝ fLQ²/D⁵ gives Q ∝ D^2.5. The ratio is 2^2.5 = 5.66, so the larger pipe carries about 5.7 times as much.
The Joukowsky formula for pressure rise from sudden closure of a valve is Δp = ρcV, where c is the speed of pressure wave in the pipe.
The Dupuit equation for an equivalent pipe uses L/D⁵, because h_f ∝ fLQ²/D⁵ for the same discharge and friction factor.

questions.q: Turbulent pipe flow Re (approx.)
questions.why: Pipe flow is turbulent for Re above about 4000. Below 2000 it is laminar, and the range between is transitional.

questions.q: Friction loss in laminar flow ∝
questions.why: For laminar flow, the Hagen–Poiseuille law gives head loss proportional to the velocity V (not V²).

questions.q: Exit loss coefficient
questions.why: At exit to a large tank, the entire velocity head V²/2g is lost, so the exit loss coefficient is K = 1.

questions.q: f for laminar Re = 1600
Re for D = 0.2 m, V = 1 m/s, ν = 10⁻⁶
questions.why: Re = VD/ν = (1 × 0.2)/10⁻⁶ = 2×10⁵, so the flow is turbulent.

questions.q: h_f ratio if V doubles (same f)
questions.why: h_f = fLV²/(2gD), so with f, L, D fixed it is proportional to V². Doubling V gives 4 times the head loss.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Parallel pipes have equal head loss.  Reason (R): They connect the same two junctions whose energy levels are fixed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. The two junctions of parallel pipes each have one energy level, so the head loss from one to the other is the same for every path. R explains A.

questions.q: Laminar Δp: μ 0.05 Pa·s, V 0.5 m/s, L 50 m, D 0.05 m
Expansion 0.05 → 0.1 m, V₁ = 4 m/s: loss
questions.why: By continuity, V₂ = V₁(A₁/A₂) = 4 × (1/4) = 1 m/s. Loss = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g = 9/19.62 ≈ 0.459 m.

questions.q: Reservoirs 15 m apart, pipe 400 m, D 0.25 m, f 0.02, K_entrance 0.5, exit 1: V
Case: A 2 km pipeline (D 0.3 m) carries 0.1 m³/s with f = 0.018. Head loss
Equivalent length of 100 m of 0.1 m pipe in terms of 0.2 m pipe
questions.why: For the same friction loss, equivalent length ∝ D⁵. 100 m of 0.1 m pipe equals 100 × (0.2/0.1)⁵ = 100 × 32 = 3200 m of 0.2 m pipe.

questions.q: Water hammer for V = 1.5 m/s, c = 1400 m/s
questions.why: Δp = ρcV = 1000 × 1400 × 1.5 = 2.1×10⁶ Pa = 2.1 MPa. This is a large pressure surge from sudden valve closure.

questions.q: Power through pipe: H = 60 m, h_f = 20 m, Q = 0.5 m³/s
Wall shear stress in laminar flow relates to Δp by
questions.why: A force balance on a fluid cylinder of length L gives Δp × πD²/4 = τ_w × πDL, so τ_w = ΔpD/(4L).

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics · Unit 4 · Dimensional analysis, boundary layer and turbomachines
courses.summary: Dimensional homogeneity, Rayleigh and Buckingham π methods, dimensionless numbers and model similitude, boundary-layer concepts (thicknesses, laminar/turbulent, separation), drag and lift, and introduction to hydraulic turbines and centrifugal pumps (heads, efficiencies, specific speed).
outcomes: Form dimensionless groups with Buckingham π
Apply Reynolds and Froude model laws
Estimate boundary-layer thickness and drag
Compute pump/turbine power, efficiency and specific speed
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Dimensional analysis and Buckingham π

scenes.text: Naval architects test a 1:25 scale model in a towing tank.
Dimensional analysis tells how to scale the results.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Dimensions M, L, T. A physically correct equation is dimensionally homogeneous.
**Buckingham π theorem:** n variables with m fundamental dimensions ⇒ n − m independent dimensionless π groups. Choose m repeating variables (geometry, flow, fluid property — e.g. D, V, ρ) that together contain all dimensions and don't form a π themselves.

steps.title: Common dimensionless numbers
steps.body:
- Reynolds Re = ρVL/μ (inertia/viscous)
- Froude Fr = V/√(gL) (inertia/gravity) — free-surface flows
- Euler Eu = Δp/(ρV²)
- Weber We = ρV²L/σ (surface tension)
- Mach Ma = V/c (compressibility)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Drag F on a sphere depends on D, V, ρ, μ: n = 5, m = 3 ⇒ 2 groups: F/(ρV²D²) = φ(ρVD/μ).

**Example 2.** Pipe pressure drop Δp = f(D, L, V, ρ, μ, ε): 7 − 3 = 4 groups: Δp/(ρV²), L/D, Re, ε/D.

**Example 3.** Dimensions of μ: [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]; of power: [ML²T⁻³].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing repeating variables that include the dependent variable.
- Choosing repeating variables that are dimensionally dependent (e.g. D and L together).
- Wrong number of groups.

activity.prompt: Variables 6, fundamental dimensions 3. Number of π groups?

quiz.why: Viscosity μ has units Pa·s = (N/m²)·s, which in base dimensions is ML⁻¹T⁻¹. The form L²T⁻¹ is for kinematic viscosity.
The Froude number is Fr = V/√(gL), the ratio of inertial to gravity forces. Mach is V/c and Reynolds is ρVL/μ.

quiz.q: Number of π groups for n = 7, m = 3
quiz.why: By the Buckingham π theorem, the number of dimensionless groups = n − m = 7 − 3 = 4, where n is the number of variables and m the number of fundamental dimensions.
Repeating variables must not include the dependent variable, because it should appear in only one π group. They should also be dimensionally independent.
The Mach number (V/c) matters when compressibility is significant, i.e. in high-speed gas flow, near or above about Mach 0.3.

lessons.title: Similitude and model laws

scenes.text: A dam spillway is tested at 1:50 scale in a lab.
Froude similarity sets the model velocity and discharge.

steps.title: Similarity
steps.body:
Geometric (shape, length ratio L_r), kinematic (velocity ratios), dynamic (force ratios equal ⇒ key π equal).
**Reynolds model law** (pipes, submerged bodies, aircraft at low Ma): (VL/ν)_m = (VL/ν)_p.
**Froude model law** (spillways, ships, open channels): V_r = √L_r, Q_r = L_r^2.5, T_r = √L_r, F_r = L_r³ (same fluid).
Distorted models use different horizontal and vertical scales (rivers).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spillway 1:50, prototype Q = 1000 m³/s ⇒ model Q = 1000/50^2.5 = 1000/17 678 = 0.0566 m³/s.

**Example 2.** Model velocity 1 m/s ⇒ prototype 1 × √50 = 7.07 m/s.

**Example 3.** Reynolds law: car 1:5 model in same air ⇒ V_m = 5V_p (often impractical — use wind tunnels with high speeds or pressurised tunnels).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Reynolds scaling for free-surface flows.
- Forgetting Q ratio exponent 2.5 (Froude).
- Expecting to satisfy Re and Fr simultaneously with the same fluid (generally impossible).

activity.prompt: Froude model 1:25, model velocity 0.8 m/s. Prototype velocity (m/s)?

quiz.why: Ship and spillway models involve a free surface, where gravity dominates. So they use Froude similarity.
With Froude scaling, V_r = √L_r and area A_r = L_r², so Q_r = V_rA_r = L_r^(1/2) × L_r² = L_r^2.5.
In pressurised pipe flow, viscous forces dominate, not gravity, so Reynolds similarity is used for the models.
Dynamic similarity needs the ratios of all the relevant forces (the π groups, such as Re and Fr) to be equal for model and prototype, along with geometric and kinematic similarity.
With Froude scaling, time ratio T_r = L_r/V_r = L_r/√L_r = √L_r.

lessons.title: Boundary layer, drag and lift

scenes.text: Dimpled golf balls fly farther than smooth ones.
Dimples trip the boundary layer to turbulence, delaying separation and cutting pressure drag.

steps.title: Boundary layer on a flat plate
steps.body:
Thickness δ (99% of U). Laminar (Blasius): δ/x = 5/√Re_x; C_f(avg) = 1.328/√Re_L. Turbulent (1/7 power law): δ/x = 0.37/Re_x^0.2; C_f = 0.074/Re_L^0.2. Transition around Re_x ≈ 5×10⁵.
Displacement thickness δ* (laminar δ/3 for linear… Blasius δ* = 1.72x/√Re_x), momentum thickness θ.
**Separation:** occurs in adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) when wall shear becomes zero ⇒ wake and pressure drag.

steps.title: Drag and lift
steps.body: F_D = C_D(½ρV²)A; F_L = C_L(½ρV²)A. Streamlined bodies: mostly skin-friction drag; bluff bodies: mostly pressure (form) drag. Sphere C_D ≈ 0.47 (subcritical); drag crisis near Re ≈ 3×10⁵ where C_D drops. Stokes' law (Re < 1): F_D = 3πμVD ⇒ terminal velocity of small particles V_t = (ρ_s − ρ)gD²/(18μ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Air (ν = 1.5×10⁻⁵) over a plate at 3 m/s, x = 1 m: Re = 2×10⁵ (laminar) ⇒ δ = 5/447 = 11.2 mm.

**Example 2.** Car C_D = 0.3, A = 2 m², 30 m/s, ρ = 1.2: F_D = 0.3 × 0.5 × 1.2 × 900 × 2 = 324 N; power = 9.7 kW.

**Example 3.** Sand grain 0.1 mm (ρ_s 2650) settling in water (μ 0.001): V_t = 1650 × 9.81 × 10⁻⁸/0.018 = 9.0 mm/s (Re ≈ 0.9, Stokes OK).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using laminar formulas beyond transition.
- Using the wrong reference area for C_D.
- Applying Stokes' law at Re ≫ 1.

activity.prompt: Car: C_D 0.32, A 2.2 m², ρ 1.2, V 25 m/s. Drag force (N, nearest whole)?

quiz.why: For laminar flow over a flat plate (Blasius solution), the boundary layer thickness is δ = 5x/√Re_x.
Separation occurs when the boundary layer moves against an adverse pressure gradient (pressure rising downstream), which slows the near-wall fluid until it reverses.
For bluff bodies, the separated wake gives a large pressure difference between the front and back, so most of the drag is pressure (form) drag, not skin friction.
Stokes' law for a sphere in creeping flow (Re < 1): drag F = 3πμVD.
Dimples trip the boundary layer into turbulence, which sticks to the ball longer and delays separation. This shrinks the wake and reduces drag.

lessons.title: Hydraulic turbines and centrifugal pumps

scenes.text: A hydro plant with 300 m head uses Pelton wheels; a low-head river plant uses Kaplan turbines.
Specific speed picks the right machine.

steps.title: Turbines
steps.body:
Power available P = ρgQH; η_o = shaft power/(ρgQH) = η_h × η_m.
Types: **Pelton** (impulse, high head, low specific speed); **Francis** (reaction, medium head); **Kaplan** (axial reaction, low head, high specific speed, adjustable blades).
Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^(5/4) (P in kW, H in m, N in rpm): Pelton ~10–35 (single jet), Francis ~60–300, Kaplan ~300–1000.
Pelton jet velocity V = C_v√(2gH); optimum bucket speed u ≈ 0.46V.

steps.title: Centrifugal pumps
steps.body: Manometric head H_m; power input = ρgQH_m/η_o. Specific speed N_s = N√Q/H^(3/4). Priming needed (displace air). **Cavitation:** local pressure below vapour pressure ⇒ bubbles collapse, damage — keep NPSH available > NPSH required. Affinity laws (same pump): Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³. Series pumps add head; parallel add flow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing turbine (P-based) and pump (Q-based) specific speeds.
- Running pumps dry (no priming).
- Ignoring NPSH ⇒ cavitation damage.

activity.prompt: Machine → typical application

quiz.why: Hydraulic power = ρgQH, the weight flow rate times head. It is the power in the water before losses.
The Pelton wheel is an impulse turbine: a high-speed jet strikes buckets at atmospheric pressure. Kaplan and Francis are reaction turbines.

quiz.q: Affinity: doubling speed multiplies head by
quiz.why: By the affinity laws, H ∝ N², so doubling the speed multiplies the head by 4 (Q ∝ N, P ∝ N³).
Cavitation is avoided by keeping the net positive suction head available (NPSH) above that required, so the pressure at the inlet stays above vapour pressure.
Kaplan turbines work at low head and high flow, which means high specific speed. Pelton wheels have the lowest.

questions.q: Reynolds number ratio expresses
questions.why: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. A large Re means inertia dominates and flow tends towards turbulence.

questions.q: Pelton turbines suit
questions.why: Pelton turbines are impulse machines used for high heads (hundreds of metres) and low flows, such as in mountain plants.

questions.q: Pumps must be primed because
questions.why: A centrifugal pump gives a pressure rise proportional to the fluid density. Air is so light that the pump cannot create enough suction, so it must be primed with water.

questions.q: Dimensions of power
questions.why: Power = force × velocity = MLT⁻² × LT⁻¹ = ML²T⁻³, or watts = J/s.

questions.q: Froude model 1:36: discharge ratio
questions.why: For Froude scaling, Q_r = L_r^2.5 = 36^2.5 = 36² × 6 = 1296 × 6 = 7776. The prototype discharge is 7776 times the model's.

questions.q: Hydro P: Q 5 m³/s, H 100 m, η 0.85
Assertion (A): Ship models are tested using Froude similarity.  Reason (R): Wave-making resistance is governed by gravity forces.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Wave-making resistance of a ship depends on gravity forces at the free surface, so the models must keep the Froude number equal. R explains A.

questions.q: BL thickness: U = 2 m/s, ν = 10⁻⁶, x = 0.5 m (laminar assumed)
questions.why: δ = 5x/√Re_x with Re_x = Ux/ν = 2 × 0.5/10⁻⁶ = 10⁶, so δ = 5 × 0.5/1000 = 2.5 mm. At Re = 10⁶ the layer would be turbulent in practice, but the question assumes laminar.

questions.q: Pump: Q 0.1 m³/s, H 40 m, η 0.8: input power
questions.why: Input power = ρgQH/η = 9810 × 0.1 × 40/0.8 = 39 240/0.8 ≈ 49 kW. Dividing by efficiency gives the larger input.

questions.q: Affinity: 1500 → 1200 rpm: power ratio
questions.why: By the affinity laws, P ∝ N³. The speed ratio is 1200/1500 = 0.8, so the power ratio is 0.8³ = 0.512.

questions.q: Case: A 1:10 model propeller in water must match Reynolds number of prototype in water. Model speed relative to prototype
questions.why: Equal Re needs V_mL_m = V_pL_p (same fluid). With the model one tenth of the size, the model speed must be 10 times higher.

questions.q: Terminal velocity (Stokes) of 0.05 mm particle (ρ_s 2600) in water (μ 0.001)
questions.why: Stokes terminal velocity v = g d²(ρ_s − ρ)/(18μ) = 9.81 × (5×10⁻⁵)² × 1600/(18 × 0.001) ≈ 2.2×10⁻³ m/s = 2.2 mm/s.

questions.q: Turbine specific speed: N 300 rpm, P 10 000 kW, H 100 m
questions.why: Specific speed N_s = N√P/H^1.25 = 300 × √10 000/100^1.25 = 300 × 100/316.2 ≈ 95, in the range of Francis turbines.

questions.q: Pelton bucket speed for H = 250 m, C_v 0.98, ratio 0.46
π groups for F = f(V, D, ρ, μ, g)
questions.why: There are 6 variables (F, V, D, ρ, μ, g) and 3 fundamental dimensions (M, L, T), so the Buckingham π theorem gives 6 − 3 = 3 groups.

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Fluid Mechanics.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Statics
steps.body:
- τ = μ du/dy; ν = μ/ρ; h_cap = 4σcos θ/(ρgd); droplet 4σ/d, bubble 8σ/d
- p = ρgh; manometer walk-through; Hg/water h = x(12.6)

- GM = I/V − BG

steps.title: Kinematics and dynamics
steps.body:
- A₁V₁ = A₂V₂; ∇·V = 0; ψ: u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x
- Bernoulli p/ρg + V²/2g + z; venturi Q = C_dA₁A₂√(2gh)/√(A₁² − A₂²); pitot √(2gh); orifice C_d a√(2gH)
- ΣF = ṁΔV; jet ρaV²; moving ρa(V − u)²

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.q: Force on vertical 2 × 2 m gate, top at surface (b 2)
quiz.why: F = ρg A h̄ = 9810 × 4 × 1 = 39.2 kN, because the centroid of a 2 m tall gate with its top at the surface is 1 m deep. The width is 2 m, so A = 2 × 2 = 4 m².

quiz.q: V₂ if D halves, V₁ = 1 m/s
quiz.why: Area ∝ D², so halving D gives a quarter of the area. Continuity gives V₂ = 4V₁ = 4 m/s.
