Case: A 3 m cantilever balcony beam (I = 5×10⁷ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa) carries 2 kN/m. Tip deflection
Rankine load: σ_c 330 MPa, A 1000 mm², λ = 100, a = 1/7500
Thin sphere d 2 m, p 1 MPa, σ_allow 80 MPa: t
questions.why: For a thin sphere, σ = pd/(4t), so t = pd/(4σ) = 1 × 2000/(4 × 80) = 6.25 mm.

questions.q: SS beam with UVL 0 → 9 kN/m over 6 m: R_A
questions.why: For a UVL from 0 to w over span L, the total load is wL/2 = 27 kN. The reaction at the zero end is wL/6 = 9 × 6/6 = 9 kN (and wL/3 = 18 kN at the heavy end).

questions.q: Strain energy in a bar of volume 10⁶ mm³ at σ = 200 MPa, E = 200 GPa
P_cr ratio fixed–pinned vs pinned–pinned
questions.why: P_cr ∝ 1/L_e². Fixed–pinned has L_e = 0.7L, so the ratio to pinned–pinned is 1/0.7² ≈ 2.04, about 2.

courses.title: Manufacturing · Unit 1 · Metal casting
courses.summary: Sand casting process, patterns and allowances, moulding sand and its properties, cores, gating system design (Bernoulli, choke, pouring time), risers and solidification time (Chvorinov's rule), casting defects, and special casting processes (die, investment, centrifugal, shell).
outcomes: Specify pattern allowances and moulding sand properties
Design gating and estimate pouring time
Size risers using Chvorinov's rule
Identify casting defects and choose special casting processes
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Patterns, allowances and moulding sand

scenes.text: Cast-iron engine blocks begin as a pattern pressed into sand.
The pattern is made slightly larger to allow for shrinkage.

steps.title: Patterns and allowances
steps.body:
Pattern materials: wood, metal, plastic, wax (investment). Types: solid, split, match-plate, cope-and-drag, loose-piece, sweep, skeleton.
Allowances: **shrinkage** (e.g. cast iron ~1%, steel ~2%, aluminium ~1.3%), **draft** (taper for withdrawal, 1–3°), **machining** (finish), **distortion** (camber), **shake** (negative — mould enlarges when rapped).

steps.title: Moulding sand
steps.body: Silica sand + clay binder (bentonite) + water (green sand) + additives (coal dust, cereal). Properties: permeability (lets gases escape), refractoriness, green and dry strength, cohesiveness, adhesiveness, collapsibility, flowability. AFS grain fineness number characterises grain size. Cores (oil/CO₂-bonded sand) form internal cavities; supported by core prints and chaplets.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Steel casting 500 mm long, shrinkage 2%: pattern = 510 mm (before machining/draft).

**Example 2.** A 200 mm deep pocket with 2° draft: wall offset = 200 tan 2° = 7.0 mm.

**Example 3.** Low permeability sand ⇒ gas trapped ⇒ blowholes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding shake allowance (it is negative).
- Forgetting cores need venting.
- Using too much water (lower strength, steam defects).

activity.prompt: Aluminium casting 400 mm, shrinkage 1.3%. Pattern length (mm, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: Draft allowance is a slight taper on vertical faces of the pattern, so it can be withdrawn from the sand mould without breaking the mould edges.
Shake allowance is a negative allowance: the pattern is rapped to loosen it, which enlarges the mould cavity, so the pattern is made slightly smaller.
Permeability is the ability of the mould sand to let gases escape. Without it, trapped gas causes blowholes in the casting.
Chaplets are metal supports that hold cores in place in the mould cavity, and they melt into the casting.
Green sand is mainly silica sand with bentonite clay as the binder, plus water, for sand moulds.

lessons.title: Gating system design

scenes.text: Molten metal must fill the mould fast enough not to freeze, but smoothly enough not to erode sand.
Gating design uses Bernoulli and continuity.

steps.title: Elements and equations
steps.body:
Pouring basin → sprue → sprue well → runner → ingates. Sprue tapers to avoid aspiration: A₁/A₂ = √(h₂/h₁).
Velocity at sprue base V = √(2gh) (with C_d for losses). Pouring time t = V_cavity/(A_choke × V) (top gating). Bottom gating: t = (A_m/A_g)(√(2/g))(√h_t − √(h_t − h_m)).
Gating ratio (sprue : runner : ingate) e.g. 1:2:2 (unpressurised, less turbulence — aluminium) or 1:0.75:0.5 (pressurised — iron). Choke = smallest area controlling flow.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sprue height 200 mm: V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.2) = 1.98 m/s.

**Example 2.** Cavity 0.002 m³, choke area 400 mm² (4×10⁻⁴ m²), V = 1.98 m/s: t = 0.002/(4×10⁻⁴ × 1.98) = 2.53 s.

**Example 3.** Sprue top area 600 mm² at h₁ = 50 mm (basin depth), bottom at h₂ = 250 mm: A₂ = 600√(50/250) = 268 mm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Straight (untapered) sprues cause air aspiration.
- Ignoring the choke location when computing time.
- Very high velocities causing sand erosion and inclusions.

activity.prompt: Sprue height 0.3 m. Ideal velocity at sprue base (m/s, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: A tapered sprue keeps the liquid metal in contact with its walls as the velocity rises downward. This prevents low pressure, which would aspirate (suck in) air.
The choke is the smallest cross-sectional area in the gating system. It controls the flow rate of the metal into the mould.
Unpressurised gating (with area increasing downstream) reduces turbulence and oxide formation, which suits metals like aluminium that form oxide films readily.
By Bernoulli, metal falling a height h reaches the base of the sprue at velocity v = √(2gh).
By continuity, volume = flow rate × time, so pouring time = cavity volume/(choke area × velocity).

lessons.title: Solidification and riser design

scenes.text: A cast part shows a hollow shrinkage pipe at its thickest section.
A riser must freeze after the casting to feed it.

steps.title: Chvorinov's rule
steps.body:
Solidification time t = C(V/A)ⁿ, n ≈ 2 (V/A = modulus). Riser must solidify later than the casting: (V/A)_riser ≥ 1.2(V/A)_casting typically.
For a cylindrical riser with H = D (side + top cooling, base on casting): V = πD³/4 and cooling area A = πD² (side) + πD²/4 (top) = 1.25πD² ⇒ V/A = D/5 (if the bottom also cools: D/6).
Shrinkage stages: liquid, solidification, solid contraction (pattern allowance covers solid only). Directional solidification towards the riser; chills accelerate cooling; exothermic sleeves and insulating toppings slow risers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cube 100 mm: V/A = 100/6 = 16.67 mm. Plate 200 × 200 × 20: V/A = 800 000/(2 × 40 000 + 4 × 4000) = 800 000/96 000 = 8.33 mm ⇒ the cube takes 4× longer (ratio²).

**Example 2.** C = 2 s/mm² for a steel: cube t = 2 × 16.67² = 556 s.

**Example 3.** Riser for the cube (sides + top exposed, H = D): need D/5 ≥ 1.2 × 16.67 = 20 ⇒ D ≥ 100 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V/A of riser equal to casting (it must be larger).
- Forgetting that the riser's contact face does not cool.
- Placing risers far from heavy sections.

activity.prompt: Chvorinov: C = 1.5 s/mm², V/A = 10 mm, n = 2. Solidification time (s)?

quiz.why: Chvorinov's rule says solidification time t = C(V/A)². It grows with the square of the volume-to-surface-area ratio (modulus).
A riser must solidify after the casting so it can keep feeding liquid metal to make up for shrinkage until the casting is solid.
Chills (metal inserts) take heat quickly, so local solidification is faster. They help produce directional solidification towards the riser.
For a cube, V/A = a³/(6a²) = a/6 = 60/6 = 10 mm.
Shrinkage allowance makes up for solid contraction after solidification. Liquid and solidification shrinkage are made up by risers.

lessons.title: Casting defects and special casting processes

scenes.text: Jet-engine turbine blades are made by investment casting with ceramic shells.
Process choice decides surface finish, accuracy and defects.

steps.title: Defects and causes
steps.body:
- **Blowholes/porosity:** trapped gas — low permeability, moisture, poor venting.
- **Shrinkage cavity:** inadequate feeding.
- **Cold shut / misrun:** metal too cold or slow pouring — streams fail to fuse / mould not filled.
- **Hot tears:** restraint during cooling — poor collapsibility.
- **Inclusions, scabs, swells, mismatch (shift), fins.**

steps.title: Special processes
steps.body:
- **Die casting** (pressure, metal dies; Al/Zn/Mg; high rate, thin walls, good finish).
- **Investment (lost-wax):** wax pattern + ceramic shell; complex, precise parts (blades, jewellery, implants).
- **Centrifugal:** pipes, liners — dense outer structure.
- **Shell moulding:** resin-bonded sand shells — good finish.
- **Continuous casting:** billets/slabs in steel plants.
- **Permanent mould (gravity die).**

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Defect: rounded smooth cavities near the top surface ⇒ blowholes ⇒ improve venting and reduce moisture.

**Example 2.** Centrifugal casting speed: G-factor = ω²R/g; for R = 0.2 m and G = 60: ω = √(60 × 9.81/0.2) = 54.2 rad/s ≈ 518 rpm.

**Example 3.** High-volume aluminium gearbox housings ⇒ pressure die casting.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing cold shut (fusion failure) with hot tear (cracking during cooling).
- Using die casting for high-melting steels (die life too short).
- Ignoring the cost of dies for small batches.

activity.prompt: Defect → likely cause

quiz.why: Lost-wax casting is investment casting. A wax pattern is coated with ceramic and then melted out, leaving a precise mould.
Pipes are commonly made by centrifugal casting. The mould is spun, and the centrifugal force pushes metal against the wall, giving dense walls with no core.
Die casting uses permanent metal dies and needs metals with low melting points, such as aluminium, zinc and magnesium alloys.
A misrun happens when the metal solidifies before the cavity is filled, due to poor fluidity or low pouring temperature.
The G-factor in centrifugal casting is the ratio of centrifugal acceleration to gravity: G = ω²R/g.

questions.q: Draft is provided on
questions.why: Draft is a taper given to the vertical faces of a pattern so it can be drawn from the mould without damaging it.

questions.q: Investment casting uses
questions.why: Investment (lost-wax) casting uses a wax pattern, which is melted out of the ceramic shell before pouring.

questions.q: Blowholes are caused by
questions.why: Blowholes are cavities caused by gas trapped in the casting, often from moisture, or poor venting of the mould.

questions.q: Pattern for 300 mm steel part (2% shrinkage)
questions.why: Pattern size = casting size × (1 + shrinkage) = 300 × 1.02 = 306 mm.

questions.q: V/A of a sphere of diameter 60 mm
questions.why: For a sphere, V/A = (πD³/6)/(πD²) = D/6 = 60/6 = 10 mm.

questions.q: Velocity at sprue base for h = 0.5 m
Assertion (A): A riser must have a higher modulus (V/A) than the casting section it feeds.  Reason (R): By Chvorinov's rule, higher modulus means longer solidification time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. By Chvorinov's rule, solidification time grows with the modulus V/A, so a riser with a higher modulus freezes later and can feed the casting. R explains A.

questions.q: Pouring time: cavity 0.003 m³, choke 500 mm², V = 2 m/s
Solidification time ratio of two cubes 50 mm and 100 mm
questions.why: t ∝ (V/A)² and for cubes V/A = a/6. The sizes ratio is 1:2, so the times are in ratio 1:4.

questions.q: Tapered sprue: top 400 mm² at 40 mm head, bottom at 160 mm head
questions.why: By continuity and Bernoulli, area ∝ 1/√h, so A_bottom = 400 × √(40/160) = 400 × 0.5 = 200 mm².

questions.q: Case: Steel castings show hot tears at junctions. Best remedy
questions.why: Hot tears form when the casting is restrained as it contracts at hot spots. Improving mould collapsibility and adding fillets (to avoid sharp junctions) relieves the restraint.
options: improve mould collapsibility and add fillets

questions.q: Riser (H = D, top+side cooling) to feed a section of modulus 12.5 mm with factor 1.2
questions.why: For a cylindrical riser with H = D cooling from top and side, V/A = D/5. For the riser modulus 1.2 × 12.5 = 15 mm, D = 5 × 15 = 75 mm.

questions.q: Centrifugal casting: R = 0.15 m, G-factor 80 — speed
Chvorinov C = 2 s/mm²: plate 100 × 100 × 10 mm, t
Gating ratio 1:2:2 is
questions.why: A gating ratio of 1:2:2 (sprue:runner:ingate) has increasing total area, so the metal flows in with low velocity and without back pressure. That makes it unpressurised.

courses.title: Manufacturing · Unit 2 · Welding and joining processes
courses.summary: Classification of welding, arc welding (SMAW, GMAW/MIG, GTAW/TIG, SAW), arc characteristics and heat input, gas welding and flames, resistance welding (spot, seam), solid-state processes (friction, ultrasonic), welding defects and inspection, soldering and brazing, and safety.
outcomes: Compare arc, gas, resistance and solid-state welding
Compute heat input and resistance-welding heat
Identify weld defects and inspection methods
Distinguish welding, brazing and soldering
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Arc welding processes

scenes.text: Shipyards weld kilometres of steel plate with submerged-arc and MIG processes.
An electric arc at about 5000+ °C melts the joint.

steps.title: Processes
steps.body:
- **SMAW (stick):** flux-coated consumable electrode; versatile, field work.
- **GMAW/MIG (and MAG):** continuous wire, shielding gas (Ar/CO₂); fast, semi-automatic.
- **GTAW/TIG:** non-consumable tungsten electrode, inert gas, filler optional; high quality, thin sheets, Al/stainless.
- **SAW:** arc under granular flux; thick plates, high deposition, flat position.
- **Plasma arc, electroslag** for special cases.
DCEN (straight polarity) — more heat in the workpiece (deeper penetration, TIG on steel); DCEP (reverse) — cleaning action (Al with AC/DCEP), more heat at the electrode.

steps.title: Heat input
steps.body: Heat input per unit length H = ηVI/v (η = arc efficiency: SAW ~0.9–0.99, SMAW/MIG ~0.7–0.85, TIG ~0.6–0.75). Higher heat input ⇒ wider heat-affected zone (HAZ), slower cooling.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** SMAW at 25 V, 200 A, 5 mm/s, η = 0.8: H = 0.8 × 25 × 200/5 = 800 J/mm.

**Example 2.** Doubling travel speed halves heat input (400 J/mm) — narrower HAZ.

**Example 3.** About 10 J/mm³ is needed to melt steel; with 50% melting efficiency the weld bead cross-section ≈ 800 × 0.5/10 = 40 mm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a consumable-electrode process name for TIG.
- Ignoring arc efficiency in heat input.
- Welding without shielding/PPE — UV burns ('arc eye'), fumes: always use a helmet with the right filter shade and ventilation.

activity.prompt: Arc: V = 20 V, I = 150 A, travel 4 mm/s, η = 0.75. Heat input (J/mm)?

quiz.why: TIG (GTAW) uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with an inert gas shield. Filler is added separately.

quiz.q: Process with arc hidden under flux
quiz.why: In submerged arc welding (SAW), the arc burns under a blanket of granular flux, so it is not visible.
DC electrode negative (DCEN, straight polarity) puts more heat on the workpiece, giving deeper penetration. DCEP heats the electrode more.
Heat input per unit length = ηVI/v, where v is the travel speed. It controls the size of the weld pool and HAZ.
AC TIG for aluminium gives a cleaning action during the positive half-cycle (which removes the oxide film) and penetration in the negative half-cycle.

lessons.title: Gas welding and resistance welding

scenes.text: A car body has thousands of spot welds made by robots in seconds.
Heat comes from the current flowing through the contact resistance.

steps.title: Gas welding (oxy-acetylene)
steps.body: C₂H₂ + O₂; flame ~3200 °C at the inner cone. Flames: **neutral** (1:1, most metals), **oxidising** (excess O₂ — brass, bronze), **carburising/reducing** (excess C₂H₂ — high-carbon steel, hard-facing). Also oxy-fuel cutting of steel.

steps.title: Resistance welding
steps.body: Heat H = I²Rt (Joule). Spot, seam (rollers — leak-tight joints), projection, flash and butt welding. Short times (0.1–0.5 s), very high currents (5–20 kA), low voltage. Electrodes: copper alloys (high conductivity, water-cooled).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spot weld: I = 10 kA, R = 100 µΩ, t = 0.2 s: H = 10⁸ × 10⁻⁴ × 0.2 = 2000 J.

**Example 2.** If only 60% of that goes into the nugget and steel needs ≈ 10 J/mm³ to melt: nugget volume ≈ 120 mm³.

**Example 3.** Neutral flame for mild steel; oxidising for brass (prevents zinc fuming).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a carburising flame on mild steel (adds carbon, brittle).
- Thinking resistance welding needs filler metal (it doesn't).
- Acetylene safety: never use above ~1 bar (15 psi) — explosive; use flashback arrestors.

activity.prompt: Flame type

quiz.why: Heat in resistance welding is by Joule heating, Q = I²Rt, using the resistance at the joint.
Seam welding is a continuous form of resistance welding using rotating roller electrodes, to make leak-tight seams.
The oxy-acetylene flame reaches about 3200 °C at the tip of the inner cone, the hottest of the common gas flames.
Spot welding electrodes are copper alloys, since they have high electrical and thermal conductivity, and they are water-cooled to avoid melting.

quiz.q: Spot weld heat: 8 kA, 150 µΩ, 0.25 s

lessons.title: Solid-state welding, defects and inspection

scenes.text: Battery packs join aluminium and copper tabs — hard by fusion welding.
Ultrasonic and friction welding join them without melting.

steps.title: Solid-state processes
steps.body: Friction welding (rotary, linear), **friction stir welding** (non-consumable rotating tool; Al ship decks, aircraft panels), ultrasonic (thin foils, wires), explosive (cladding), diffusion bonding, forge welding. No melting ⇒ fewer solidification defects, dissimilar metals possible.

steps.title: Defects and inspection
steps.body:
Defects: porosity, slag inclusion, incomplete fusion, incomplete penetration, undercut, overlap, cracks (hot/cold/hydrogen), distortion, residual stresses.
Remedies: clean joints, dry electrodes (low-hydrogen), correct current/speed, preheat for high-carbon steels, post-weld heat treatment.
Inspection (NDT): visual, dye penetrant (surface cracks), magnetic particle (ferromagnetic, near-surface), ultrasonic (internal), radiography (X/γ — internal volumetric defects), eddy current.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cracks found hours after welding high-strength steel ⇒ hydrogen-induced cold cracking ⇒ use low-hydrogen electrodes, preheat.

**Example 2.** Aluminium aircraft panels ⇒ friction stir welding (no melting, low distortion).

**Example 3.** Internal porosity check in a pressure vessel weld ⇒ radiography or ultrasonic testing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using magnetic particle testing on aluminium (non-ferromagnetic).
- Skipping preheat on high-carbon/alloy steels.
- Confusing undercut (groove at toe) with lack of penetration (root).

activity.prompt: NDT method → best for

quiz.q: Friction stir welding melts the metal?
quiz.why: Friction stir welding is a solid-state process. A rotating tool softens the metal by friction and stirs it, but the metal does not melt.
Hydrogen cracking needs hydrogen, a hard microstructure and stress. Low-hydrogen electrodes and preheating (slower cooling) lower these risks.
Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic materials, because it needs the part to be magnetised so a flaw disturbs the field and holds the particles.
Undercut is a groove melted into the base metal along the toe of a weld and not filled, which can act as a stress concentration.
options: a groove at the weld toe

quiz.why: Ultrasonic welding uses high-frequency vibration to join thin foils, wires and sheets, without much heat.

lessons.title: Soldering, brazing and adhesive bonding

scenes.text: Electronics are joined by soldering at about 220 °C.
Plumbers braze copper pipes at much higher temperatures — the base metal never melts in either.

steps.title: Differences
steps.body:
- **Welding:** base metals melt (fusion) or bond in solid state.
- **Brazing:** filler melts above 450 °C (below base metal melting), flows by capillary action (brass, silver alloys); strong joints.
- **Soldering:** filler melts below 450 °C (Sn–Ag–Cu lead-free solders ~217–220 °C; traditional Sn–Pb ~183 °C); electronics.
Flux removes oxides and promotes wetting. Joint clearance small (0.025–0.15 mm) for capillary flow.
**Adhesive bonding:** epoxies, cyanoacrylates — dissimilar materials, distributes stress; limited temperature resistance.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Copper water pipes ⇒ brazing (or soldering for low-temperature plumbing) with capillary fittings.

**Example 2.** Lap length for a brazed joint in shear to match the base strip strength: L = σ_t t/τ_filler; σ_t = 300 MPa, t = 2 mm, τ = 100 MPa ⇒ L = 6 mm.

**Example 3.** Lead-free solder required for consumer electronics in many markets (RoHS rules).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling brazing a welding process (base metal doesn't melt).
- Too large a joint gap (capillary action fails).
- Breathing flux fumes — ventilate and avoid lead exposure.

statements.s: In brazing, the base metal melts.
Soldering uses fillers melting below 450 °C.
Flux removes oxides and helps wetting.
Large gaps help capillary flow.

quiz.why: By definition, brazing uses a filler metal that melts above 450 °C but below the melting point of the base metals. Below 450 °C it is soldering.
Typical lead-free (tin–silver–copper) solders melt around 217–220 °C, which is higher than older tin–lead solders (about 183 °C).

quiz.q: Filler flows into the joint by
quiz.why: In brazing and soldering, molten filler is drawn into the narrow gap between close-fitting parts by capillary action, provided it wets the surfaces.

quiz.q: Lap length for σ 250 MPa, t 3 mm, τ 75 MPa
quiz.why: Equal strength of plate and joint: σ × t = τ × L, so L = σt/τ = 250 × 3/75 = 10 mm.
Adhesives are polymers, so they lose strength at higher temperatures. They can join dissimilar materials and spread the stress, so those are not limitations.

questions.q: Non-consumable electrode process
questions.why: TIG uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode. SAW, MIG and SMAW (stick) electrodes are consumed and become the filler metal.

questions.q: Spot welding is a type of
questions.why: Spot welding joins sheets by heat from electrical resistance at a point, so it is a form of resistance welding.

questions.q: Flame for mild steel
questions.why: A neutral flame (equal oxygen and acetylene) is used for mild steel, as it neither adds carbon nor oxidises the metal.

questions.q: Heat input: 30 V, 250 A, 6 mm/s, η 0.9
Spot weld: 12 kA, 80 µΩ, 0.3 s
Internal porosity best detected by
questions.why: Internal porosity is a volume defect. Radiography (X-ray or gamma) sees through the weld, while dye penetrant and visual only find surface defects.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Friction stir welding is suitable for aluminium alloys that are hard to fusion weld.  Reason (R): It joins metal in the solid state without melting, avoiding solidification cracking.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. Many aluminium alloys crack when fusion welded as they solidify. Friction stir welding stays below the melting point, so there is no solidification cracking. R explains A.

questions.q: Halving current (same V, speed, η) changes heat input to
questions.why: Heat input is ηVI/v, linear in current. Halving I halves the heat input, with V, speed and efficiency constant.

questions.q: Cold cracking in high-strength steel is linked to
questions.why: Cold (hydrogen-induced) cracking occurs in the HAZ of high-strength steels when hydrogen, a hard microstructure and residual stress are present together.

questions.q: Brazed lap length: σ 400 MPa, t 1.5 mm, τ 120 MPa
questions.why: For equal strength, σt = τL, so L = 400 × 1.5/120 = 5 mm.

questions.q: Case: A fabricator must weld 40 mm thick steel plates in the flat position at high deposition rate. Best process
questions.why: Submerged arc welding gives very high deposition rates and deep penetration, which suits thick plates (40 mm) in the flat position. TIG is too slow, and soldering is too weak.

questions.q: Case: Welding thin (1 mm) stainless steel sheets for food equipment with best finish
questions.why: TIG gives precise, clean, low-spatter welds on thin stainless steel, which gives the best finish for food equipment.

questions.q: Energy to melt 50 mm³ of steel at 10 J/mm³ with 25% process efficiency (energy supplied)
questions.why: Energy needed in the metal = 50 × 10 = 500 J. At 25% efficiency, the energy supplied = 500/0.25 = 2000 J.

questions.q: Spot weld nugget heat needed 3000 J with R = 120 µΩ, t = 0.25 s: current
Magnetic particle inspection on austenitic stainless steel welds
questions.why: Austenitic stainless steel is non-magnetic, so magnetic particle inspection does not work. Dye penetrant or radiography is used instead.

courses.title: Manufacturing · Unit 3 · Metal forming
courses.summary: Hot and cold working, recrystallisation, flow stress and true strain, rolling (draft, roll force, maximum draft), forging (open/closed die, forging force), extrusion and wire drawing (reduction, forces), and sheet-metal operations (shearing, blanking/punching force, clearance, bending, deep drawing).
outcomes: Distinguish hot and cold working using recrystallisation temperature
Compute true strain, draft and roll-force estimates
Estimate forging, extrusion and drawing loads
Compute blanking force, clearance and deep-drawing limits
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Hot and cold working; true stress and strain

scenes.text: Bend a paper clip back and forth and it gets harder, then snaps.
That is strain hardening — hot working avoids it by recrystallising as it goes.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Recrystallisation temperature ≈ 0.4–0.5 T_m (K). **Hot working** above it (low forces, no strain hardening, poorer finish/tolerance, scale). **Cold working** below it (strain hardening, better finish and accuracy, higher forces, reduced ductility). Warm working in between.
True strain ε = ln(L/L₀) = ln(A₀/A); flow stress σ_f = Kεⁿ (n = strain-hardening exponent). Volume constancy in plastic deformation: A₀L₀ = AL.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Lead (T_m ≈ 600 K): recrystallisation ≈ 240–300 K ⇒ room-temperature working of lead is hot working!

**Example 2.** Bar from 50 mm to 40 mm dia: ε = ln(2500/1600) = 0.446.

**Example 3.** K = 500 MPa, n = 0.2 at ε = 0.446: σ_f = 500 × 0.446^0.2 = 425 MPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using engineering strain for large deformations.
- Forgetting temperatures in kelvin for 0.4T_m.
- Assuming hot working gives better surface finish.

activity.prompt: True strain for reducing a rod area from 400 mm² to 200 mm² (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Hot working is done above the recrystallisation temperature, so new strain-free grains form as the metal deforms and it does not strain-harden.
Cold working, below the recrystallisation temperature, raises the dislocation density and so the strength and hardness: strain hardening.
True strain is ε = ln(L/L₀), the sum of small increments dL/L. Engineering strain is (L − L₀)/L₀.
In plastic deformation, volume stays constant, as metals are essentially incompressible when yielding.
Cold working gives better dimensional accuracy and finish than hot working, because there is no scale and little thermal contraction.

lessons.title: Rolling

scenes.text: A steel mill reduces a 200 mm slab to a 2 mm sheet through many roll passes.
Friction pulls the metal into the roll gap — up to a maximum draft.

steps.title: Rolling relations
steps.body:
Draft Δh = h₀ − h_f. Maximum draft Δh_max = μ²R (R = roll radius, μ = friction coefficient). Bite angle condition μ ≥ tan α.
Projected contact length L ≈ √(RΔh). Roll force (approx.) F = σ̄_f w L (σ̄_f = average flow stress). Torque per roll T = F L/2; power (two rolls) P = 2πNFL/60 (approx.).
Neutral point: roll and strip speeds equal; forward slip beyond it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R = 250 mm, μ = 0.12: Δh_max = 0.0144 × 250 = 3.6 mm.

**Example 2.** Strip 300 mm wide from 25 to 22 mm, R = 250 mm, σ̄_f = 180 MPa: L = √(250 × 3) = 27.4 mm; F = 180 × 300 × 27.4 = 1.48 MN.

**Example 3.** Torque per roll = 1.48×10⁶ × 0.0274/2 = 20.3 kN·m; at 50 rpm both rolls: P = 2 × 2π × 50 × 20.3×10³/60 = 213 kW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter instead of radius in μ²R.
- Forgetting both rolls in power.
- Too large a draft ⇒ the strip won't be drawn in (skidding).

activity.prompt: Maximum draft: μ = 0.1, roll radius 300 mm (mm)?

quiz.why: For rolling, the strip is drawn in if μ ≥ tanα, which gives the maximum draft Δh_max = μ²R.
The projected contact length in rolling is L = √(RΔh), from the geometry of the roll arc.
At the neutral point in rolling, the strip speed equals the roll surface speed. Before it the strip is slower, and after it the strip is faster.
options: strip and roll speeds are equal

quiz.why: Maximum draft is μ²R, so a larger roll radius allows a bigger reduction per pass. But it increases the contact length and so the roll force.
Hot rolling oxidises the surface, giving scale, and thermal contraction on cooling makes the dimensions less accurate than cold rolling.

lessons.title: Forging, extrusion and wire drawing

scenes.text: Crankshafts are forged for strength; copper wires are drawn through dies.
Grain flow follows the shape in forging — tougher parts.

steps.title: Forging
steps.body:
Open-die (simple shapes, large parts), closed/impression-die (flash), upsetting, coining. Forged parts have continuous grain flow ⇒ better fatigue strength.
Forging force (cylinder, with friction): F = σ_f A (1 + 2μr/(3h)) (r = radius, h = height).

steps.title: Extrusion and drawing
steps.body:
Extrusion: direct (forward), indirect (backward), impact, hydrostatic. Extrusion ratio R = A₀/A_f; ideal pressure p = σ̄_f ln R (real higher due to friction: Johnson's p = σ̄_f(a + b ln R), a ≈ 0.8, b ≈ 1.2–1.5).
Wire drawing: stress σ_d = σ̄_f ln(A₀/A_f) (ideal); must be below σ_f of the drawn wire ⇒ max ideal reduction per pass: ln(A₀/A_f) = 1 ⇒ 63% reduction (practically ~30–45%).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Upsetting Ø50 × 50 mm to 25 mm height: final r = 35.36 mm; σ_f = 300 MPa, μ = 0.2: A = 3927 mm²; F = 300 × 3927 × (1 + 2 × 0.2 × 35.36/(3 × 25)) = 1.178 MN × 1.189 = 1.40 MN.

**Example 2.** Extrusion 100 → 50 mm dia: R = 4; ideal p = σ̄_f ln 4 = 1.386 σ̄_f; with σ̄_f = 150 MPa ⇒ 208 MPa.

**Example 3.** Wire 5 → 4 mm: ln(25/16) = 0.446 ⇒ σ_d = 0.446 σ̄_f — feasible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using initial area for forging force at the end of the stroke.
- Ignoring friction and redundant work (ideal estimates are low).
- Excessive reduction per pass in drawing ⇒ wire breaks.

activity.prompt: Extrusion ratio 8, average flow stress 100 MPa. Ideal extrusion pressure (MPa, 1 decimal)?

quiz.q: Forged parts are strong due to
quiz.why: Forging gives a continuous grain flow that follows the part's shape, which adds strength and toughness, unlike casting or machining from bar.
The ideal extrusion pressure (no friction) is p = σ̄_f ln R, where R = A₀/A_f is the extrusion ratio.

quiz.q: Max ideal reduction in wire drawing per pass
quiz.why: In ideal wire drawing, σ_d = σ̄_f ln(A₀/A). With σ_d at most equal to σ̄_f, ln(A₀/A) ≤ 1, so A₀/A ≤ e, and the maximum reduction is 1 − 1/e ≈ 63%.
In indirect (backward) extrusion, the billet stays still relative to the container and the die moves. There is no relative sliding, so friction is lower.
options: container and billet move together; less friction

quiz.why: Flash forms in closed-die forging. Excess metal squeezes out between the die halves, and also helps fill the die cavity.

lessons.title: Sheet-metal operations

scenes.text: A press punches thousands of washers per hour from steel strip.
Blanking force and die clearance decide tool size and edge quality.

steps.title: Shearing
steps.body:
Blanking (keep the piece) vs punching/piercing (keep the strip). Force F = L t τ_s (L = cut perimeter, τ_s ≈ 0.7–0.8 UTS). Clearance per side c ≈ k t (k ≈ 0.03–0.1 depending on material).
Blanking: die = blank size, punch = die − 2c. Punching: punch = hole size, die = punch + 2c.
Shear on punch (angled) reduces peak force.

steps.title: Bending and deep drawing
steps.body:
Bending: minimum bend radius ∝ t (depends on ductility); springback (more for high strength, large R/t) — compensate by overbending. Bend allowance BA = α(R + kt) (α in radians, k ≈ 0.33–0.5).
Deep drawing: limiting drawing ratio LDR = D_blank/d_punch ≈ 2; blank diameter for a cup (no flange) D = √(d² + 4dh); blank holder prevents wrinkling; drawing force F ≈ πd t UTS (D/d − 0.7).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Washer: outer Ø40, hole Ø20, t = 2 mm, τ_s = 300 MPa. Blanking F = π × 40 × 2 × 300 = 75.4 kN; punching F = 37.7 kN.

**Example 2.** Clearance 5% of t = 0.1 mm per side: blanking die 40.00, punch 39.80 mm; piercing punch 20.00, die 20.20 mm.

**Example 3.** Cup d = 50, h = 40: D = √(2500 + 8000) = 102.5 mm ⇒ D/d = 2.05 ⇒ needs two draws (LDR ≈ 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting clearance on the wrong tool (die for blanking, punch side for piercing).
- Using UTS instead of shear strength.
- Ignoring springback in bending.

activity.prompt: Blank a 50 mm square (perimeter 200 mm) from 3 mm sheet, τ = 250 MPa. Force (kN)?

quiz.why: Blanking force F = L × t × τ_s, the cutting perimeter times the thickness times the shear strength, which is the shear area times τ.

quiz.q: In blanking, clearance is applied to
quiz.why: In blanking, the die opening is made to the blank size and the punch is smaller (clearance on the punch). In punching holes it is the other way round.
The limiting drawing ratio (blank diameter/punch diameter) for a single draw is typically about 2. Beyond it the cup tears.
Springback is the elastic recovery after bending. It is larger for high-yield-strength materials and for larger bend radius to thickness ratios.

quiz.q: Blank diameter of cup d 40, h 30
quiz.why: For a cup, equal surface area gives blank D = √(d² + 4dh) = √(1600 + 4 × 40 × 30) = √6400 = 80 mm.

questions.q: Recrystallisation temperature ≈
questions.why: The recrystallisation temperature is typically 0.4 to 0.5 of the absolute melting point T_m. Hot working is above it.

questions.q: Wire drawing is
questions.why: In wire drawing, the wire is pulled through a die, which reduces its diameter. The material has to be in tension, so pushing would buckle it.

questions.q: Blanking: useful part is
questions.why: In blanking, the piece punched out is the useful part, and the remaining strip is scrap. In piercing, the slug is the scrap.

questions.q: Max draft for μ 0.15, R 400 mm
True strain for L 100 → 150 mm
Punching force: hole Ø25, t 4, τ 300 MPa
questions.why: F = π d t τ = π × 25 × 4 × 300 ≈ 94 200 N = 94.2 kN. It is the shear area (perimeter × thickness) times the shear strength.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cold-worked parts have better surface finish than hot-worked parts.  Reason (R): No oxide scale forms at low temperatures.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. At low temperatures, no oxide scale forms, so the surface stays smooth and bright. In hot working, scale roughens it. R explains A.

questions.q: Rolling contact length R 300, Δh 3 mm
Flow stress K 600, n 0.25 at ε = 0.5
Roll force: w 200 mm, L 20 mm, σ̄ 200 MPa
questions.why: Roll force = σ̄ × w × L = 200 × 200 × 20 = 800 000 N = 0.8 MN, using the projected contact area (w × L).

questions.q: Case: A 1.5 mm steel strip (τ 350 MPa) is blanked into Ø60 discs. Press capacity needed with 20% margin
questions.why: F = π d t τ = π × 60 × 1.5 × 350 ≈ 98.96 kN. With a 20% margin: 98.96 × 1.2 ≈ 119 kN of press capacity.

questions.q: Upsetting force: σ_f 250 MPa, final A 2000 mm², μ 0.1, r 25, h 20
questions.why: Ideal force = σ_f × A = 250 × 2000 = 0.5 MN. Friction raises it by the factor (1 + 2μr/(3h)) = 1 + 2 × 0.1 × 25/60 = 1.083, so F ≈ 0.542 MN.

questions.q: Number of draws for cup d 40, h 60 (LDR 2)
questions.why: The blank D = √(d² + 4dh) = √(1600 + 9600) = 105.8 mm. D/d = 2.65, which is more than the limiting ratio of 2, so two or more draws are needed.

questions.q: Ideal drawing stress ratio σ_d/σ̄_f for 6 → 5 mm wire
questions.why: Ideal drawing stress ratio = ln(A₀/A) = ln(6²/5²) = ln(1.44) ≈ 0.365. It must stay below 1.

questions.q: Punch diameter for piercing a Ø30 hole, clearance 0.15 mm per side
questions.why: When piercing a hole, the hole size is set by the punch, so the punch is 30.00 mm. The die is larger by the clearance on both sides: 30 + 2 × 0.15 = 30.30 mm.

lessons.title: Mechanics of orthogonal cutting

scenes.text: A lathe peels long curly chips off a steel shaft.
Chip thickness reveals the shear angle and cutting forces.

steps.title: Relations
steps.body:
Chip thickness ratio r = t₁/t₂ (< 1). Shear angle tan φ = r cos α/(1 − r sin α) (α = rake angle).
Merchant's theory: 2φ + β − α = 90° (β = friction angle, μ = tan β).
Forces: F_c (cutting), F_t (thrust). Friction force F = F_c sin α + F_t cos α; normal N = F_c cos α − F_t sin α; μ = F/N.
Shear force F_s = F_c cos φ − F_t sin φ; shear stress τ = F_s/A_s with A_s = bt₁/sin φ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inverting the chip ratio (t₁/t₂, not t₂/t₁).
- Using degrees inconsistently in trig functions.
- Assuming Merchant's equation is exact (it's an idealisation).

activity.prompt: Chip ratio r = 0.5, rake α = 0°. Shear angle φ (degrees, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The chip thickness ratio r = t₁/t₂ (uncut thickness/chip thickness). Since the chip is thicker than the uncut layer, r is below 1.
Merchant's relation (minimum energy): 2φ + β − α = 90°, where φ is the shear angle, β the friction angle and α the rake angle.
A larger rake angle makes the cutting easier: the shear angle rises, the shear plane gets shorter, so the forces and power fall.

quiz.q: Friction coefficient on the tool face
quiz.why: The coefficient of friction on the tool face is μ = F/N, the ratio of the friction force to the normal force there.

quiz.q: Orthogonal cutting means the edge is
quiz.why: In orthogonal cutting, the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity, giving a simple 2-D plane strain model.

lessons.title: Cutting power, tool materials and tool life

scenes.text: A shop switches from HSS tools to carbide inserts and quadruples cutting speed.
Taylor's equation predicts how long each tool lasts.

steps.title: Power and specific energy
steps.body: Cutting power P = F_c V. Material removal rate (turning) MRR = V f d (f feed, d depth of cut). Specific cutting energy u = P/MRR = F_c/(f d) (J/mm³ or N/mm²).

steps.title: Tool materials and Taylor
steps.body:
Increasing hot hardness: carbon steel < HSS < cast alloys < cemented carbide (coated) < cermets < ceramics < CBN < diamond (PCD — not for steel; reacts with iron).
**Taylor's equation:** VTⁿ = C (n ≈ 0.1 HSS, 0.2–0.3 carbide, 0.5–0.7 ceramics). Extended: VTⁿf^a d^b = C.
Tool wear: flank wear (VB criterion ~0.3 mm), crater wear, notch; chipping. Economics: minimum-cost tool life T = (1/n − 1)(C_t/C_m + t_c).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F_c = 1000 N, V = 120 m/min = 2 m/s: P = 2 kW. MRR at f = 0.25 mm, d = 2 mm: 2000 × 0.25 × 2 = 1000 mm³/s ⇒ u = 2 J/mm³.

**Example 2.** Carbide n = 0.25: tool life 60 min at 100 m/min ⇒ C = 100 × 60^0.25 = 278.3. At 150 m/min: T = (278.3/150)^4 = 11.9 min.

**Example 3.** Doubling speed with n = 0.125 (HSS): T falls by 2^8 = 256 times.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using m/min with N to get watts (convert to m/s).
- Using diamond tools on steel.
- Rearranging Taylor: T = (C/V)^(1/n).

activity.prompt: Taylor: n = 0.2, C = 300 (m/min, min). Tool life at V = 150 m/min (min)?

quiz.why: Taylor's tool life equation is VTⁿ = C, linking cutting speed V and tool life T.
Diamond reacts with iron (carbon diffuses into steel) at cutting temperatures, so it wears quickly. It is not used for steel, but for non-ferrous metals and ceramics.
Specific cutting energy is the energy per unit volume of metal removed: F_c/(f d), the cutting force over the chip cross-section.
The Taylor exponent n is about 0.1–0.15 for HSS, 0.2–0.3 for carbide and 0.4–0.6 for ceramics.
A common tool-life criterion is a flank wear VB of about 0.3 mm (ISO uses 0.3 mm for uniform wear).

lessons.title: Machining operations and time estimation

scenes.text: A production planner estimates cycle times for turning, drilling and milling a part.
Simple formulas give machining time per operation.

steps.title: Time formulas
steps.body:
- **Turning:** N = 1000V/(πD) rpm; time per pass t = L/(fN) (L includes approach/overtravel).
- **Drilling:** t = (L + 0.3D)/(fN) (approach for the drill point ≈ 0.3D for 118°).
- **Milling (slab/face):** table feed f_m = f_z z N (mm/min); t = (L + approach)/f_m; MRR = w d f_m.
- **Grinding:** fine finish, abrasive wheels (Al₂O₃ for steel, SiC for cast iron/non-ferrous); dressing restores sharpness.
Surface roughness (turning, ideal) R_max = f²/(8r) (r = nose radius).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Turn Ø50 × 200 mm at V = 100 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev: N = 636.6 rpm; t = 200/(0.2 × 636.6) = 1.57 min per pass.

**Example 2.** Drill Ø20 × 40 mm, V = 25 m/min, f = 0.25: N = 398 rpm; t = (40 + 6)/(0.25 × 398) = 0.46 min.

**Example 3.** Face mill: 8 teeth, f_z = 0.1 mm, N = 500 rpm ⇒ f_m = 400 mm/min; 300 mm length + 100 approach ⇒ 1 min.

**Example 4.** R_max for f = 0.2 mm, r = 0.8 mm: 0.04/6.4 = 6.25 µm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius in N = 1000V/(πD).
- Forgetting approach/overtravel.
- Units: f_z per tooth vs per revolution.

activity.prompt: Turning speed: V = 120 m/min on Ø40 mm. Spindle speed (rpm, nearest whole)?

quiz.why: Spindle speed N = 1000V/(πD) rpm, with V in m/min and D in mm.
Milling table feed = feed per tooth × number of teeth × spindle speed: f_z × z × N.
The ideal peak-to-valley roughness in turning is R_max = f²/(8r), where f is the feed and r the nose radius.
Silicon carbide wheels suit cast iron, and non-ferrous and non-metallic materials. Aluminium oxide is for steels.
A 118° drill point has a cone height of (D/2)/tan(59°) ≈ 0.3D, so the drill travels this extra distance before reaching full diameter.

lessons.title: Non-traditional machining, CNC and additive manufacturing

story.title: Making a turbine blade cooling hole

scenes.text: Tiny angled cooling holes in superalloy blades are drilled by EDM or lasers.
Prototype brackets are 3-D printed overnight.

steps.title: Non-traditional processes
steps.body:
- **EDM:** sparks erode conductive workpieces (dies, hard materials); wire-EDM for profiles.
- **ECM:** anodic dissolution (no tool wear, stress-free).
- **USM:** abrasive slurry + vibrating tool (brittle materials: glass, ceramics).
- **AJM/WJM:** abrasive/water jets (cutting composites, stone).
- **LBM/EBM:** lasers/electron beams (micro-holes, cutting, welding).
- **Chemical machining (etching).**

steps.title: CNC and additive manufacturing
steps.body:
CNC: G-codes (G00 rapid, G01 linear feed, G02/G03 arcs, G90 absolute, G91 incremental), M-codes (M03 spindle on CW, M05 stop, M08 coolant, M30 end). CAD/CAM generates toolpaths; DNC/flexible manufacturing.
Additive manufacturing (ISO/ASTM 52900 categories): material extrusion (FDM/FFF), vat photopolymerisation (SLA/DLP), powder bed fusion (SLS, SLM/DMLS, EBM), material jetting, binder jetting, directed energy deposition, sheet lamination. Strengths: complex geometry, lattices, customisation; limits: speed, surface finish, anisotropy, post-processing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Hardened tool steel die cavity ⇒ EDM (sinker).

**Example 2.** Glass micro-holes ⇒ USM.

**Example 3.** CNC snippet: G90 G01 X50 Z−20 F0.2 — absolute linear move to (50, −20) at 0.2 mm/rev.

**Example 4.** Titanium patient-specific implant ⇒ powder bed fusion (SLM/EBM).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- EDM on non-conducting ceramics (won't work).
- Confusing G02 (clockwise) and G03 (counter-clockwise).
- Assuming 3-D printed parts are isotropic and production-ready without post-processing.

activity.prompt: Process → best application

quiz.why: G01 is linear interpolation at the programmed feed rate. G00 is rapid positioning and G02/G03 are circular arcs.
M03 turns the spindle on in the clockwise direction. M05 stops it, and M30 ends the program.

quiz.q: EDM requires the workpiece to be
quiz.why: Electrical discharge machining removes metal with sparks between electrode and workpiece, so the workpiece must be electrically conductive.
FDM (fused deposition modelling) pushes melted thermoplastic filament through a nozzle, which is material extrusion in 3D-printing terms.
In electrochemical machining, the tool does not touch the work and is not worn away, so tool wear is practically zero.

questions.q: Chip thickness ratio is always
questions.why: The chip is thicker than the uncut layer (t₂ > t₁), so t₁/t₂ is always below 1.

questions.q: Highest hot hardness among
questions.why: Cubic boron nitride keeps its hardness at the highest temperatures of the options listed, so CBN has the highest hot hardness.

questions.q: G02 means
questions.why: G02 is clockwise circular interpolation, and G03 is counter-clockwise.

questions.q: Cutting power: F_c 800 N, V 90 m/min
Turning time: L 150 mm, f 0.3 mm/rev, N 500 rpm
questions.why: Feed rate = f × N = 0.3 × 500 = 150 mm/min. Time = L/(feed rate) = 150/150 = 1 min.

questions.q: Taylor n 0.25, C 400: V for T 16 min
Assertion (A): A higher rake angle generally reduces cutting forces.  Reason (R): It increases the shear angle, reducing the shear plane area.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. A larger rake angle raises the shear angle, which shortens the shear plane and lowers the shear force and the cutting force. R explains A.

questions.q: Shear angle: r 0.35, α 10°
MRR turning: V 100 m/min, f 0.2 mm, d 3 mm
R_max for f 0.25 mm, r 1.0 mm
Case: A shop doubles cutting speed with carbide (n = 0.25). Tool life becomes
questions.why: T ∝ V^(−1/n) = V⁻⁴ for n = 0.25. Doubling the speed gives life 2⁻⁴ = 1/16. Cutting speed strongly affects tool life.

questions.q: Milling: 10 teeth, f_z 0.08 mm, N 600 rpm: table feed
questions.why: Table feed = f_z × z × N = 0.08 × 10 × 600 = 480 mm/min.

questions.q: Merchant φ for α = 10°, β = 40°
Specific energy if F_c = 1500 N, f = 0.3, d = 2.5 mm
Drilling time: Ø10 × 25 mm, V 20 m/min, f 0.15 mm/rev

lessons.title: Formula sheet: casting, welding, forming

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Manufacturing Processes.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Casting and welding
steps.body:
- Allowances: shrinkage, draft, machining, distortion, shake (−)
- V = √(2gh); t_pour = V/(A_c V); A₁/A₂ = √(h₂/h₁)
- Chvorinov t = C(V/A)²; riser modulus ≥ 1.2× casting
- H = ηVI/v; resistance H = I²Rt; brazing > 450 °C, soldering < 450 °C

steps.title: Forming
steps.body:

- Δh_max = μ²R; L = √(RΔh); F = σ̄wL
- Extrusion p = σ̄ ln R; drawing σ_d = σ̄ ln(A₀/A)

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

u for F_c 1000 N, f 0.2, d 2
quiz.why: Specific energy = F_c/(f d) = 1000/(0.2 × 2) = 2500 N/mm² = 2.5 J/mm³.

Read each explanation, even for the ones you got right.

steps.title: How to attempt
steps.body:

- For numericals write the formula, substitute with units, then simplify.
- Mark doubtful ones and return.

steps.title: Coverage
steps.body: This paper mixes every unit of Manufacturing Processes. Scores below 60% mean: re-read the unit whose questions you missed, then retake.

steps.title: Common mistakes in exams

activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: The negative allowance in patterns is the shake allowance: rapping the pattern enlarges the cavity, so the pattern is made smaller.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Process with non-consumable tungsten electrode
quiz.why: TIG (GTAW) uses a non-consumable tungsten electrode with inert gas shielding.
Hot working takes place above the recrystallisation temperature of the metal.
Taylor's tool life equation is VTⁿ = C.
Ultrasonic machining (USM) suits brittle, non-conducting materials like glass and ceramics, using abrasive slurry and vibration. EDM and ECM need a conductive work.
M30 ends the program and resets it to the start. M03 is spindle clockwise, M06 is tool change and M08 coolant on.
A riser must solidify after the casting so that it can feed liquid metal to the casting while shrinkage occurs.

questions.q: Sand property letting gases escape
questions.why: Permeability is the ability of the moulding sand to let gases escape. Cohesiveness is about holding together, refractoriness about heat resistance, and collapsibility about yielding to casting shrinkage.

questions.q: Soldering temperature limit
questions.why: Soldering uses a filler that melts below 450 °C. Brazing uses one that melts above 450 °C but below the base metal's melting point.

questions.q: Extrusion pushes metal
questions.why: In extrusion, a billet is pushed (or pulled) through a die opening to give a long constant-section product.

questions.q: Fastest-wearing tool when V doubles (n smallest)
questions.why: Tool life varies as T ∝ V^(−1/n). The smaller the n, the more strongly life falls when speed rises, so HSS (n about 0.1–0.15) suffers the most.

questions.q: Pattern for 250 mm cast iron (1% shrinkage)
questions.why: Pattern size = 250 × 1.01 = 252.5 mm. The pattern is made bigger to allow for the shrinkage of the casting.

questions.q: Pouring time: 0.0015 m³ cavity, choke 300 mm², V 2.5 m/s
Heat input 25 V, 180 A, 4.5 mm/s, η 0.8
Cup blank: d 60, h 45
Assertion (A): Closed-die forging produces flash.  Reason (R): Excess metal escapes into the flash gutter to ensure complete die filling.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both are true. In closed-die forging, extra metal is deliberately supplied. It squeezes out as flash, which makes sure that the die fills fully. R explains A.

questions.q: Roll force: w 250, Δh 4, R 400, σ̄ 160 MPa
questions.why: Contact length L = √(RΔh) = √(400 × 4) = 40 mm. Force = σ̄ w L = 160 × 250 × 40 = 1.6×10⁶ N = 1.6 MN.

questions.q: Shear angle r 0.4, α 0°
questions.why: For α = 0, tanφ = r = 0.4, so φ = tan⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 21.8°.

questions.q: Chvorinov C 3 s/mm², cylinder D 60 (all faces cooling, H = D): t
questions.why: For a cylinder with H = D, V/A = (πD³/4)/(1.5πD²) = D/6 = 10 mm. t = C(V/A)² = 3 × 100 = 300 s.

questions.q: Taylor: tool life 30 min at 100 m/min (n 0.25). Life at 80 m/min
questions.why: Taylor's equation gives T ∝ V^(−1/n) = V⁻⁴. At a lower speed, T₂ = 30 × (100/80)⁴ = 30 × 2.44 ≈ 73 min. A 20% speed cut gives more than double the tool life.

questions.q: Case: A 2 mm steel washer (OD 50, ID 25, τ 320 MPa) is made in a single stroke compound die (blank + pierce together). Total force
questions.why: A compound die cuts both the outer blank and the inner hole in one stroke, so the force adds up the two cut perimeters: π(50 + 25) × 2 × 320 = π × 75 × 2 × 320 ≈ 150.8 kN.

questions.q: Specific energy 3 J/mm³, MRR 800 mm³/s: power
questions.why: Power = specific energy × material removal rate = 3 J/mm³ × 800 mm³/s = 2400 W = 2.4 kW.

questions.q: Extrusion Johnson: σ̄ 120 MPa, R 10, a 0.8, b 1.5
questions.why: Johnson's extrusion formula is p = σ̄(a + b ln R). With R = 10, ln R = 2.303, so p = 120 × (0.8 + 1.5 × 2.303) = 120 × 4.25 ≈ 510 MPa. It is higher than the ideal σ̄ ln R because of friction and redundant work.

questions.q: Wire drawing 3 → 2.5 mm, σ̄ 400 MPa: ideal drawing stress
questions.why: The ideal drawing stress is σ_d = σ̄ ln(A₀/A) = 400 × ln(3²/2.5²) = 400 × ln 1.44 = 400 × 0.365 ≈ 146 MPa.

questions.q: Milling MRR: w 60, d 3, f_m 300 mm/min
questions.why: MRR = w × d × feed rate = 60 × 3 × 300 = 54 000 mm³/min. Divide by 60 for mm³/s: 900 mm³/s.

questions.q: Merchant: α 15°, μ 0.7 (β ≈ 35°): φ
questions.why: By Merchant's relation, φ = 45° + α/2 − β/2 = 45 + 7.5 − 17.5 = 35°, using β = tan⁻¹(0.7) ≈ 35°.

questions.q: Max reduction per pass (ideal) in drawing
questions.why: The ideal drawing stress cannot exceed the flow stress, so ln(A₀/A) ≤ 1 and A₀/A ≤ e. The maximum reduction in area is 1 − 1/e ≈ 63%.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Conduction: laws, composite walls, radial systems, heat generation
courses.summary: Modes of heat transfer, Fourier's law, the general conduction equation, composite plane/cylindrical/spherical walls, critical radius and internal heat generation — covering topics commonly taught in B.Tech Heat & Mass Transfer.
outcomes: Apply Fourier, Newton and Stefan–Boltzmann laws
Solve resistance networks for walls and pipes
Find critical radius

lessons.title: Lab: Three modes of heat transfer

scenes.text: A furnace door at 500 K sits in a 300 K workshop. A fitter wants to know how much heat leaves each square metre.
Heat leaves by conduction through the steel, convection to air, and radiation to the walls.

steps.title: Fourier, Newton, Stefan–Boltzmann
steps.body:
**Heat transfer** is energy in transit due to a temperature difference (thermodynamics tells how much; heat transfer tells how fast).

- **Conduction** (Fourier): q'' = −k dT/dx (W/m²); k in W/m·K. Needs a medium; molecular/electron transport.
- **Convection** (Newton): Q = h A (Ts − T∞); h in W/m²·K. Conduction + bulk fluid motion; free (natural) or forced.
- **Radiation** (Stefan–Boltzmann): Q = ε σ A (Ts⁴ − Tsur⁴), σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴, T in **kelvin**. Needs no medium.

Typical k: copper ≈ 385, aluminium ≈ 205, mild steel ≈ 45–60, brick ≈ 0.7, glass wool ≈ 0.04, air ≈ 0.026 W/m·K.

steps.title: Where you see it
steps.body: A tea-cup loses heat by all three modes; a thermos defeats each: vacuum stops conduction/convection, silvered walls (low ε) cut radiation. Spacecraft rely almost entirely on radiation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in the radiation formula (must be kelvin).
- Using mm instead of m for L.
- Reading the minus sign in Fourier's law as 'negative heat': it only says heat flows from hot to cold.
- Treating h as a material property; it depends on flow, geometry and fluid.

lessons.title: Lab: Composite wall and overall U

scenes.text: A cold-room wall: 200 mm brick (k 0.7), 50 mm polystyrene (k 0.04), 20 mm plaster (k 0.8).
Inside −5 °C with h = 8, outside 25 °C with h = 25. What is the heat gain per m²?

steps.title: Thermal resistance network
steps.body: For 1-D steady conduction, **R_cond = L/(kA)** (K/W) for a plane wall; convection **R = 1/(hA)**. Layers in series add: **R_tot = ΣR**; then **Q = ΔT/R_tot**. **U = 1/(A R_tot)** is the overall heat-transfer coefficient (W/m²K). Parallel paths add as conductances (1/R_eq = Σ1/R). Interface temperatures follow from ΔT_i = Q R_i.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Per m²: R_in = 1/8 = 0.125; brick 0.2/0.7 = 0.286; foam 0.05/0.04 = 1.250; plaster 0.02/0.8 = 0.025; R_out = 1/25 = 0.040.

ΣR = **1.726 m²K/W**, U = **0.579 W/m²K**.

q'' = U × 30 K = **17.38 W/m²**. The foam is 72% of the total resistance — that is why we insulate.

steps.title: Design insight
steps.body: Thin high-k layers (plaster, steel) barely matter; a thin low-k layer dominates. Find which resistance controls before changing anything.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding k values instead of resistances.
- Forgetting the film resistances 1/h.
- Using the parallel formula for series layers.
- Mixing mm and m.

activity.prompt: Heat gain per m² of this wall (W/m²).

quiz.why: Same heat flow passes through each.

quiz.q: U in terms of ΣR (per m²)

lessons.title: Lab: Cylinders, spheres and critical radius

scenes.text: A steel pipe carries hot fluid; a fitter wonders whether more lagging always cuts loss.
For small pipes more insulation can increase loss — until the critical radius is passed.

steps.title: Radial conduction
steps.body:
Cylinder: **Q = 2πkL(T1−T2)/ln(r2/r1)**, R = ln(r2/r1)/(2πkL). Sphere: **R = (1/r1 − 1/r2)/(4πk)**.

**Critical radius of insulation:** cylinder r_c = **k_ins/h_o**; sphere r_c = **2k_ins/h_o**. If the outer radius is below r_c, adding insulation *increases* loss because the outer surface area (convection) grows faster than the conduction resistance. For electrical wires this is a benefit.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Steel pipe r1=50 mm, r2=60 mm, k=45; lagging to r3=110 mm, k=0.06; h_o=12; inner surface 200 °C, ambient 30 °C, L=1 m.

R_steel = ln(1.2)/(2π·45) = 0.00064 K/W; R_lag = ln(110/60)/(2π·0.06) = 1.6078; R_conv = 1/(12·2π·0.11) = 0.1206.

ΣR = 1.7290 → **Q = 170/ΣR = 98.3 W per metre**.

Critical radius for k=0.08, h=12 on a cylinder: 0.08/12 = **6.67 mm**.

steps.title: Bare vs lagged
steps.body: The lagging above is well past r_c, so it helps; on a 3 mm wire with k=0.08 insulation it would hurt up to r = 6.7 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the plane-wall formula for pipes.
- log10 instead of ln.
- Using diameter instead of radius in r_c.
- Applying r_c to thick pipes (r already above r_c).

activity.prompt: Heat loss per metre of lagged pipe (W/m).

lessons.title: Lab: Heat generation in a wire and slab

scenes.text: A 4 mm copper conductor carries 100 A. Its resistance heats it from inside.
What is the centreline temperature if the surface sits at 40 °C?

steps.title: Conduction with internal heat generation
steps.body:
Steady 1-D with volumetric generation q_g (W/m³):

- Plane wall, thickness 2L, both faces at Ts: **T_max − Ts = q_g L²/(2k)** (mid-plane).
- Long solid cylinder radius R: **T(r) = Ts + q_g(R² − r²)/(4k)**, so **T_c − Ts = q_g R²/(4k)**.
- Solid sphere: **T_c − Ts = q_g R²/(6k)**.

Energy balance: q_g × volume = h A (Ts − T∞).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
I = 100 A, ρ_e = 1.7×10⁻⁸ Ω·m, D = 4 mm, k = 380.

A = πD²/4 = 1.257e-05 m²; R' = ρ_e/A = 1.3528e-03 Ω/m; q_g = I²R'/A = **1.077e+06 W/m³**.

T_c − Ts = q_g R²/(4k) = 0.003 K → T_c = **40.00 °C**. The rise is tiny because k is large.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Nuclear fuel rods, resistive heaters, bus-bars, curing concrete (hydration heat). Designers check T_max against the material limit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full thickness instead of half-thickness L in the slab formula.
- Forgetting that q_g is per unit volume.
- Using the cylinder formula (÷4k) for a sphere (÷6k).

lessons.title: Lab: General conduction equation and boundary conditions

scenes.text: A steel billet is dropped into a bath. Before solving anything we need the governing equation.
Everything in conduction comes from one energy balance on a tiny control volume.

steps.title: Derivation sketch
steps.body:
Energy balance on dx dy dz: (net conduction in) + (generation) = (storage). For constant k:

**∇²T + q_g/k = (1/α) ∂T/∂t**, with **α = k/(ρ c_p)** (m²/s), the thermal diffusivity.

Steady, no generation → Laplace ∇²T = 0. 1-D steady plane wall → d²T/dx² = 0 → linear T(x). Cylinder (radial): T = C1 ln r + C2. Sphere: T = C1/r + C2.

**Boundary conditions:** (1) fixed temperature, (2) fixed flux / insulated (dT/dx = 0), (3) convection: −k dT/dx = h(T − T∞). An **initial condition** is needed for transient problems.

steps.title: Reading α
steps.body: Large α means heat diffuses quickly (metals); small α (insulators, wood) means a slow response.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating an insulated boundary as T = constant (it is dT/dx = 0).
- Applying the linear profile to cylinders.
- Mixing α and k.

lessons.title: Lab: Fin equation and heat from a pin fin

scenes.text: A power-electronics heat sink uses 10 mm diameter, 100 mm long aluminium pins (k=200) in 25 W/m²K air.
The base is 100 K above ambient. How much heat does one pin shed?

steps.title: Extended surfaces
steps.body:
Fins add area where h is low (usually gas side). Energy balance on a slice gives **d²θ/dx² − m²θ = 0**, θ = T − T∞, **m = √(hP/kA_c)** (1/m). For a pin: m = √(4h/kD).

Heat from the fin base (θ0 = T_b − T∞), M = √(hPkA_c) θ0:
- **Infinitely long:** q = M
- **Insulated tip:** q = M tanh(mL)
- **Convecting tip:** use the full formula, or the corrected length L_c = L + A_c/P (= L + D/4 for a pin) in the insulated-tip formula.

Temperature: θ/θ0 = cosh m(L−x)/cosh mL (insulated tip).

steps.title: When do fins help?
steps.body: A fin is worthwhile if h is small (air) and k large. Rule of thumb: fin effectiveness ε_f > 2 to justify cost; with liquids (high h) fins add little.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using radius for D in m.
- Taking perimeter as πD² (it is πD).
- Forgetting θ0 is T_base − T∞, not T_base.
- Using the long-fin formula when mL < 2.5.

lessons.title: Lab: Fin efficiency, effectiveness and fin arrays

scenes.text: A designer compares fins to see which gives most heat per rupee.
Efficiency and effectiveness are the two numbers that decide.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Fin efficiency** η_f = actual heat / heat if the whole fin were at base temperature. For insulated tip η_f = tanh(mL)/(mL). **Fin effectiveness** ε_f = heat with fin / heat without fin from the same base area = q_f/(h A_c θ0). Relation: ε_f = η_f A_fin/A_c.

**Overall surface efficiency** of an array: η_o = 1 − (N A_f/A_t)(1 − η_f). Total heat: Q = η_o h A_t θ0 (or N q_f + h A_unfinned θ0).

steps.title: Trade-off
steps.body: Longer fins add area but efficiency drops (the tip is cooler). Optimum balances weight, cost and flow blockage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing efficiency (≤1) with effectiveness (can be ≫1).
- Forgetting the un-finned base area in totals.
- Using fins on high-h surfaces (ε_f < 2).

lessons.title: Lab: Lumped capacitance and Biot number

scenes.text: A 20 mm copper sphere at 300 °C is dropped into 25 °C air stream with h = 100.
How long until it cools to 100 °C — and can we treat it as one temperature?

steps.title: Lumped system analysis
steps.body:
If internal resistance ≪ surface resistance, the body is at one temperature. Criterion: **Bi = hL_c/k < 0.1**, L_c = V/A_s.

Energy balance ρVc dT/dt = −hA(T−T∞) gives **(T−T∞)/(Ti−T∞) = exp(−t/τ)**, time constant **τ = ρVc/(hA_s)** (s). Equivalent: exp(−Bi·Fo). After t = τ the excess falls to 36.8%; after 4τ it is 98% gone. Heat lost up to t: Q = ρVc(Ti − T).

steps.title: Thermocouples
steps.body: A thermocouple junction must have small τ to track changes — use a small bead and high h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full radius, not V/A, in Bi.
- Using the fluid's k in Bi (it is the solid's k).
- Applying lumped analysis when Bi ≥ 0.1.

lessons.title: Lab: Semi-infinite solid and Heisler-chart thinking

scenes.text: A thick steel block initially at 20 °C has its surface suddenly held at 500 °C.
What is the temperature 20 mm deep after one minute?

steps.title: When Bi ≥ 0.1
steps.body:
Temperature varies inside. **Semi-infinite solid** (early times or very thick body), surface held at Ts: **(T−Ti)/(Ts−Ti) = erfc(x/(2√(αt)))**. Penetration depth ≈ 4√(αt). Surface flux q''(t) = k(Ts−Ti)/√(παt).

**Finite slab/cylinder/sphere** (Heisler charts or one-term series): Fo = αt/L²; for Fo > 0.2 the first term suffices: θ*₀ = C1 exp(−ζ1² Fo), where ζ1 is the first root of ζ tan ζ = Bi (slab). Charts give centre temperature, a position correction, and Q/Q0.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Steel α = 50/(7800×480) = 13.35×10⁻⁶ m²/s. At x = 0.02 m, t = 60 s: x/(2√αt) = 0.3533; erfc = 0.6174.

T = Ti + (Ts−Ti)·erfc = 20 + 480×0.6174 = **316.3 °C**.

Slab check: h=500, k=50, half-thickness 20 mm → Bi = 0.20 > 0.1, so lumped analysis is **not** allowed.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Quenching, ground temperature below frost line (soil as semi-infinite), skin burn depth, laser heating.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full thickness for a slab heated on both sides (use half-thickness).
- Using the one-term series for Fo < 0.2.
- Confusing erf and erfc.

activity.prompt: Temperature 20 mm below the surface after 60 s (°C).

lessons.title: Lab: Two-dimensional steady conduction and shape factors

scenes.text: A 0.3 m diameter hot pipe is buried 1.5 m deep (axis), 10 m long, at 60 °C in soil at 10 °C (k=1.2).
Estimate the loss with a conduction shape factor.

steps.title: Shape factors
steps.body:
When geometry is 2-D/3-D, **Q = S k (T1−T2)**, S in m. Long cylinder (D, length L) buried at axis depth z: **S = 2πL/cosh⁻¹(2z/D)**; sphere in infinite medium: S = 4πr.

For numerical work: finite-difference nodal equation for an interior node with Δx=Δy: **T_i,j = (T_{i+1,j}+T_{i−1,j}+T_{i,j+1}+T_{i,j−1})/4**. Solve by Gauss–Seidel iteration.

steps.title: Why numerical
steps.body: Real parts have corners, fins, mixed boundaries; FD/FE are standard. The 4-neighbour mean is the discrete Laplace equation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using D instead of 2z/D in the cosh⁻¹ argument.
- Applying the interior nodal formula on boundary nodes without modification.

courses.summary: Velocity/thermal boundary layers, dimensionless groups, forced convection over plates and cylinders, internal flow in tubes, Reynolds–Colburn analogy and dimensional analysis.
outcomes: Use Re, Pr, Nu correctly

lessons.title: Lab: Boundary layers and dimensionless groups

scenes.text: Air at 5 m/s flows over a flat plate. 0.5 m from the leading edge a probe reads the layer thickness.
Engineers describe it with Re, Pr and Nu rather than raw numbers.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**Velocity boundary layer:** thickness δ where u = 0.99 U∞; **thermal boundary layer** δ_t. Ratio δ/δ_t ≈ Pr^(1/3).

Dimensionless groups: **Re = ρUL/μ = UL/ν** (inertia/viscous); **Pr = ν/α = μc_p/k** (momentum/thermal diffusivity); **Nu = hL/k** (convective/conductive); **St = Nu/(Re Pr) = h/(ρ c_p U)**; **Gr = gβΔT L³/ν²** (buoyancy/viscous), **Ra = Gr·Pr**.

Flat plate: transition at Re_x ≈ 5×10⁵. Laminar: **δ = 5x/√Re_x**, **C_fx = 0.664/√Re_x**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
x = 0.5 m, U = 5 m/s, ν = 1.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s: Re_x = 156250 (laminar). δ = 5×0.5/√156250 = **6.32 mm**. C_fx = **0.00168**.

Air has Pr ≈ 0.7 → δ_t slightly larger than δ; for oils (Pr ≫ 1) δ_t ≪ δ.

steps.title: Pr values
steps.body: Liquid metals ≈ 0.01–0.03; gases ≈ 0.7; water ≈ 2–7 (20→100 °C ≈ 7→1.7); light oils ≈ 50–1000; engine oil ≈ 10³–10⁴.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using kelvin vs °C does not matter for Re but property values must be at film temperature.
- Mixing L (plate length) with D (diameter) in Re/Nu.
- Using k of the solid in Nu (it must be the fluid's).

lessons.title: Lab: Forced convection over a flat plate

scenes.text: A 1 m × 1 m electronic panel at 80 °C is cooled by 40 °C air at 3 m/s along its length.
Estimate average h and the heat removed.

steps.title: Correlations (constant wall temperature)
steps.body:
Properties at film temperature T_f = (T_s+T∞)/2.

- Laminar (Re_L < 5×10⁵): **Nu_x = 0.332 Re_x^½ Pr^⅓** (local); **Nu_L = 0.664 Re_L^½ Pr^⅓** (average, = 2× local at L). Valid Pr ≥ 0.6.
- Turbulent: Nu_x = 0.0296 Re_x^⅘ Pr^⅓.
- Mixed: Nu_L = (0.037 Re_L^⅘ − 871) Pr^⅓.
- Constant heat flux: 0.453 Re^½ Pr^⅓ (local).

steps.title: Average vs local
steps.body: Average h over length L is twice the local h at x = L for laminar flow (h ∝ x^−½).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying laminar correlation to Re > 5×10⁵.
- Using properties at T∞ not film temperature.
- Using local-x formula for average coefficients.

lessons.title: Lab: Internal flow in tubes

scenes.text: Water at 1 m/s flows in a 25 mm tube. The wall is hotter than the water.
Estimate h with Dittus–Boelter and the bulk temperature rise over 3 m.

steps.title: Internal flow
steps.body:
Re_D = U_m D/ν: laminar < 2300, turbulent > ~10 000. Hydrodynamic entry length laminar ≈ 0.05 Re D; turbulent ≈ 10 D.

- Fully developed laminar: **Nu = 3.66** (constant T_w), **4.36** (constant flux).
- Turbulent: **Dittus–Boelter Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^n**, n = 0.4 heating, 0.3 cooling; 0.6 < Pr < 160, Re > 10⁴.
- Energy balance: **Q = ṁ c_p (T_out − T_in)**; constant flux ⇒ T_b rises linearly; constant T_w ⇒ (T_w − T_b) decays exponentially: ln[(T_w−T_out)/(T_w−T_in)] = −hP L/(ṁ c_p).
- Hydraulic diameter D_h = 4A/P for non-circular ducts.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Water at 40 °C: ν = 0.658×10⁻⁶, k = 0.63, Pr = 4.3. Re = 1×0.025/0.658×10⁻⁶ = **37994** (turbulent).

Nu = 0.023×Re^0.8×4.3^0.4 = **190.1**; h = Nu k/D = **4789 W/m²K**.

For a wall at 80 °C and bulk 40 °C, over 3 m: Q ≈ hπDLΔT = 45.1 kW; ṁ = ρ·U·A = 0.487 kg/s; ΔT_b ≈ Q/(ṁ c_p) = **22.19 K** (small, so the constant-ΔT assumption holds).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Dittus–Boelter for laminar flow.
- Using velocity as inlet instead of mean velocity.
- Forgetting n = 0.3 for cooling.

lessons.title: Lab: Cross flow over cylinders and the Reynolds–Colburn analogy

scenes.text: Wind at 5 m/s crosses a 50 mm diameter pipe.
Friction data can also predict heat transfer through the Reynolds–Colburn analogy.

steps.title: Cross flow and analogies
steps.body:
Cylinder in cross flow (Hilpert): **Nu_D = C Re_D^m Pr^⅓**; for 4000 < Re < 40 000, C = 0.193, m = 0.618. Flow separates near θ ≈ 80–120°, so local h is highest at the stagnation point.

**Reynolds analogy** (Pr = 1): St = C_f/2. **Chilton–Colburn** (0.6 < Pr < 60): **St·Pr^(2/3) = C_f/2 = j_H**. Valid when form drag is absent (flat plate, tubes) — not for bluff bodies.

**Dimensional analysis:** Buckingham π reduces h = f(ρ,U,L,μ,k,c_p) to **Nu = f(Re, Pr)** — two groups instead of seven variables.

steps.title: Why separation matters
steps.body: After separation the wake is turbulent and h rises again on the rear half — the local Nu curve of a cylinder has two humps at high Re.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using D as 'L' of a plate formula.
- Applying the Reynolds analogy to flows with large pressure drag.
- Forgetting the Pr^⅓ factor.

lessons.title: Lab: Natural convection on a vertical plate

scenes.text: A 0.5 m tall panel at 60 °C stands in 20 °C still air.
Air moves only because heated air is lighter — buoyancy-driven flow.

steps.title: Free convection
steps.body:
Density differences in a gravity field drive the flow. Governing group: **Grashof Gr = gβ(Ts−T∞)L³/ν²**; **Rayleigh Ra = Gr·Pr**. For ideal gases β = 1/T_film (K). Vertical-plate laminar/turbulent transition at Ra ≈ 10⁹.

**Churchill–Chu (all Ra):** Nu = {0.825 + 0.387 Ra^(1/6)/[1+(0.492/Pr)^(9/16)]^(8/27)}². Simple laminar form: Nu = 0.59 Ra^¼ (10⁴ < Ra < 10⁹). Free convection h is small: 2–25 W/m²K for gases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C for β of a gas (use 1/T in K).
- Using properties at the wall temperature.
- Using forced-convection correlations without a free-stream velocity.

lessons.title: Lab: Horizontal surfaces, cylinders and mixed convection

scenes.text: A 0.4 m square plate at 70 °C faces up in 30 °C air.
Orientation changes h because plumes rise differently.

steps.title: Orientation matters
steps.body:
Characteristic length for plates: L_c = A/P. Hot surface facing up (or cold facing down): **Nu = 0.54 Ra^¼** (10⁴–10⁷), **0.15 Ra^⅓** (10⁷–10¹¹). Hot facing down: Nu = 0.27 Ra^¼. Horizontal cylinder (Churchill–Chu): Nu_D = {0.6 + 0.387Ra_D^(1/6)/[1+(0.559/Pr)^(9/16)]^(8/27)}².

**Mixed convection:** compare Gr/Re². < 0.1 forced dominates; > 10 natural dominates; between: both matter, combine Nu^n = Nu_F^n ± Nu_N^n (n = 3 typical).

**Enclosures:** for small Ra the layer is conduction only (Nu = 1); above critical Ra ≈ 1708 (horizontal layer heated below) cells form.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: If Gr/Re² ≈ 1 you must not neglect either effect — e.g. slow air over a hot vertical surface.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong face (upward/downward) correlation.
- Using side length instead of A/P.
- Ignoring radiation in free convection — it is often equal in size!

lessons.title: Lab: Pool boiling and critical heat flux

scenes.text: A heater in water at 1 atm increases surface temperature in steps.
Beyond a limit, the bubbles merge into a vapour film and the metal can burn out.

steps.title: Boiling regimes (Nukiyama curve)
steps.body:
Excess temperature ΔT_e = T_s − T_sat.

1. **Natural convection** (ΔT_e < ~5 K).
2. **Nucleate boiling** (5–30 K): bubbles form, h very high (10⁴–10⁵ W/m²K); Rohsenow correlation.
3. **Critical (burnout) heat flux q''_max** — peak of curve.
4. **Transition boiling:** unstable, falling flux.
5. **Film boiling** (beyond Leidenfrost point): vapour blanket, radiation adds; h low.

**Zuber/Kutateladze:** q''_max = 0.131 h_fg ρ_v^½ [σ g(ρ_l − ρ_v)]^¼. Heat-flux-controlled heaters jump from nucleate to film boiling at q''_max (burnout); temperature-controlled surfaces trace the whole curve.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Boilers, nuclear fuel (DNB limit), electronics immersion cooling, quenching steel (Leidenfrost slows cooling).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the Leidenfrost point (min film boiling) with CHF.
- Using ΔT in °C and K incorrectly — differences are the same.
- Forgetting that heat-flux-controlled surfaces burn out.

lessons.title: Lab: Film condensation (Nusselt theory)

scenes.text: Saturated steam at 100 °C condenses on a 1 m vertical plate held 10 K colder.
How much condensate forms per metre width?

steps.title: Condensation
steps.body:
**Filmwise:** liquid wets the surface and forms a film — thermal resistance. **Dropwise:** drops roll off, h is 5–10× higher but hard to sustain.

Nusselt vertical plate (laminar film): **h̄ = 0.943 [ρ_l(ρ_l−ρ_v) g h_fg k_l³/(μ_l L ΔT)]^¼**, ΔT = T_sat − T_w, liquid properties at film temperature. For horizontal tubes replace 0.943 by 0.729 and L by D. Condensation rate ṁ = Q/h_fg. Film Reynolds number Re_f = 4ṁ'/μ; above ~30 ripples, ~1800 turbulent (use corrections). Non-condensable gases (air) greatly reduce h; vent condensers.

steps.title: Tube banks
steps.body: For N tubes stacked vertically, h̄ falls as N^(−¼) because condensate drips down onto lower tubes (Nusselt).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using vapour properties for the liquid film.
- Using ΔT = T_w − T∞ (it is T_sat − T_w).
- Forgetting that the 0.943 is for a vertical plate and 0.729 for a horizontal tube.

lessons.title: Lab: Choosing the right heat-transfer correlation

steps.title: Decision procedure
steps.body:
1. Is there bulk forced motion? (fan/pump) → forced, else natural.
2. Geometry: flat plate, tube interior, cylinder in cross flow, sphere, enclosure.
3. Regime: compute Re (or Ra). Laminar/turbulent limits.
4. Properties at film or bulk temperature as the correlation specifies.
5. Get Nu → h = Nu·k/L_c.

Typical h (W/m²K): free convection gases 2–25; forced gases 25–250; free convection liquids 50–1000; forced liquids 100–20 000; boiling water 2500–100 000; condensing steam 4000–25 000.

steps.title: Worked classification
steps.body: A fan blows air along a heated board (forced, flat plate, Re_L check); stagnant water around a hot vertical wire (natural, vertical/cylinder, Ra); oil in a heated tube (internal flow, check Re, Pr, viscosity correction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Dittus–Boelter for oils (use Sieder–Tate with viscosity ratio).
- Neglecting radiation for hot surfaces in air.
- Choosing correlation before checking the Reynolds regime.

lessons.title: Lab: Heat-exchanger types and overall coefficient U

scenes.text: A plant uses a shell-and-tube cooler. Water inside the tubes, oil outside.
Before sizing, the designer needs overall U including fouling.

steps.title: Types and U
steps.body:
**Recuperators** (separate streams): double-pipe (parallel/counter), shell-and-tube (1–2 pass, baffles), plate, compact finned, cross-flow. **Regenerators** store/release heat (rotary wheel). **Direct-contact** (cooling towers).

Overall coefficient (per unit outer area A_o): **1/U_oA_o = 1/(h_iA_i) + R_fi/A_i + ln(r_o/r_i)/(2πkL) + R_fo/A_o + 1/(h_oA_o)**. Fouling factors R_f (m²K/W) are typically 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ (river water ≈ 0.0002–0.0004; oils 0.0002–0.0009).

Heat duty: **Q = U A ΔT_m = ṁ_h c_h (T_h,i − T_h,o) = ṁ_c c_c (T_c,o − T_c,i)**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Thin-wall tube, h_i = 1500, h_o = 800 W/m²K.

Clean: U = 1/(1/1500 + 1/800) = **521.7 W/m²K**.

With R_fi = 0.0002, R_fo = 0.0001 m²K/W: 1/U = 0.00222 → U_d = **451.1 W/m²K** — fouling cost 14% of capacity. Cleanliness factor U_d/U_c = 0.86.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding h instead of resistances.
- Referring U to the wrong area (inner vs outer).
- Forgetting fouling and then under-sizing.

lessons.title: Lab: LMTD method and correction factor F

scenes.text: Oil cools from 150 °C to 90 °C while 2 kg/s of water heats from 30 °C to 70 °C.
How much area is needed for counterflow versus parallel flow if U = 500?

steps.title: LMTD
steps.body:
For parallel or counter flow: **ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂)** where ΔT₁, ΔT₂ are the end-to-end differences (parallel: inlet-inlet and outlet-outlet; counter: hot-in − cold-out and hot-out − cold-in). If ΔT₁ = ΔT₂, ΔT_lm = ΔT. **Q = U A ΔT_lm**.

Multi-pass/cross-flow: **Q = U A F ΔT_lm,cf**, F ≤ 1 from charts using P = (T_co − T_ci)/(T_hi − T_ci) and R = (T_hi − T_ho)/(T_co − T_ci). F < 0.75 is poor design; add shells.

Counterflow is always at least as good as parallel flow: it permits T_c,o > T_h,o and gives larger ΔT_lm.

steps.title: Phase change
steps.body: If one fluid changes phase at constant temperature, parallel and counterflow give the same ΔT_lm and F = 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Pairing wrong ends in counterflow.
- Using arithmetic mean difference blindly.
- Forgetting F for shell-and-tube.
