lessons.title: Lab: ε–NTU method

scenes.text: A counterflow exchanger with UA = 3000 W/K has hot gas (C = 4000 W/K) at 120 °C and cold air (C = 2000 W/K) at 30 °C.
Outlet temperatures are unknown — LMTD would need iteration; ε–NTU does not.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
C = ṁc_p (W/K). C_min, C_max, **C_r = C_min/C_max**. Maximum possible heat Q_max = C_min(T_h,i − T_c,i). **Effectiveness ε = Q/Q_max**. **NTU = UA/C_min**.

Counterflow: **ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1−C_r))]/[1 − C_r exp(−NTU(1−C_r))]** (C_r = 1: ε = NTU/(1+NTU)).
Parallel flow: **ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1+C_r))]/(1+C_r)**.
C_r = 0 (condenser/evaporator): **ε = 1 − exp(−NTU)** for every geometry.

Use ε–NTU when outlet temperatures are unknown (rating); LMTD when all four temperatures are known (sizing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using C_max in NTU.
- Mixing up ε definitions when the hot stream is C_min (still use C_min).
- Applying counterflow formula to cross-flow.

steps.title: Phase-change exchangers
steps.body:
When one fluid is isothermal, C_max → ∞, C_r = 0 and **ε = 1 − e^(−NTU)** for parallel, counter and cross-flow alike. Cooling-water outlet: T_c,o = T_c,i + ε(T_sat − T_c,i). Steam condensed: ṁ_s = Q/h_fg.

Capacity-rate cases: if C_h = C_c (balanced) counterflow ΔT is constant. Cross-flow with one mixed, one unmixed stream has its own ε formulas (charts).

steps.title: Power plants
steps.body: Condenser vacuum depends on cooling-water temperature; each K of rise in condensing temperature costs turbine output.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the cooling water as C_max.
- Forgetting the units of h_fg (kJ vs J).
- Applying F ≠ 1 to a condenser.

lessons.title: Lab: Design workflow, fouling and pressure drop

scenes.text: A client sends a duty sheet; the engineer must follow a defined sequence.
Fouling, vibration and pressure-drop limits all shape the final design.

steps.title: Design sequence
steps.body:
1. Fix duty Q from process data (energy balance). 2. Choose type/arrangement; put fouling or corrosive fluid in tubes (easier to clean). 3. Estimate U from tables; compute ΔT_lm and F. 4. A = Q/(U F ΔT_lm); choose tube size, pitch, passes. 5. Compute tube- and shell-side h, update U. 6. Check pressure drops (allowable ≈ 0.5–0.7 bar liquids), velocity (water 1–2.5 m/s in tubes; < 3 to reduce erosion), vibration. 7. Add 10–25% margin and repeat until converged.

**Fouling types:** scaling, particulate, biological, corrosion, chemical reaction. Mitigation: velocity > 1 m/s, cleaning, filters, water treatment.

steps.title: Worked mini-check
steps.body: Tube-side water 1.5 m/s in 19 mm ID tubes: ṁ per tube = ρ·V·A = 995×1.5×2.835×10⁻⁴ = 0.423 kg/s. For ṁ = 12.7 kg/s you need ≈ 30 tubes per pass.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not iterating after refining h.
- Ignoring pressure drop (pump cost).
- Zero fouling allowance.

lessons.title: Lab: Blackbody radiation, Planck, Wien and emissivity

scenes.text: A bar heated in a forge goes dull red, then orange, then white.
Hotter bodies emit more energy at shorter wavelengths.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
A **blackbody** absorbs all radiation and emits the maximum at each T and λ. **Stefan–Boltzmann:** E_b = σT⁴ (W/m²). **Planck** gives spectral emissive power E_bλ(λ,T) = C1/{λ⁵[exp(C2/λT) − 1]}. **Wien's displacement:** λ_max T = 2897.8 μm·K. Fraction of emission in a band is read from the F(λT) table.

Real surfaces: emissivity ε = E/E_b (0–1); absorptivity α, reflectivity ρ, transmissivity τ with **α + ρ + τ = 1** (opaque: α + ρ = 1). **Kirchhoff:** α_λ = ε_λ; for a **gray** body α = ε. Diffuse surfaces emit equally in all directions; intensity I = E/π.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
E_b at 1000 K = 5.67×10⁻⁸×10¹² = **56.7 kW/m²**.

Sun (T ≈ 5800 K): λ_max = 2897.8/5800 = **0.500 μm** (visible). Body at 300 K: λ_max = **9.66 μm** (infrared).

A gray surface ε = 0.6 at 800 K emits E = 0.6σT⁴ = **13.94 kW/m²**.

steps.title: Greenhouse effect
steps.body: Glass transmits solar (short-wave) radiation but is nearly opaque to the long-wave (~10 μm) emission of warm interiors — τ depends on wavelength.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using °C in T⁴.
- Assuming ε = α for all radiation sources: only valid for gray surfaces (or same-temperature source).
- Forgetting that a body in an enclosure also receives radiation.

activity.prompt: λ_max for a 5800 K blackbody (μm).

lessons.title: Lab: View factors

scenes.text: A radiant heater faces a workpiece. How much of the heater's emission lands on the work?
That fraction is the view factor.

steps.title: View (configuration) factor F_ij
steps.body:
F_ij = fraction of radiation leaving surface i that strikes surface j. Properties:
- **Reciprocity:** A_i F_ij = A_j F_ji.
- **Summation (enclosure):** Σ_j F_ij = 1.
- **Flat or convex surface:** F_ii = 0; concave: F_ii > 0.
- Surface fully enclosed by another: F_12 = 1, F_21 = A_1/A_2.
- **Long three-surface duct:** F_12 = (L1 + L2 − L3)/(2L1) (Hottel's crossed-string idea).
- Superposition: F_i→(j+k) = F_ij + F_ik. Standard charts for parallel discs, perpendicular rectangles.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
Concentric spheres r₁ = 0.1, r₂ = 0.2 m: F₁₂ = 1; F₂₁ = A₁/A₂ = (r₁/r₂)² = **0.25**; F₂₂ = 1 − F₂₁ = **0.75**.

Equilateral triangular duct, sides 1: F₁₂ = (1+1−1)/(2×1) = **0.5**. Check: F₁₂ + F₁₃ = 1 ✓.

Unknown F₂₁ given A₁ = 2, A₂ = 5, F₁₂ = 0.4: F₂₁ = A₁F₁₂/A₂ = **0.16**.

steps.title: Counting unknowns
steps.body: For an N-surface enclosure you need N(N−1)/2 independent F values; the rest follow from reciprocity and summation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using F_12 = F_21 when areas differ.
- Giving F_ii = 0 for a concave surface.
- Not checking summation to 1.

steps.title: Radiosity network
steps.body:
Radiosity J = εE_b + ρG (total leaving). Net heat from a gray surface: **Q = (E_b − J)/[(1−ε)/(εA)]**. Space resistance between i and j: **1/(A_iF_ij)**.

**Two-surface enclosure:** Q₁₂ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/[(1−ε₁)/(ε₁A₁) + 1/(A₁F₁₂) + (1−ε₂)/(ε₂A₂)].
- Large parallel plates: **q = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1)**.
- Concentric cylinders/spheres: **Q = σA₁(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/[1/ε₁ + (A₁/A₂)(1/ε₂ − 1)]**. If A₁/A₂ → 0 (small body in large room), Q = ε₁σA₁(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ε₁ε₂ in the denominator.
- Using A₂ for A₁ in the sphere/cylinder formula.
- Using °C.

lessons.title: Lab: Radiation shields and reradiating surfaces

scenes.text: A thin metal sheet placed between a hot and a cold surface cuts radiant heat dramatically.
How much, and how hot does the shield get?

steps.title: Shields
steps.body:
A shield adds two surface resistances (its two faces) and one space resistance. For N identical shields between identical-emissivity large plates ε: **q_with/q_without = 1/(N+1)**. With different emissivities add (1/ε_s1 + 1/ε_s2 − 1) per shield to the denominator.

**Reradiating (adiabatic) surface:** net heat Q₃ = 0, so J₃ = E_b3 and its temperature floats: it only redirects radiation. Equivalent F factor for two black surfaces with a reradiating wall: F_eff = F₁₂ + 1/(1/F₁₃ + 1/F₂₃).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
Plates as before, add one shield with ε = 0.1 on both sides: denominator = (1/0.8 + 1/0.6 − 1) + (1/0.1 + 1/0.1 − 1) = 1.917 + 19 → q = **329.4 W/m²** versus 3595 without — a 91% cut. Shield temperature ≈ **514 K**.

Equilateral duct, 1 m wide, black surfaces 1 at 600 K, 2 at 300 K, surface 3 reradiating: F_eff = 0.5 + 1/(2+2) = 0.75; Q = σ·1·(600⁴−300⁴)·0.75 = **5167 W/m**; T₃ = ((T₁⁴+T₂⁴)/2)^¼ = **512 K**.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Cryogenic tanks (multi-layer insulation), thermos flasks, thermocouple radiation shields, furnaces with refractory walls.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the same ε for all shield faces.
- Forgetting two surface resistances per shield.
- Treating a reradiating wall as insulation: it still affects the exchange.

lessons.title: Lab: Solar absorption and equilibrium temperature

scenes.text: A black plate and a selective-coating plate both sit in 1000 W/m² sunlight.

steps.title: Solar radiation
steps.body:
Solar constant ≈ 1361 W/m² at top of atmosphere; ground-level clear-sky ≈ 800–1000 W/m². Sun ≈ blackbody at 5800 K. Surface properties split into **solar absorptivity α_s** (short wave) and **emissivity ε** (long wave ~ room temperature).

Insulated plate in equilibrium (no convection): **α_s G = ε σ T⁴ → T = (α_s G/(εσ))^¼**. Selective surfaces (high α_s/ε) used in solar collectors; white paint (low α_s/ε) in cooling.

With convection: α_s G = εσ(T⁴ − T_sky⁴) + h(T − T∞).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: G = 1000 W/m². Black-ish paint α_s = ε = 0.9: T = (1000/σ)^¼ = **364 K**. Selective coating α_s = 0.9, ε = 0.1: T = (0.9×1000/(0.1×5.67×10⁻⁸))^¼ = **631 K** (358 °C) — much hotter, until convection losses limit it.

steps.title: Roof design
steps.body: A white roof (α_s ≈ 0.2, ε ≈ 0.9) can be 20–30 K cooler than a dark one in sun.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ε for absorption of sunlight (use α_s).
- Ignoring convection in real life — equilibrium without convection is an upper bound.
- Forgetting to convert K to °C at the end.

lessons.title: Lab: Fick's law and steady molecular diffusion

scenes.text: Water evaporates from the bottom of a 10 cm vertical tube; dry air blows across the top at 25 °C.
The vapour must diffuse up through stagnant air.

steps.title: Diffusion basics
steps.body:
Mass transfer needs a **concentration (partial-pressure) gradient**. **Fick's law:** J_A = −D_AB dC_A/dz (molar flux relative to the mixture, mol/m²s); D_AB in m²/s (gas ≈ 10⁻⁵, liquid ≈ 10⁻⁹, solid ≈ 10⁻¹²–10⁻¹⁵). Total flux N_A = J_A + y_A(N_A + N_B). D varies with T^1.75/P in gases.

**Equimolar counter-diffusion** (N_B = −N_A): N_A = D_AB(C_A1 − C_A2)/L = D_AB(p_A1 − p_A2)/(RTL).

**Diffusion through a stagnant film** (N_B = 0, Stefan): **N_A = [D_AB P/(RTL)] ln[(P − p_A2)/(P − p_A1)]**. Larger than the equimolar value due to bulk flow.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Water/air at 298 K, D = 2.56×10⁻⁵ m²/s, p_A1 = 3169 Pa (saturated), p_A2 ≈ 0, L = 0.1 m.

N_A = (2.56×10⁻⁵×101325)/(8.314×298×0.1) × ln(101325/(101325−3169)) = **0.3327 mmol/m²s** → mass flux 5.988 mg/m²s.

Compare equimolar: 0.3274 mmol/m²s — the stagnant-film result is ~1.6% higher.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Fick's law with J when N is needed.
- Mixing mol and kg units.
- Using the equimolar formula for evaporation into air (bulk motion ≠ 0).

lessons.title: Lab: Convective mass transfer and the heat–mass analogy

scenes.text: Air at 2 m/s flows over a 0.5 m × 0.5 m wet tray at 25 °C; air is 40% relative humidity.
How much water evaporates per hour?

steps.title: Dimensionless groups
steps.body:
Convective mass transfer: **N_A'' = h_m (ρ_A,s − ρ_A,∞)** (kg/m²s), h_m in m/s.

**Sherwood Sh = h_m L/D_AB** (analogue of Nu), **Schmidt Sc = ν/D_AB** (analogue of Pr), **Lewis Le = α/D_AB = Sc/Pr**.

Analogy: replace Nu → Sh, Pr → Sc in any heat-transfer correlation. Laminar plate: **Sh_L = 0.664 Re_L^½ Sc^⅓**; turbulent tube: **Sh = 0.023 Re^0.83 Sc^⅓**. Chilton–Colburn: h/(h_m ρ c_p) = Le^(2/3).

Vapour density from partial pressure: ρ_v = pM/(RT) (ideal gas).

steps.title: Quick conversion
steps.body: If you know a Nu correlation you know Sh: swap Pr→Sc. For air–water Le ≈ 0.85–0.9 so heat and mass transfer are nearly analogous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Pr where Sc is needed.
- Mass flux in mol vs kg inconsistency.
- Using total density instead of species-density difference.

scenes.text: A low-carbon steel gear (0.2 wt% C) is carburised at 927 °C with surface carbon held at 1.0 wt%.
How long to reach 0.5 wt% C at 0.5 mm depth?

steps.title: Fick's second law
steps.body:
∂C/∂t = D ∂²C/∂x²: exactly the heat equation with α → D. For a **semi-infinite solid** with surface concentration C_s held constant:

**(C_x − C_0)/(C_s − C_0) = 1 − erf(x/(2√(Dt)))**.

Hence a given concentration is reached at depth x ∝ √(Dt). D rises exponentially with T: **D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT)** (Arrhenius).

Applications: carburising/nitriding, doping of silicon, drug release, moisture in wood, gas permeation.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: Doubling the case depth needs ~4× the time — depth ∝ √t.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 1 − erf (erfc).
- Using mm for x with m²/s for D.
- Using D at the wrong temperature.

lessons.title: Lab: Evaporation losses and simultaneous heat and mass transfer

scenes.text: A 10 m × 5 m pool at 25 °C sits in air at 50% relative humidity.
How much water evaporates in a day, and what heat does it carry away?

steps.title: Evaporation as heat loss
steps.body:
Evaporative flux **ṁ'' = h_m(ρ_v,s − ρ_v,∞)**; latent heat loss **q'' = ṁ'' h_fg** (h_fg ≈ 2442 kJ/kg at 25 °C). Wet-bulb temperature is the steady value at which sensible heat from air equals latent heat for evaporation: h(T∞ − T_wb) = h_m h_fg (ρ_s − ρ_∞).

Cooling towers, wet-bulb thermometers, sweating and drying all rely on this. Evaporation lowers surface temperature below air temperature; the effect is greatest at low humidity.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Take h_m = 0.01 m/s (light air movement), ρ_s = 0.0230 kg/m³, ρ_∞ = 0.0115.

ṁ'' = 0.01×(0.0230−0.0115) = 115 mg/m²s; for 50 m²: **497 kg/day** (≈ 9.9 mm of depth).

Latent loss = ṁ'' h_fg = 281 W/m² ≈ **14.0 kW** over the pool — why covers save heating energy.

steps.title: Humidity matters
steps.body: At 100% RH there is no driving force (ρ_s = ρ_∞) and evaporation stops, even at high temperature.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the relative-humidity factor on ρ_∞.
- Ignoring latent heat in energy balances for wet surfaces.
- Using dry-bulb instead of surface temperature for ρ_s.

lessons.title: Lab: Two-film theory and overall mass-transfer resistance

scenes.text: An absorber removes a solute from gas into water. Resistance exists on both sides of the interface.
Which side controls the rate?

steps.title: Two-film (Lewis–Whitman) theory
steps.body:
Interface at equilibrium (Henry's law y* = m x). Fluxes in series: N = k_y(y − y_i) = k_x(x_i − x). Overall: **1/K_y = 1/k_y + m/k_x**, **1/K_x = 1/(m k_y) + 1/k_x**. If m is small (very soluble gas) gas-film resistance controls; if m is large (sparingly soluble, e.g. O₂ in water) the liquid film controls.

Enhance transfer on the controlling side: raise gas velocity (gas control) or agitate (liquid control). Membranes: N = P Δp/δ with permeability P = D·S.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
k_y = 2.0×10⁻³, k_x = 5.0×10⁻⁵ mol/m²s (per unit mole fraction), m = 0.8.

1/K_y = 1/(2×10⁻³) + 0.8/(5×10⁻⁵) = 500 + 16000 = 16500 → K_y = **6.06×10⁻⁵** mol/m²s.

Liquid-side share = 97.0% → **liquid-film controlled**; stirring the liquid helps far more than blowing more gas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding k's rather than resistances.
- Forgetting m in the overall formula.
- Assuming gas control for sparingly soluble gases.

steps.title: Conduction & fins
steps.body:
- Fourier q'' = −k dT/dx; plane wall R = L/kA; cylinder R = ln(r₂/r₁)/2πkL; sphere R = (1/r₁−1/r₂)/4πk.
- Critical radius: cylinder k/h, sphere 2k/h.
- Generation: slab q_gL²/2k; cylinder q_gR²/4k; sphere q_gR²/6k.
- Fin: m = √(hP/kA_c); insulated tip q = √(hPkA_c)θ₀ tanh mL; η = tanh mL / mL.
- Lumped: Bi = hL_c/k < 0.1; θ/θ₀ = e^(−t/τ), τ = ρVc/hA.
- Semi-infinite: θ/θ₀ = erfc(x/2√αt).

steps.title: Convection
steps.body:
- Re = UL/ν; Pr = ν/α; Nu = hL/k; Gr = gβΔTL³/ν²; Ra = Gr·Pr; St = Nu/(Re·Pr).
- Laminar plate Nu_L = 0.664Re^½Pr^⅓ (Re < 5×10⁵).
- Tube: laminar Nu = 3.66 (T_w) / 4.36 (q''); turbulent Dittus–Boelter 0.023Re^0.8Pr^0.4 (heating).
- Natural, vertical plate: Churchill–Chu; Nu = 0.59Ra^¼ simple laminar.

steps.title: Exchangers & radiation & mass
steps.body:
- Q = UAΔT_lm F; ΔT_lm = (ΔT₁−ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂). ε–NTU: NTU = UA/C_min; counter ε = [1−e^(−NTU(1−C_r))]/[1−C_r e^(−NTU(1−C_r))]; C_r=0: 1−e^(−NTU).

scenes.text: A lagged copper rod is heated at one end by a known power; two thermocouples 0.2 m apart read 95 °C and 55 °C.

steps.title: Aim, theory, apparatus
steps.body: **Aim:** determine k of a metal rod by steady axial conduction. **Theory:** Q = kA(T₁−T₂)/L. **Apparatus:** rod (D = 25 mm) lagged with glass wool, band heater with wattmeter/dimmerstat, thermocouples + selector, cold-end water jacket, stopwatch.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: See the ordering task. Wait until readings change < 0.5 °C in 10 min (steady state) before recording. Heat leak through lagging is the main error source.

steps.title: Observation and calculation
steps.body:
Q = V·I = 20 W (assume all enters rod), L = 0.2 m, A = π(0.025)²/4 = 4.909e-04 m², ΔT = 40 K.

k = QL/(AΔT) = 20×0.2/(4.909e-04×40) = **203.7 W/m·K** — this is like aluminium; check heat leak or whether the rod is not copper.

steps.title: Precautions & errors
steps.body:
- Do not touch the hot heater; insulate thoroughly.
- Ensure steady state.
- Thermocouple contact errors; lagging losses make k read low or high depending on position.

lessons.title: Lab: Engine geometry, swept volume and compression ratio

scenes.text: A showroom brochure says 'four-cylinder, 3.8-litre, bore 100 mm, stroke 120 mm, compression ratio 9:1'.
Karan, a final-year student, wants to check whether the numbers are consistent.

steps.title: Terminology
steps.body:
- **TDC / BDC:** top and bottom dead centres — the extreme piston positions.
- **Stroke L:** distance between TDC and BDC (= 2 × crank radius).
- **Bore D:** cylinder diameter.
- **Swept (displacement) volume** Vs = (π/4) D² L per cylinder; engine capacity = Vs × number of cylinders.
- **Clearance volume** Vc: volume above the piston at TDC.
- **Compression ratio** r = (Vs + Vc)/Vc = V₁/V₂, so Vc = Vs/(r − 1).

Classification: by cycle (Otto/Diesel), strokes (4S/2S), ignition (SI/CI), cooling (air/water), cylinder arrangement (inline, V, flat/boxer, radial), valve gear (SV, OHV, OHC/DOHC), fuel (petrol, diesel, CNG, LPG).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Brochure check
steps.body:
D = 100 mm = 0.1 m, L = 120 mm = 0.12 m, 4 cylinders.
- Step 1: Vs = (π/4)(0.1)²(0.12) = 9.425 × 10⁻⁴ m³ = **942.5 cc**.
- Step 2: capacity = 4 × 942.5 = 3770 cc = **3.77 L ≈ 3.8 L** ✓.
- Step 3: with r = 9, Vc = 942.5/(9 − 1) = **117.8 cc** per cylinder.

The brochure is consistent. Stroke/bore = 1.2, so this is an *undersquare* (long-stroke) engine — good low-speed torque.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Piston speed
steps.body: Mean piston speed Sp = 2 L N / 60 (N in rpm, L in m). At 3000 rpm: Sp = 2 × 0.12 × 3000/60 = **12 m/s**. Production engines are limited to roughly 18–25 m/s by inertia stresses and friction, which is why long-stroke engines have lower redlines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using r = Vs/Vc (forgetting the +Vc): r = (Vs+Vc)/Vc.
- Confusing bore with radius in the π/4 D² formula.
- Forgetting to multiply by cylinder count, or mixing cc, litres and m³ (1 L = 10⁻³ m³ = 1000 cc).

lessons.title: Lab: Otto cycle — derivation and efficiency

story.title: Why petrol engines love high compression

scenes.text: Meera notices sports bikes quote compression ratios of 11–13:1 while old scooters had 7:1.
Her professor says the ideal Otto efficiency depends only on that ratio and γ.

steps.title: The ideal Otto (constant-volume) cycle
steps.body:
Air-standard assumptions: fixed mass of air as ideal gas with constant cp, cv; combustion replaced by heat addition; exhaust replaced by heat rejection; all processes reversible.

Processes: **1→2** isentropic compression; **2→3** heat addition at constant volume (Q₁ = cv(T₃−T₂)); **3→4** isentropic expansion; **4→1** heat rejection at constant volume (Q₂ = cv(T₄−T₁)).

steps.title: Derivation of efficiency
steps.body:
η = 1 − Q₂/Q₁ = 1 − (T₄ − T₁)/(T₃ − T₂).
For isentropic processes T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₄ = r^(γ−1), so (T₄−T₁)/(T₃−T₂) = 1/r^(γ−1).

**η_Otto = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1)**, γ = 1.4 for air. It rises with r but with diminishing returns; in real engines r is limited by knock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using γ = 1.3 or the wrong exponent (it is γ − 1, not γ).
- Thinking efficiency depends on heat added — for the ideal Otto cycle it does not.
- Quoting real engine efficiency (≈ 25–35 %) as the air-standard value.

lessons.title: Lab: Diesel and Dual cycles

scenes.text: Ravi compares a truck diesel (r = 18) with a car petrol engine (r = 9) and asks why the truck uses less fuel per unit of work.
The answer lies in the Diesel cycle: only air is compressed, so there is no knock limit.

steps.title: Diesel cycle (constant pressure)
steps.body:
1→2 isentropic compression of air only; 2→3 heat addition at **constant pressure**; 3→4 isentropic expansion; 4→1 constant-volume heat rejection.

Cut-off ratio ρ = V₃/V₂ = T₃/T₂.

**η_Diesel = 1 − (1/r^(γ−1)) · (ρ^γ − 1)/(γ(ρ − 1))**

The bracket (ρ^γ − 1)/(γ(ρ−1)) is always > 1, so at the same r the Diesel cycle is *less* efficient than Otto; but diesel engines run at 16–22:1, which wins overall.

steps.title: Dual (limited-pressure) cycle
steps.body:
Heat is added partly at constant volume (2→3) then at constant pressure (3→4). Pressure ratio α = P₃/P₂, cut-off ρ = V₄/V₃.

**η_Dual = 1 − (1/r^(γ−1)) · (αρ^γ − 1)/((α−1) + γα(ρ−1))**

With α = 1 it reduces to Diesel; with ρ = 1 it reduces to Otto. It best represents modern high-speed diesels.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Effect of load
steps.body: At light load ρ falls toward 1, bracket → 1: with ρ = 1.5, ρ^1.4 = 1.764; bracket = 0.764/(1.4 × 0.5) = 1.091; η = 1 − 1.091/3.178 = **65.7 %**. So ideal Diesel efficiency *increases* at part load (real engines also gain, because quantity governing avoids throttling losses).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing cut-off ratio ρ (V₃/V₂) with compression ratio r.
- Forgetting the Diesel bracket exceeds 1.
- Claiming Diesel > Otto at the same r — the reverse is true.

lessons.title: Lab: Mean effective pressure and cycle comparison

scenes.text: Two engines have the same swept volume. Which produces more work per cycle?
Mean effective pressure answers this: the constant pressure that gives the same work over the stroke.

steps.title: Mean effective pressure
steps.body:
mep = net work per cycle / swept volume = W_net / (v₁ − v₂).
For Otto: mep = W_net / [v₁(1 − 1/r)], with v₁ = RT₁/P₁.
mep is a measure of how well the displacement is used; for real engines imep and bmep are the key performance numbers (Unit 4).

steps.title: Comparing cycles
steps.body:
**Same compression ratio and heat input:** Otto > Dual > Diesel in efficiency.
**Same maximum pressure and heat input:** Diesel > Dual > Otto — because the Diesel cycle can use a much higher r when pressure is the structural limit.
This is why engineers say 'Otto is best for fixed r, Diesel for fixed peak pressure'.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Size from power
steps.body: A four-stroke engine must give 60 kW at 3000 rpm with bmep 8 bar. Power = bmep × Vs_total × N/120 → Vs = 60 000/(8×10⁵ × 3000/120) = 60 000/(2×10⁷) = 3×10⁻³ m³ = **3.0 L**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing work by total volume instead of swept volume.
- Using N instead of N/2 for four-stroke power strokes.
- Mixing kPa and bar (1 bar = 100 kPa).

lessons.title: Four-stroke and two-stroke operation, valve timing and firing order

scenes.text: Sana hears the smooth beat of a 4-cylinder car and asks why the cylinders do not fire 1-2-3-4.
Her mechanic says the firing order 1-3-4-2 spreads the load on the crankshaft.

steps.title: Four-stroke cycle
steps.body: Suction (inlet valve open, piston down) → compression (both valves closed) → power (after ignition) → exhaust (exhaust valve open, piston up). Two crank revolutions (720°) per cycle; one power stroke per cylinder per two revolutions.

steps.title: Two-stroke cycle
steps.body: Inlet/transfer/exhaust ports in the cylinder wall replace valves. Compression and power happen on the upward and downward strokes while the crankcase pumps the fresh charge; one power stroke per revolution. Advantages: simple, light, high power-to-weight. Disadvantages: poor scavenging, short-circuiting of fresh charge (HC emissions), lubricant mixed with fuel, lower efficiency.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Firing intervals
steps.body: A 4-cylinder four-stroke has 720°/4 = **180°** between firings; a 6-cylinder: 120°; an 8-cylinder: 90°. Common orders: 4-cyl **1-3-4-2** or 1-2-4-3; 6-cyl inline **1-5-3-6-2-4**. At 2400 rpm a 4-cyl 4-stroke has 4 × 2400/120 = **80 power strokes/s**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Valve timing
steps.body: Typical petrol valve timing: IVO 10–20° before TDC, IVC 30–50° after BDC, EVO 40–50° before BDC, EVC 10–20° after TDC. The period when both valves are open near TDC is **valve overlap** (aids scavenging, raises volumetric efficiency at high speed, but causes rough idle and HC emissions). Intake closes late because the incoming column keeps moving by inertia (ram effect).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a four-stroke engine fires every revolution (it is every second).
- Believing two-stroke engines have twice the power of four-stroke ones of equal size — real gain is about 1.3–1.6× because of scavenging losses.
- Mixing up firing order (cylinder numbering) and crank phasing.

lessons.title: Lab: Air–fuel ratio, stoichiometry and mixture requirements

story.title: Why the engine runs rich when cold

scenes.text: Aman's old car needs the choke on a cold morning and gives black smoke if he forgets to turn it off.
The reason is the mixture the engine needs at different conditions.

steps.title: Stoichiometric mixture
steps.body:
Air–fuel ratio AFR = mass of air / mass of fuel. For isooctane C₈H₁₈ + 12.5 (O₂ + 3.76 N₂) → 8 CO₂ + 9 H₂O + 47 N₂.
Per kmol of fuel the air is 12.5 × 4.76 = 59.5 kmol = 1724 kg, against 114.2 kg of fuel → **AFR ≈ 15.1**. Commercial petrol: about **14.7:1**.

Equivalence ratio φ = AFR_stoich/AFR_actual. φ > 1 rich, φ < 1 lean. Lambda λ = 1/φ.

steps.title: What the engine needs
steps.body:
- **Idle / cold start:** rich (φ ≈ 1.1–1.3), because poor vaporisation and residual gas.
- **Cruise:** slightly lean (φ ≈ 0.9) for economy.
- **Full load / acceleration:** rich (φ ≈ 1.1–1.2) for maximum power and cooling.
- Maximum power is near φ ≈ 1.1; best economy near φ ≈ 0.9; zero CO/NOx/HC compromise needs φ = 1 for the three-way catalyst.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Equivalence ratio
steps.body: Actual AFR 12:1, stoichiometric 14.7:1 → φ = 14.7/12 = **1.225** (rich, ≈ 22 % excess fuel). λ = 0.816.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Fuel flow
steps.body: An engine takes 0.06 kg/s of air at AFR 14.7: fuel = 0.06/14.7 = 4.08 g/s = **14.7 kg/h**. At AFR 12 the fuel rises to 5 g/s (18 kg/h), 22 % more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling AFR 16:1 'rich' (it is lean).
- Mixing mass and volume basis.
- Ignoring that CO and HC rise when rich and NOx peaks slightly lean (φ ≈ 0.9).

lessons.title: Lab: Simple carburettor and venturi airflow

scenes.text: Dev's older motorbike coughs at altitude and runs rich when the air filter clogs.
He wants to understand how the venturi meters air and fuel together.

steps.title: Working principle
steps.body: Air accelerates through the **venturi (choke tube)**; the static pressure falls (Bernoulli); fuel flows from the float chamber through the main jet because of this depression and is atomised by the air. The **float chamber** keeps the fuel level just below the jet tip; the **throttle valve** controls airflow.

steps.title: Air flow equation
steps.body: ṁ_a = C_da · A_t · √(2 ρ_a Δp), where Δp is the depression at the throat. Fuel: ṁ_f = C_df · A_j · √(2 ρ_f (Δp − ρ_f g z)), z = jet height above the float level. The simple carburettor gives an increasingly rich mixture as throttle opens, hence extra systems: **compensating jet, idling system, accelerator pump, economiser (power enrichment), choke**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter instead of area.
- Forgetting that ṁ ∝ √Δp: doubling depression raises flow only 41 %.
- Calling the choke a throttle: choke is a restriction *upstream* of the venturi that enriches the mixture for cold start.

lessons.title: Lab: Electronic fuel injection — MPFI and GDI

scenes.text: After BS-IV and BS-VI norms, manufacturers dropped carburettors on cars and then motorcycles.
The ECU measures air and meters fuel with millisecond precision.

steps.title: Systems
steps.body:
- **Throttle-body (single-point) injection:** one injector above the throttle.
- **MPFI (port injection):** one injector per cylinder spraying onto the back of the inlet valve; sequential timing.
- **GDI/FSI:** injector in the chamber at 50–200 bar; allows stratified-charge lean burn and cooling that permits higher r.

Sensors: MAF/MAP, throttle position, crank/cam position, coolant temperature, intake-air temperature, **lambda (O₂) sensor**, knock sensor. The ECU gives a base pulse width from a map and corrects it with **short-term/long-term fuel trims** (closed loop).

steps.title: Solved example · Pulse width
steps.body:
1.2 L four-cylinder at 3000 rpm, ηv = 0.85, ρ_a = 1.2 kg/m³, AFR 14.7. Cylinder displacement 0.3 L.
- Air per cylinder cycle = 1.2 × 0.0003 × 0.85 = 3.06 × 10⁻⁴ kg
- Fuel = 3.06×10⁻⁴/14.7 = 2.08 × 10⁻⁵ kg = **20.8 mg**
- Injector static flow 2.5 g/s = 2.5 mg/ms → pulse width = 20.8/2.5 = **8.3 ms**.
- Cycle time = 120/3000 = 40 ms, so duty cycle ≈ 21 %.

steps.title: Why injection wins
steps.body: Accurate per-cylinder metering, better cold start (no choke), precise λ = 1 control for the catalyst, higher volumetric efficiency (no venturi), fuel cut-off on overrun and altitude compensation by sensors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing lambda sensor (O₂) with MAF.
- Using a pulse width longer than the cycle time at high rpm — injectors saturate; dead time (opening lag) must be added at low battery voltage.
- Saying GDI is always cleaner: it can emit particulates, which is why GPFs appear.

lessons.title: Ignition systems — coil, magneto and CDI

scenes.text: Priya's car cranks but does not start; the mechanic checks for a spark first.
Ignition must deliver 15–30 kV at exactly the right crank angle.

steps.title: Battery-coil ignition
steps.body: A 12 V battery supplies the **primary winding** (low turns) through the contact breaker or ECU-driven transistor. When the primary is interrupted the collapsing flux induces a high voltage in the **secondary** (many turns): V₂ = N₂/N₁ × V₁(induced). The capacitor/snubber prevents arcing and speeds collapse. Modern **coil-on-plug** systems have one coil per cylinder, no distributor and ECU-controlled dwell and advance.

steps.title: Magneto and CDI
steps.body: A **magneto** generates its own current from a rotating magnet (two-wheelers, small engines). **CDI (capacitor discharge ignition)** charges a capacitor to 200–400 V and discharges it into a primary — a very fast rise time that tolerates fouled plugs. **Spark advance** is needed because burning takes time (about 30–40° of crank): advance with speed (centrifugal/ECU map) and decrease with load (vacuum/map).

steps.title: Solved example · Voltage
steps.body: Primary inductance 5 mH, current 5 A interrupted in 0.1 ms: e = L di/dt = 5×10⁻³ × 5/10⁻⁴ = **250 V**. With a turns ratio of 100, the secondary can reach 250 × 100 = **25 kV**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the battery directly supplies 30 kV.
- Confusing dwell (coil charging time) with advance (timing).
- Wrong plug heat range: too hot causes pre-ignition; too cold fouls.

lessons.title: Lab: Combustion, knock and octane rating

scenes.text: Rohit climbs a ghat road in top gear with low-grade petrol and hears a metallic 'ping'.
That sound is knock — an engine-damaging combustion event.

steps.title: Normal combustion — three stages
steps.body: (1) **Ignition lag** (spark to ~10 % burn); (2) **flame propagation** (turbulent flame front at 10–30 m/s, most of the heat release, 10 %–90 %); (3) **after-burning**. Peak pressure should occur at ~10–15° ATDC for best torque (MBT timing).

steps.title: Knock
steps.body:
The unburnt **end gas** is compressed by the advancing flame and heated until it auto-ignites before the flame arrives. Pressure waves hit the walls → audible ping, hot spots, piston/ring damage. 
**Factors increasing knock:** high r, advanced spark, high inlet temperature/pressure (turbo), lean-rich extremes at ≈φ 1.1, long flame travel (large bore, off-centre plug), hot spots, low-octane fuel, low speed. **Cures:** retard spark, richer mixture, lower r, central plug, compact chambers, intercooling, EGR, knock-sensor feedback.

steps.title: Octane rating
steps.body: **RON/MON** compare the fuel with isooctane (100) and n-heptane (0). A 90:10 isooctane:n-heptane blend by volume is **90 octane**. Anti-knock additives: tetra-ethyl lead (banned in India since 2000) and now ethanol, MTBE, aromatics. India's E20 petrol (20 % ethanol) has high octane (ethanol RON ≈ 108) but lower energy density, so slightly higher volumetric consumption.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up knock (end-gas autoignition) with surface-ignition/pre-ignition (hot spot ignites before the spark).
- Believing higher octane fuel gives more power in an engine not designed for it — it only prevents knock.
- Mixing cetane (diesel) and octane (petrol).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — diagnose a pinging engine

scenes.text: A 1.2 L turbo-petrol car shows knock under full load on summer afternoons; the customer used 91 RON fuel.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Read ECU knock-retard counters and fuel trims.
2. Check intake temperature and intercooler flow.
3. Check fuel grade (the car needs 95+ RON).
4. Inspect plugs for correct heat range and deposits.
5. Verify ignition timing is not mechanically over-advanced and EGR/coolant function is normal.

steps.title: Ranking causes
steps.body: Cheapest-first: fuel octane → deposits/hot spots → cooling/intercooler → timing/sensors → internal compression ratio (rare).

steps.title: Do not
steps.body: Do not simply raise rail pressure or boost to restore power: removing knock margin kills pistons.

lessons.title: Lab: Diesel fuel injection systems and fuel per stroke

scenes.text: A farmer's tractor starts instantly with a puff of smoke; its pump meters fuel to the cylinders.
Karthik studies how a pump and nozzle deliver a few tens of cubic millimetres per stroke.

steps.title: Requirements
steps.body: The system must **meter** exactly the right quantity per load, **time** the start of injection (typically 5–25° BTDC), **atomise** the fuel (droplets 10–50 µm) and **distribute** it through the chamber. Pressure: 200 bar (old inline pump) to 2000+ bar (common rail).

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Jerk-type inline pump** (Bosch): plunger lifted by a cam, helix on the plunger varies the effective stroke for quantity; delivery valve gives sharp cut-off.
- **Distributor (rotary) pump:** single plunger serves all cylinders.
- **Unit injector / pump-line-nozzle.**
- **Common rail (CRDi):** a high-pressure pump fills a rail; electronically controlled solenoid/piezo injectors allow pilot, main and post injections, flexible timing and quiet, clean combustion.
Nozzles: pintle, single-hole, multi-hole (DI). Pump is driven at half crank speed.

steps.title: Solved example · Fuel per stroke
steps.body:
A four-cylinder four-stroke diesel at 2000 rpm consumes 8 kg/h; ρ = 830 kg/m³.
- Fuel rate = 8000/3600 = 2.222 g/s
- Injection events/s per cylinder = 2000/120 = 16.67
- Fuel per injection = 2.222/(4 × 16.67) = 0.0333 g = **33.3 mg**
- Volume = 33.3 mg/0.83 = **40.2 mm³** per injection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using N instead of N/2 for injection frequency in a four-stroke.
- Forgetting to divide by the number of cylinders.
- Mixing mm³ and cm³ (1 cm³ = 1000 mm³).

lessons.title: Lab: Stages of CI combustion, ignition delay and diesel knock

story.title: The clatter of a cold diesel

scenes.text: On a cold morning Neha hears a harsh clatter from an old diesel autorickshaw.
The cause is a long ignition delay followed by a violent premixed burn.

steps.title: Four stages
steps.body:
1. **Ignition delay** (start of injection to start of pressure rise from combustion): physical delay (atomise, vaporise, mix) + chemical delay (pre-reactions).
2. **Uncontrolled (premixed) burning:** fuel injected during the delay burns rapidly → steep pressure rise.
3. **Controlled (diffusion) burning:** rate set by injection/mixing.
4. **After-burning.**
Diesel knock = excess premixed fuel because of a long delay.

steps.title: SI knock vs diesel knock
steps.body: SI knock is at the *end* of combustion (end-gas autoignition); diesel knock is at the *beginning* (long delay). Cures are opposite: for diesel, **shorten** the delay: high cetane, high r, high intake temperature, **small** injection at first (pilot), high swirl. Cetane number (CN): n-hexadecane (cetane) = 100, α-methylnaphthalene = 0; Indian diesel ≥ 51 (BS-VI).

steps.title: Solved example · Delay in crank degrees
steps.body: Ignition delay 1.2 ms at 2400 rpm: 2400 rpm = 14 400°/s = 14.4°/ms, so delay = 1.2 × 14.4 = **17.3° crank**. At 1200 rpm the same time delay is only 8.6°, so knock is worse at *high* speed in angle terms but hotter engines have shorter time delay.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying diesel knock cures are the same as SI (high octane).
- Treating ignition delay as a fixed angle: it is mostly fixed in *time*.
- Mistaking blue/white smoke (unburnt fuel at cold start) for black smoke (rich/soot).

lessons.title: Combustion chambers of CI engines and the SI–CI comparison

scenes.text: Large trucks use direct-injection chambers; small old car diesels used swirl chambers.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Direct injection (open chamber):** fuel injected into a bowl in the piston; multi-hole nozzle at 200–2000 bar; best fuel economy (≈ 10–15 % better), but needs high injection pressure and is noisier; hard to cold start without glow assistance on small engines.
- **Indirect injection:** swirl chamber, pre-combustion chamber and air-cell; lower injection pressure, better mixing by turbulence, smoother and quieter but higher heat loss and fuel consumption, needs glow plugs.
Modern passenger diesels are all common-rail DI.

steps.title: SI vs CI engines
steps.body:
| Aspect | SI | CI |
|---|---|---|
| Fuel | Petrol (volatile) | Diesel |
| Mixture | homogeneous, throttled | heterogeneous, quality governed |
| Ignition | spark | compression |
| r | 8–12 | 16–22 |
| Efficiency | 25–35 % | 35–45 % |
| Peak pressure | lower | higher, heavier build |

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying CI engines have no throttling: they have none on the intake; the load is controlled by fuel quantity.
- Believing diesels are cleaner in all respects: NOx and PM are the key diesel issues.

lessons.title: Lab: Supercharging and turbocharging

scenes.text: A 1.5 L turbo-diesel gives power comparable to a 2.2 L naturally aspirated one.
The turbo raises the air density entering the cylinder.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body: Power ∝ air mass per cycle. **Supercharging** raises inlet pressure with a compressor: mechanically driven (belt/gear, Roots/centrifugal) or exhaust driven (**turbocharger**: turbine on the exhaust, compressor on the intake). An **intercooler** cools the compressed air to restore density and lower NOx/knock. A **wastegate/VGT** controls boost. Turbo lag arises from rotor inertia.

steps.title: Solved example · Compressor outlet
steps.body:
P₂/P₁ = 1.8, T₁ = 300 K, ηc = 0.70, γ = 1.4.
- Isentropic: T₂′ = 300 × 1.8^0.2857 = 300 × 1.1829 = 354.9 K (rise 54.9)
- Actual rise = 54.9/0.70 = 78.4 K → **T₂ = 378.4 K**
- Density ratio = 1.8 × (300/378.4) = **1.427** → ≈ 43 % more air (with the same ηv), allowing about 43 % more fuel and power in a diesel (limited by smoke and structure).

steps.title: Solved example · With intercooler
steps.body: Cool the air back to 320 K at the same pressure: density ratio = 1.8 × 300/320 = **1.69** — nearly 70 % more air than naturally aspirated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ηc without converting temperature rise correctly (divide the *isentropic rise* by η).
- Forgetting that turbocharged SI engines need lower r or retarded timing to avoid knock.
- Thinking the turbine robs crank power: it uses exhaust energy that would otherwise be wasted (though some back-pressure penalty exists).

lessons.title: Fuels, emissions and Bharat Stage control technologies

scenes.text: Maya's city has moved to BS-VI fuel since April 2020; tailpipe emissions dropped sharply.
What exactly is in exhaust and how is it cleaned?

steps.title: Fuels
steps.body: Approximate lower heating values: petrol ≈ 44 MJ/kg, diesel ≈ 43 MJ/kg, CNG (methane) ≈ 50 MJ/kg, LPG ≈ 46 MJ/kg, ethanol ≈ 27 MJ/kg, hydrogen ≈ 120 MJ/kg (but very low volumetric density). **Biodiesel** (FAME) is blended with diesel; **ethanol** (E10→E20) and **CNG** reduce petroleum use; hydrogen ICE and fuel-cell vehicles are emerging.

steps.title: Pollutants and formation
steps.body:
- **CO:** incomplete combustion in rich mixtures.
- **HC:** quench layers, crevices, misfire, short-circuit in 2-stroke.
- **NOx:** thermal (Zeldovich) NO forms above ~1800 K, peaks slightly lean — more in diesels.
- **PM/soot:** fuel-rich pockets in diesel; **SOx** from fuel sulphur.
- **CO₂** is a greenhouse gas tied to fuel use.
**Diesel NOx–PM trade-off:** retarding injection lowers NOx but raises soot.

steps.title: Control technologies
steps.body:
- **Three-way catalyst** (SI at λ = 1): oxidises CO, HC and reduces NOx simultaneously.
- **EGR:** recirculates cooled exhaust to lower flame temperature → lower NOx.
- **DPF** traps soot, regenerated by burning; **SCR** with urea (AdBlue/DEF) reduces NOx to N₂; **LNT**; **GPF** for GDI.
- India moved directly from BS-IV to **BS-VI on 1 April 2020** (diesel sulphur ≤ 10 ppm), skipping BS-V.

steps.title: Solved example · CO₂ per litre
steps.body: Diesel: ρ ≈ 0.83 kg/L, carbon fraction ≈ 0.86 → carbon = 0.714 kg/L → CO₂ = 0.714 × 44/12 = **2.62 kg CO₂ per litre**. A car doing 20 km/L emits about 131 g/km.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a catalyst works at any air–fuel ratio (needs λ ≈ 1).
- Claiming EGR increases power: it reduces peak temperature.
- Mixing BS norms with Euro: BS-VI is broadly equivalent to Euro 6 standards.

lessons.title: Lab: Indicated power, brake power, torque and efficiencies

scenes.text: The college test cell has a four-cylinder diesel coupled to an eddy-current dynamometer.
Isha records imep, speed and torque to find the engine's efficiencies.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Indicated power** IP = imep · L · A · n · K/60 (n = N for 2-stroke or N/2 for 4-stroke; K = cylinders).
- **Brake power** BP = 2πNT/60 (T in N·m) — what the shaft delivers.
- **Friction power** FP = IP − BP.
- **Mechanical efficiency** ηm = BP/IP.
- **bsfc** = ṁ_f/BP (kg/kWh).
- **Brake thermal efficiency** ηbth = BP/(ṁ_f · CV); indicated thermal efficiency uses IP.
- **Volumetric efficiency** ηv = actual air drawn/(ρ_a · swept volume rate).
- **bmep** = BP/(L A n K).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Efficiencies
steps.body:
A petrol engine uses 6 kg/h of fuel, CV = 44 000 kJ/kg, BP = 22 kW.
- Heat input = 6 × 44 000/3600 = 73.3 kW
- ηbth = 22/73.3 = **30.0 %**
- bsfc = 6/22 = **0.273 kg/kWh**
- Volumetric efficiency check: 1.5 L engine at 3000 rpm draws 0.040 kg/s; theoretical = 1.18 × 1.5×10⁻³ × 3000/120 = 0.04425 kg/s → ηv = **90.4 %**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total swept volume with the wrong speed factor (four-stroke needs N/2).
- Putting torque in kN·m with power in kW without checking units.
- Taking friction power as the oil pump alone; it includes rubbing, pumping and accessories.

lessons.title: Lab: Morse test, Willans line and heat balance

scenes.text: Friction power can't be measured directly in a running multi-cylinder engine.

steps.title: Morse test
steps.body: For a multi-cylinder engine at constant speed: measure full BP; then short-circuit (cut) one cylinder at a time keeping speed constant by reducing the dynamometer load. The drop in BP = indicated power of the cut cylinder (the friction remains). IP total = Σ (BP_all − BP_i); ηm = BP/IP.

steps.title: Willans line and heat balance
steps.body: **Willans line:** plot fuel consumption vs BP at constant speed — approximately linear for CI engines; extrapolating to zero fuel gives negative BP equal to friction power. **Heat balance sheet:** heat input is split into BP, coolant, exhaust, and unaccounted (radiation, friction): typical SI: 25–30 % BP, 30 % coolant, 30–35 % exhaust.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Morse test
steps.body:
Full BP = 40 kW. BP with cylinder 1 off: 28; 2 off: 29; 3 off: 27; 4 off: 30 kW.
IP₁ = 12, IP₂ = 11, IP₃ = 13, IP₄ = 10 → **IP = 46 kW**. ηm = 40/46 = **87.0 %**; FP = 6 kW.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Heat balance
steps.body: Fuel 6 kg/h, CV 44 000 kJ/kg → 73.3 kW. BP = 22 kW (30.0 %). Coolant flow 0.4 kg/s, cp = 4.18, rise 15 K → 25.1 kW (34.2 %). Exhaust + unaccounted = 73.3 − 22 − 25.1 = **26.2 kW (35.8 %)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting speed change during the Morse test.
- Using it for single-cylinder engines (not possible).
- Forgetting that the coolant heat is only part of the total loss.

lessons.title: Cooling systems and lubrication

scenes.text: Vikram's car temperature gauge rises in a traffic jam; the radiator fan has failed.
He must understand how the engine rejects heat and keeps its moving parts oiled.

steps.title: Cooling
steps.body: About 25–35 % of fuel energy goes to the coolant. **Air cooling:** fins (motorcycles, small engines). **Water cooling:** water pump circulates coolant (water + ethylene glycol, 50:50 protects from −37 °C and raises boiling point), through the block, head and **radiator**; **thermostat** opens at ~82–95 °C to keep the engine hot enough for efficiency but cool enough for strength; pressure cap (≈ 1 bar gauge) raises boiling temperature by ~ 15 °C; fan (viscous/electric).

steps.title: Lubrication
steps.body: Functions: reduce friction, cool, clean, seal rings, protect from corrosion. **Splash, pressure (wet sump), dry sump** systems; gear pump through a filter and relief valve; bearings run on a hydrodynamic oil film. **Viscosity grades** (SAE 5W-30: 5W = cold cranking behaviour, 30 = viscosity at 100 °C); viscosity index; additives (detergents, anti-wear ZDDP, VI improvers). Oil pressure falling at hot idle indicates worn bearings or low level.

steps.title: Solved example · Radiator heat
steps.body:
Engine rejects 25 kW to coolant; water allowed to rise 8 K: ṁ = Q/(cp ΔT) = 25/(4.18 × 8) = **0.748 kg/s ≈ 45 L/min**.
Oil: a 20 L/min pump with a 4 L sump circulates the whole sump volume every 4/20 = 0.2 min = **12 s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using plain water in winter or highly concentrated glycol (poor heat transfer).
- Removing the thermostat (engine then runs cold and wears).
- Opening a hot pressure cap: scalding steam.

lessons.title: Lab: Flywheel sizing, firing order and balancing

story.title: The engine that shakes at idle

scenes.text: Nitin's single-cylinder bike thumps at idle while a four-cylinder car is smooth.
A flywheel stores energy between power strokes; firing order spreads torque pulses.

steps.title: Flywheel
steps.body: Torque from a reciprocating engine fluctuates. Energy fluctuation ΔE = Iω²Cs, where **Cs = (ω_max − ω_min)/ω_mean** is the coefficient of fluctuation of speed (0.01–0.02 for generator sets, 0.05–0.1 for automobiles). I = ΔE/(Cs ω²). A single-cylinder four-stroke needs the largest flywheel; multi-cylinder engines need less.

steps.title: Balancing basics
steps.body: Primary (once per revolution) and secondary (twice per revolution) inertia forces arise from reciprocating mass. Inline-four is primary-balanced but has a secondary force; inline-six is fully balanced in forces and couples; flat/boxer engines cancel many forces. Counterweights on the crank balance rotating masses and part of the reciprocating masses.

steps.title: Solved example · Flywheel
steps.body:
ΔE = 1200 J, N = 1500 rpm (ω = 157.08 rad/s), Cs = 0.02.
I = 1200/(0.02 × 157.08²) = 1200/493.5 = **2.43 kg·m²**.
For a solid disc I = ½mr²: with r = 0.15 m, m = 2I/r² = 4.86/0.0225 = **216 kg**? – too heavy, so a rim-type wheel (I ≈ mr²) with m = 108 kg is used, or a larger radius.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rpm rather than rad/s in ω².
- Confusing Cs with efficiency.
- Thinking the flywheel increases power: it only smooths speed.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — full test-cell report

scenes.text: A 1.5 L four-cylinder petrol engine has been tested at 3000 rpm: torque 105 N·m, fuel flow 6.5 kg/h (CV 44 MJ/kg), air flow 0.040 kg/s.
Write the performance summary.

steps.title: Calculations
steps.body:
- BP = 2π × 3000 × 105/60 = **33.0 kW**
- Heat input = 6.5 × 44 000/3600 = **79.4 kW**
- ηbth = 33.0/79.4 = **41.6 %**? — high for a petrol engine: recheck: 33/79.4 = 0.4157. Real engines rarely exceed 38 %, so the test point is exceptional or the measurement is suspect.
- bsfc = 6.5/33.0 = **0.197 kg/kWh** (≈ 197 g/kWh, again very good).
- AFR = 0.040 × 3600/6.5 = **22.2:1** — a lean mixture, so a lean-burn GDI engine would be required.
Conclusion: treat the data as suspect and recheck instrumentation before reporting.

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body: Sanity-checking is a key professional skill: compare results with typical ranges (SI ηbth 25–38 %, CI 30–45 %; bsfc 220–300 g/kWh SI, 190–250 g/kWh CI).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Reporting results without uncertainty; ignoring corrections for temperature and pressure (SAE/DIN correction factors); mixing volume and mass flows.

lessons.title: Lab: Vehicle layout, chassis and road-load power

scenes.text: Aditi's family hatchback weighs 1200 kg and cruises at 100 km/h on the highway.
She wants to know the power the engine must deliver at the wheels.

steps.title: Layouts and chassis
steps.body: Major parts: **chassis** (frame, suspension, wheels, steering, brakes), **powertrain**, **body**. Layouts: front-engine front-drive (FWD, most hatchbacks), front-engine rear-drive (RWD, SUVs/trucks), rear-engine, mid-engine, all-wheel-drive. Construction: ladder frame (trucks), **monocoque/unibody** (cars) for lighter weight and crash design.

steps.title: Road load
steps.body: Resistances: rolling R_r = C_rr m g; aerodynamic R_a = ½ ρ C_d A v²; gradient R_g = m g sin θ; plus inertia m a. Total tractive effort F = R_r + R_a + R_g + m a. Power at wheels = F·v; engine power = that / drivetrain efficiency (≈ 0.85–0.92).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Gradient
steps.body: A 5 % grade (sin θ ≈ 0.05) adds 1200 × 9.81 × 0.05 = 588.6 N → total 1061.5 N → P = **29.5 kW** at 100 km/h — more than double. Aerodynamic power grows with v³, so 120 km/h needs (1.2)³ = 1.73 × the aerodynamic power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using km/h in v² instead of m/s.
- Forgetting that drag power ∝ v³.
- Taking sin θ = grade % without checking the angle is small.

lessons.title: Lab: Clutch, gearbox and tractive effort

scenes.text: Sameer's car crawls up a steep ramp in first gear but cruises quietly in fifth.

steps.title: Single-plate friction clutch
steps.body: Spring-loaded pressure plate squeezes a friction disc between the flywheel and pressure plate. Torque capacity T = μ W R_m n (n = friction surfaces, = 2 for one disc). Uniform wear: R_m = (R₁ + R₂)/2; uniform pressure: R_m = (2/3)(R₁³ − R₂³)/(R₁² − R₂²). Design uses uniform wear (conservative).

steps.title: Gearbox
steps.body: Sliding-mesh, constant-mesh and **synchromesh** helical gears; ratios chosen for hill starting (first, 3.5–4:1) to economy (top < 1 overdrive). Overall ratio = gear × final drive. Tractive force F = T_e × G × G_f × η/r_w; vehicle speed v = 2π r_w N/(60 G G_f).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Tractive force and speed
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using diameter for rolling radius.
- Applying n = 1 for a single-plate clutch (two friction faces).
- Quoting top-gear tractive force as if it were first gear.

story.title: Why the outer wheel spins faster

scenes.text: On a roundabout Zoya's outer wheels travel a longer path than the inner wheels.
The differential lets them rotate at different speeds while sharing torque.

steps.title: Final drive and differential
steps.body: The **propeller shaft** with universal joints and the **final drive** (crown wheel & pinion; hypoid gears) turn the power through 90° and give ratio = crown teeth/pinion teeth. The **differential** (bevel gear spider) has N_L + N_R = 2N_crown and equal torque to both wheels; a **limited-slip or locking differential** solves wheel-spin on slippery surfaces. Axles: semi-floating, three-quarter and full-floating (trucks).

steps.title: Tyres
steps.body: Code **205/55 R16**: 205 mm section width, aspect ratio 55 % (sidewall = 0.55 × 205), radial, 16-inch rim. Tubeless radials dominate. Tyre pressure, tread wear, slip angle and rolling resistance affect safety and economy.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cornering
steps.body: Crown wheel 600 rpm, left wheel 560 rpm → right wheel = 2 × 600 − 560 = **640 rpm**. Final drive: 41-tooth crown with 10-tooth pinion → **4.1:1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the differential adds torque (it only splits it).
- Forgetting the spider equation when one wheel is lifted: the other stays still while the lifted wheel spins at twice crown speed.
- Fitting tyres of different diameter, which skews the speedometer.

lessons.title: Steering geometry and suspension

scenes.text: After hitting a pothole Dinesh's car pulls left and the tyre wears on one edge.
Wheel alignment (camber, caster, toe) was disturbed.

steps.title: Steering
steps.body: Rack-and-pinion or recirculating-ball boxes, with hydraulic/electric power assistance. **Ackermann condition** for true rolling in a turn: cot φ − cot θ = c/b (φ outer, θ inner wheel angle, c = distance between kingpins, b = wheelbase). Alignment: **camber**, **caster** (self-centring), **toe-in**, **kingpin inclination**, **scrub radius**.

steps.title: Suspension
steps.body: Springs (leaf, coil, torsion bar, air), dampers (shock absorbers) and linkages (MacPherson strut, double wishbone, multi-link, solid axle). Quarter-car natural frequency f = (1/2π)√(k/m); damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(km)) is typically 0.2–0.4 for comfort. Human comfort is best near 1–1.5 Hz.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Ride frequency
steps.body: Sprung mass 300 kg per wheel, k = 30 000 N/m: ω = √(30000/300) = 10 rad/s → f = **1.59 Hz**. Reducing k to 20 000 N/m gives 1.30 Hz (softer ride).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the inner and outer wheel in the Ackermann formula.
- Treating dampers as springs: they dissipate energy.
- Confusing camber (tilt seen from the front) with caster (kingpin tilt seen from the side).

scenes.text: A car at 60 km/h brakes hard on dry asphalt.

steps.title: Braking systems
steps.body: **Hydraulic brakes** use Pascal's law: p = F/A transmitted equally. Disc brakes (calipers + pads) fade less than drums. **Servo (vacuum booster)**, **ABS** (prevents wheel lock, keeps steering), **EBD**, **ESC**. Air brakes in heavy vehicles; parking brake mechanical. Brake fluid is hygroscopic: replace every 2–3 years.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Stopping distance
steps.body: v = 60 km/h = 16.67 m/s, μ = 0.7: d = v²/(2 μ g) = 277.8/(2 × 0.7 × 9.81) = **20.2 m** (braking only; add reaction distance 1 s × 16.67 = 16.7 m → 36.9 m total).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Hydraulic force
steps.body: Pedal force 200 N, lever ratio 5 → 1000 N on a master cylinder of diameter 20 mm (A = 314.2 mm²): p = 3.18 MPa. Caliper piston diameter 40 mm (A = 1256.6 mm²): F = 3.18 × 1256.6 = **4000 N**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the reaction (thinking) distance.
- Using the wrong μ on wet roads (≈ 0.4) or ice (≈ 0.1).
- Thinking ABS shortens distance on every surface (on loose gravel it can lengthen it).

steps.title: EV and hybrid basics
steps.body: **BEV:** battery pack, inverter, traction motor (PMSM or induction), single-speed reduction gear, regenerative braking. **HEV/PHEV:** engine + motor combinations (series, parallel, power-split). Regenerative braking recovers roughly 60 % of braking energy in ideal conditions. Charging: AC (3.3–11 kW) vs DC fast (50–150+ kW). Cold weather and highway speed reduce range.

- At 7.4 kW AC from 20→80 %: 36/(7.4 × 0.9) = 5.4 h.

lessons.title: Formula and key-point sheet

scenes.text: Tara has one hour to revise IC engines.
She builds a one-page sheet of formulae and traps.

steps.title: Core formulae
steps.body:
- Vs = (π/4)D²L; r = (Vs+Vc)/Vc
- η_Otto = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1); η_Diesel = 1 − (1/r^(γ−1))(ρ^γ − 1)/(γ(ρ−1))
- IP = imep·L·A·(N/2)·K/60 (4S); BP = 2πNT/60
- ηm = BP/IP; ηbth = BP/(ṁ_f·CV); bsfc = ṁ_f/BP
- ηv = actual air/(ρ_a·Vs·N/2)
- Equivalence ratio φ = AFR_s/AFR
- Flywheel I = ΔE/(Cs ω²)
- Compressor T₂ = T₁[1 + ((p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) − 1)/η_c]

steps.title: Key points
steps.body:
- Same r: Otto > Dual > Diesel. Same peak pressure: Diesel > Dual > Otto.
- SI knock = end-gas autoignition; CI knock = long delay.
- Octane for petrol, cetane for diesel.
- NOx peaks slightly lean/high T; CO rises when rich; soot in diesel when rich pockets.
- BS-VI from 1 April 2020.

steps.title: Common traps
steps.body: Mixing N and N/2; kPa vs bar; degrees vs radians; using total instead of swept volume; forgetting the exponent (γ−1).

statements.s: Otto efficiency depends on heat added.
statements.why: It depends only on r and γ.

statements.s: Diesel knock occurs at the beginning of combustion.
Cetane number measures knock resistance of petrol.
statements.why: Octane does; cetane is for diesel.

statements.s: A three-way catalyst works near λ = 1.

lessons.title: Lab: Morse test on a four-cylinder petrol engine

scenes.text: The lab batch has a four-cylinder SI engine on a hydraulic dynamometer.
You have 90 minutes to perform the Morse test and write the report.

steps.title: Aim and apparatus
steps.body: Aim: to find indicated power and mechanical efficiency by cutting each cylinder in turn. Apparatus: engine with hydraulic dynamometer, tachometer, spark-cut switches, fuel measuring burette, thermometers.

lessons.title: Lab: Valve timing and port timing diagram

scenes.text: The cut-away four-stroke engine in the lab can be turned by hand.
You mark valve opening and closing points on the flywheel degree scale.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Rotate the crank slowly; note the flywheel angle when the inlet valve just starts to lift (IVO), when it just closes (IVC), and similarly for exhaust (EVO, EVC). Plot these on a circular diagram with TDC at the top: the angular positions relative to TDC and BDC give the valve timing diagram.

steps.title: Observation and calculation
steps.body:
IVO 15° BTDC, IVC 45° ABDC, EVO 40° BBDC, EVC 10° ATDC.
- Inlet open period = 15 + 180 + 45 = **240°**
- Exhaust open period = 40 + 180 + 10 = **230°**
- Valve overlap = IVO before TDC + EVC after TDC = 15 + 10 = **25°**.

steps.title: Viva hint
steps.body: Why does the exhaust valve open before BDC? To let the pressure fall so the piston does less pumping work on the exhaust stroke ('blow-down').

lessons.title: Viva voce and previous-year-style questions

scenes.text: The external examiner asks Pooja rapid-fire questions about her engine experiments.
She must give crisp, correct answers.

steps.title: Tips
steps.body: Answer in one or two sentences; state the formula, then the physical meaning; quote typical numbers.

steps.title: Model answer: Otto vs Diesel at the same r
steps.body: At the same compression ratio the Otto cycle rejects less heat because all heat is added at the highest temperature (constant volume). The Diesel cycle adds part of its heat during expansion (constant pressure) at lower temperature, so its mean heat-addition temperature is lower and its efficiency is lower. In practice diesel engines win because r is 16–22 and there is no throttling loss.

steps.title: How to answer a viva
steps.body: Give the definition, the governing formula, one typical number (e.g. r, efficiency, octane/cetane), and a one-line consequence. Example: 'Knock is end-gas autoignition; raise octane or retard spark.'

steps.title: Frequent viva slips
steps.body: Saying 'octane' for diesel; saying 'two-stroke fires every two revolutions'; quoting ideal air-standard efficiency as engine efficiency.

activity.prompt: Answer these viva questions

items.q: Why is the Otto cycle more efficient than Diesel at the same compression ratio?
items.a: Its heat rejection is lower for the same r because the Diesel cycle adds heat over a part of the stroke at constant pressure, giving a higher mean heat-rejection temperature.

items.q: Why does a diesel engine have no throttle?
items.a: Load is controlled by fuel quantity (quality governing) with full air always, which avoids pumping losses.

items.q: What is knock in SI engines?
items.a: Autoignition of the end gas ahead of the flame, causing pressure waves and a metallic ping.

items.q: Why is a catalytic converter poisoned by leaded petrol?
items.a: Lead coats the catalytic sites; hence unleaded petrol only.
